title: Hierarchical Gene Regulatory Networks Improve Gene Prioritization in TWAS by Constraining Trans-Regulatory Search
synopsis: Standard TWAS models use only cis variants, so this paper adds trans-regulation without searching the whole genome. GRNTWAS ranks upstream regulators by propagating over hierarchical gene regulatory networks, then models expression from cis variants together with these GRN-selected trans variants. In GEUVADIS and Mayo RNA-seq it predicted expression more accurately and for more genes than the benchmarked methods. Across 12 neuropsychiatric traits, including Alzheimer's disease, the genes it prioritized were backed by independent evidence.

title: A method to disentangle enhancer-gene interactions from latent factors in single-cell multi-omics data
synopsis: CREMAP links non-coding regulatory elements to target genes within each cell type, a step needed to interpret GWAS variants. It learns shared technical and biological variation as latent factors from single-cell multiome data and removes them before testing each peak-gene pair, instead of using sample covariates that also remove genuine genetic effects. Against CRISPRi and fine-mapped eQTL benchmarks it was more accurate than existing methods in 2 cell lines and 13 cell types, and in kidney proximal tubule it kept eQTL-supported links that other methods lost.

title: A pangenomic approach identifies new structural variants associated with gene expression in the CARTaGENE cohort
synopsis: The authors genotyped about 646,000 structural variants with a pangenome reference in 2,173 CARTaGENE participants and ran eQTL analyses conditioned on known small variants. They found 99 SV-eQTLs (41 replicated in 1000 Genomes), and these were enriched in ENCODE cis-regulatory elements. Two-thirds of them are in strong LD with Open Targets fine-mapped credible sets, which makes them candidate causal variants at GWAS loci.

title: Allele-specific open chromatin analysis revealed allelic bias of alcohol-induced gene expression in human microglia
synopsis: The authors looked for functional non-coding variants at alcohol use disorder GWAS loci by combining microglia allele-specific open chromatin with GWAS, eQTL, expression and ATAC data. They nominated rs7307261, whose minor allele looks more like ETS-family binding motifs and is linked to higher CD163 expression. When rs7307261 was knocked out or edited in iPSC-derived microglia, ethanol no longer induced CD163 and phagocytosis changed.

title: Single-Cell Gene Expression Heritability Informed by Genotype x Cell-Context Interactions
synopsis: scHINT is a fast method that splits single-cell expression heritability into a main genetic part and a genotype-by-cell-state part. In brain snRNA-seq the cell-state part was common and on average larger than the main part, and it was concentrated in constrained genes and in disease heritability. A cell-state-aware TWAS built on it found 68% more disease-risk genes than state-agnostic TWAS, including TREM2.

title: Estimated Glucose Disposal Rate, Genetic Susceptibility and Risks of Incident and Recurrent Coronary Artery Disease: Evidence From the UK Biobank Study
synopsis: This study examines how insulin resistance and polygenic risk together relate to incident and recurrent coronary artery disease. Insulin resistance was measured with the estimated glucose disposal rate (eGDR). In 460,859 UK Biobank participants followed for a median of 13.8 years, eGDR was derived from waist circumference, hypertension status and HbA1c, then combined with a CAD polygenic risk score in Cox models. Compared with low eGDR and medium or high polygenic risk, high eGDR with low polygenic risk had the lowest risk of incident CAD (HR 0.25) and recurrent CAD (HR 0.67). The interaction was significant for incident disease. Using both measures improved prediction, which supports profiling metabolic and genetic risk together.

title: Heterogeneity of glaucoma polygenic risk score reporting
synopsis: This systematic review asks how polygenic risk scores for primary open-angle glaucoma have been built and how well they predict disease. The authors searched four databases, screened 2018 articles, and assessed risk of bias with PROBAST. They included 65 studies: 20 developed an original score and 45 related a score to clinical traits. The models varied widely in size, from 4 to over 9 million SNPs and from 672 to over 449,000 individuals. Outcome reporting was inconsistent, with odds ratios per decile ranging from 1.74 to 45.48. Adding demographic factors improved prediction, and ancestry-specific scores performed best in matching populations. The findings point to a need for standardized reporting and validation in more diverse cohorts.

title: An Integrated Single-cell Multi-Omics Atlas of the Human Optic Nerve
synopsis: This study builds a cell atlas of the human optic nerve, a central nervous system tract affected by neurodegenerative and neuroinflammatory disease. It integrates single-nucleus RNA-seq, single-nucleus ATAC-seq and Xenium spatial transcriptomics from about 2.1 million cells across 108 donors. The atlas identifies 10 major cell classes and more than 60 populations, along with their regulatory elements, transcription factor programs and spatial gradients along the nerve. It also reconstructs adult oligodendroglial and astrocyte lineages and describes age-related loss of progenitor-like glia and microglia. Integration with genome-wide association data sheds light on the genetic basis of glaucoma and related disorders, giving the field a reference resource for optic nerve biology and disease.

title: Beyond Abundance: Integrated Splicing and Expression Quantitative Trait Loci Refine Causal Gene Mapping in IBD
synopsis: Splicing QTLs have been studied much less than expression QTLs in inflammatory bowel disease. This study mapped both in 1,149 colon samples from IBD participants, finding 20,566 genes with eQTLs and 9,906 with sQTLs. Colocalization with GWAS prioritized 239 eGenes and 164 sGenes across 147 of 320 IBD risk loci, and 58 genes were supported by both. In five genes, risk alleles were linked to opposite shifts in total expression and in the use of junctions predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay, which fits NMD as the mechanism. IBD sGenes were enriched in immune pathways and included drug targets, so splicing may help explain differences in how patients respond to therapy.

title: EditFinder: A Sequence-Based Model for A-to-I RNA Editing Identification and Characterization of Genetic Variant Effects
synopsis: This paper asks how to identify A-to-I RNA editing sites more completely and how genetic variants change editing. The authors built EditFinder, a model that predicts editing sites from sequence alone. It outperformed other methods on an independent reference validation set and on a read-based sequencing dataset. Applied across the genome, it produced a larger catalog of candidate editing sites. Variant analysis showed that the nucleotide immediately 3' of the site has an especially strong effect. Flanking variants may change the predicted editing status of about 10% of REDIportal entries. These tools help link genetic variation, RNA editing and disease.

title: Exhaustive rearrangement of an enhancer reveals that dependency-syntax encodes tissue specificity
synopsis: This study asks how the arrangement of transcription factor binding sites within an enhancer, its syntax, controls activity and tissue specificity. The authors tested 460,800 arrangements of ETS and GATA binding sites in Ciona embryos. Every arrangement had the same number, type and affinity of sites, yet only 18% were active. Flipping the orientation of a single site turned 54,000 inactive elements into working enhancers. A new single-cell whole-embryo reporter assay, SEMPRA, showed that some syntaxes depend on where higher- and lower-affinity sites sit, and these keep enhancers tissue-specific. Other, robust syntaxes are active regardless of that placement and drive broad expression. The results show that syntax alone can encode where an enhancer is active.

title: FiberTron enables regulatory variant effect prediction and testing from multi-omic long reads of a single sample
synopsis: This paper asks whether a single sample can supply enough data to train a regulatory sequence-to-function model from scratch. Using Fiber-seq and Nanopore direct RNA-seq from HG002, the authors trained FiberTron, a 12M-parameter model. From reference sequence it predicts methylation, chromatin accessibility and transcript coverage at base-pair resolution, reaching median Pearson r of 0.85 to 0.97 on held-out chromosomes. It matched AlphaGenome on dsQTL and eQTL variant-effect tasks despite being far smaller. The sample's own phased reads can then test its predictions. FiberTron recovered 79% of allele-specific accessibility variants in a melanoma line, along with known oncogenic and fusion-transcript effects. Such models can be trained by individual laboratories.

title: Functional interrogation of osteoarthritis-associated regulatory variants and effector genes
synopsis: Genome-wide association studies have found hundreds of osteoarthritis risk loci, but for most of them the causal regulatory variants and target genes are still unknown. This study combined massively parallel reporter assays in primary human chondrocytes with chromatin accessibility, H3K27ac and chromatin conformation data to prioritize candidate elements, then tested them with CRISPR activation and interference. The work linked risk regions to PAPPA and SPRY4. At 9q33, the risk allele of rs1895062 increased regulatory activity in an element that loops to the PAPPA promoter. Activating this element raised PAPPA expression and changed extracellular matrix pathways, making rs1895062 a likely causal variant.

title: ISOMPRA enables the disambiguation of transcriptional and post-transcriptional effects of genetic variants
synopsis: Classic massively parallel reporter assays often cannot tell whether a sequence element acts on transcription or on RNA stability after transcription. This paper introduces ISOMPRA, which measures pre-spliced RNA to estimate transcription rate. It also measures spliced RNA, corrected for transcription rate, to detect 3'-UTR elements that change RNA stability. Tests on predicted enhancers and 3'-UTR elements, including regions carrying mutations from autism patients, found many functional elements and a subset of high-impact mutations. Ignoring either layer of regulation produced many likely false positives and false negatives. The method was also adapted for cell-type-specific use in the mouse brain, so variant effects and traits such as sex can be studied in vivo.

title: Limited cross-model agreement in predicted RNA effects of complete non-reference human insertions
synopsis: This study asks whether sequence-to-function models agree on the RNA effects of complete human insertions that are missing from the GRCh38 and CHM13 references. On a fixed benchmark of 400 natural insertions, AlphaGenome and Borzoi both produced scores for 318 loci. Their predictions barely agreed: Spearman rho was -0.052, and the sign of the effect matched at only 48.7% of loci. Agreement was much higher for 500 reference single-nucleotide variants (rho 0.626), although that comparison is only descriptive. Too few loci had expression data to check the predictions against biology. Pangenome annotations of insertions should therefore report coverage, sensitivity to sequence context and biological calibration separately.

title: Measuring Cell Type Resolved Aging Through Long-Read Sequencing
synopsis: Bulk blood methylation clocks mix up real epigenetic aging inside cells with age-related changes in which blood cell types are present. This study builds cell-type-resolved aging clocks from cohort-scale long-read whole-genome sequencing of bulk blood, with no physical cell sorting. Individual reads are assigned to seven blood cell types by scoring their methylation against a purified-cell atlas. On held-out samples, the clocks reached mean absolute errors of 2.8-5.7 years. Associations with epigenetic age deviation differed by cell type, for example lower B-cell and NK-cell deviation in males, myeloid links to blood pressure and heart rate, and higher NK-cell deviation in asthma.

title: Multi-layer colocalization prioritizes adipose RNA regulatory features beyond gene expression at type 2 diabetes loci
synopsis: Most colocalization studies of type 2 diabetes loci use only total gene expression, which may miss other RNA-level mechanisms. This study tested 338 fine-mapped T2D signals for colocalization with five GTEx RNA phenotypes in subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue: gene expression, exon expression, transcript usage, transcriptional-event usage and splice-junction usage. Adding these phenotypes raised the number of testable signals from 253 to 293. It identified 77 colocalized pairs across 30 signals, and 87% of these involved features other than gene expression. At BDNF-AS and PGM1, specific RNA features colocalized while bulk expression pointed to different variants, which shows that gene-level analyses can misattribute regulatory signals.

title: Network-guided discovery and virtual perturbation identify clinically associated gene modules in acute myeloid leukemia
synopsis: This study asks whether network-guided analysis can find gene modules in acute myeloid leukemia that are linked to clinical outcome and whose network connections actually help prediction. The authors fit a network-based linear discriminant model of one-year survival in the BEAT2 cohort, using 660 KEGG pathway genes plus age, and then tested it in seven more cohorts by removing modules or cutting their links in the frozen model. The model kept 200 genes in seven modules. Cutting the connections of the first module lowered evaluation AUC by 0.0145, more than matched reference sets. That module also showed AML-specific CRISPR dependency (q = 0.0238) and mapped to myeloid cells. Higher gene scores went with lower odds of induction remission (odds ratio 0.616 in BEAT2 and 0.532 in GSE146173), which points to candidate programs for functional study.

title: Sequence-to-function embeddings across individuals capture rare and common variant heritability
synopsis: Sequence-to-function models learn from variation along the genome, and this paper asks whether their internal representations also capture genetic differences between individuals. The authors introduce EMBHER, a variance-component framework that estimates how much expression heritability these embeddings explain. Applied to Borzoi in whole blood, the embeddings recovered much of the heritability explained by genotypes and far more than the model's final predictions. Deeper layers focused more on functional, evolutionarily constrained sequence and carried less ancestry information. The embeddings also explained more rare-variant heritability than genotypes, possibly by pooling information across variants too rare to study one at a time. This approach connects deep sequence models with statistical genetics.

title: Single-cell multiomics analysis reveals Cxcl12 enhancer inactivation in LepRhigh-MSCs driving niche dysfunction in murine myeloid malignancies
synopsis: This study asks how myeloid malignancies remodel the bone marrow niche, focusing on leptin receptor-high mesenchymal stromal cells that support normal blood formation. Using single-cell multiomic RNA and ATAC sequencing of stromal cells from mouse models of myeloid malignancy, the authors mapped where chromatin closes near niche-factor genes. They found a previously unrecognized enhancer downstream of Cxcl12 that is open only in healthy stromal cells. The transcription factor Foxc1 regulates it, and Foxc1 is downregulated in disease. Disrupting the enhancer lowered Cxcl12 expression, and deconvolved patient data showed a similar trend. Together, the results point to a regulatory axis whose loss may explain niche dysfunction in blood cancers.

title: SurvStudio for browser-based survival analysis and model comparison in cancer genomics
synopsis: Molecular prognostic studies have to show that a marker improves survival prediction beyond clinical variables, but the analyses this takes are usually spread across separate tools. SurvStudio is a locally installed browser workspace that brings together survival curves, clinically adjusted marker estimates, selection-stability summaries and comparison of nine machine-learning and deep-learning models on the same test patients. In two external glioma cohorts, adding IDH/1p/19q groups to age, sex and grade raised the concordance index by 0.118 and 0.084. In 381 breast cancer patients the nine models performed similarly (C 0.632-0.646). Its input checks catch coding errors: in one gastric cancer cohort, correct event coding changed estimated five-year survival from 89.3% to 52.2%.

title: CellColocDB: a disease-centred resource linking GWAS loci to genes, cell contexts, and fine-mapping evidence
synopsis: CellColocDB is a resource that links GWAS loci to candidate genes and cellular contexts. It does this through GWAS-QTL colocalization across bulk, sorted-cell and single-cell QTL datasets. The current release covers 2805 GWAS datasets for 1201 traits, 40,516 GWAS windows, 316 QTL contexts and 89,842 molecular features. It contains over 3.5 million coloc.abf results with PP.H4 above 0.5, of which 1.6 million reach 0.8 or higher. Coloc-SuSiE and SMR/HEIDI add complementary evidence, and top SNPs are linked to fine-mapping results from seven methods. Because results are organized by window and context, users can compare cell types and genes within a single GWAS region.

title: MGnify analyses in 2027: enhancing the depth and breadth of analyses across metabarcoding, unassembled metagenomes, and assembled datasets
synopsis: This update describes the latest MGnify analysis pipelines (version 6). MGnify provides standardized, versioned workflows for the taxonomic and functional characterization of microbiome sequence data. The release adds amplicon sequence variant analysis and expanded functional annotation of assemblies, including viral and mobilome features. It also adds a streamlined minimal analysis of raw reads. The pipelines now use Nextflow, with execution orchestrated by Prefect, and the programmatic and bulk access services were rebuilt for large-scale computational use. These changes aim to make MGnify outputs easier to reuse, including for machine learning applications, across metabarcoding, unassembled metagenome and assembled datasets.

title: MIsoTEx: a mammalian transcript-isoform classification framework and database for exploring tissue distribution, expression stability, and abundance patterns
synopsis: MIsoTEx is a database and classification framework for the tissue expression patterns of protein-coding transcript isoforms in human, mouse and rat. Using normal adult tissue RNA-seq from GTEx, ARCHS4 and curated SRA studies, it classifies ubiquitously detected isoforms as uniformly or variably abundant. Tissue-associated isoforms are classified as predominant, exclusive, poor or absent in a tissue, with relative-abundance subclasses and confidence scores. The resource covers about 147,000 isoforms and supports cross-species ortholog comparison and analysis of user-supplied data. Validation against independent RNA-seq, RT-PCR and published datasets supported parts of the classification. The resource helps with transcript-level expression analysis and the choice of candidate reference isoforms.

title: MatriSpace: Identification and visualization of spatially resolved ECM gene expression patterns in health and disease
synopsis: The extracellular matrix (ECM) comprises more than 150 proteins made by different cell populations, and its composition varies across organs and disease states. This paper presents MatriSpace, a computational framework for mining spatial transcriptomics data with a focus on matrisome genes. Users can analyze their own datasets or explore a large collection of public ones. The tool returns spatially resolved maps of ECM gene expression in relation to cell populations, from single genes up to tissue niches and functional ECM units. Released as an R package and an online Shiny app, it aims to help identify which cells produce ECM and how it changes in disease, which may point to therapeutic targets.

title: Overview of recruitment strategies to reach the million milestone and characterization of the Million Veteran Program cohort
synopsis: This study evaluates the recruitment campaign that brought the Million Veteran Program, a large VA genetic and health cohort, to one million participants. Between 2022 and 2024, a multi-channel campaign contacted more than 6.5 million Veterans and enrolled 109,912. Recruitment calls had the highest enrollment rate (13.7%), but emails produced the most enrollments (46,999, or 43% of the total) despite a 0.8% rate. New enrollees differed only slightly in demographics from earlier ones. The cumulative cohort of 1,016,584 mostly male participants resembles the wider VA user population. The results can guide recruitment for large biobanks, and the cohort's link to health records makes it a major resource for precision medicine research.

title: VEuPathDB: 2026 update on data, tools, and infrastructure for eukaryotic pathogens, vectors, and hosts
synopsis: This update describes VEuPathDB, an open resource of genomic and other large-scale data for protozoan and fungal pathogens, arthropod vectors and their hosts. As of Release 71, it supports over 800 organisms and 2602 datasets across 12 component databases. Since the last update, 292 datasets were added and OrthoMCL grew to over 819,000 orthology groups covering 9.2 million proteins. AI-assisted curation and annotation are now subject to expert or user review, and new tools let users upload their own data and run differential expression analysis without programming. The infrastructure moved to a single PostgreSQL platform with Nextflow pipelines. After losing its federal funding and briefly closing in 2024, the resource now runs on community support and remains free to use.

title: Epigenetic clocks and adverse childhood experiences: a meta-analysis
synopsis: This meta-analysis asks which epigenetic clocks best capture the biological effects of adverse childhood experiences and early-life stress. It follows PRISMA guidelines and pools 17 studies (n = 10,940) with random-effects models. Those studies used eight clocks measured in peripheral tissues, including Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge and DunedinPACE. GrimAge and DunedinPACE showed the strongest and most consistent associations with total adversity counts and with abuse, neglect and household dysfunction subdomains. Only DunedinPACE stayed robust across strata, with age differences but no sex effects. The results show that the choice of clock matters a great deal in research on stress biology.

title: Mechanisms and gene therapy of GJB2 related deafness
synopsis: This review looks at how mutations in GJB2, the gene for the gap junction protein connexin 26, cause hearing loss. GJB2 mutations account for more than half of nonsyndromic hearing loss, and more than 100 pathogenic variants are known, yet genotype-phenotype correlations are still unclear. The authors draw mainly on mouse models. These suggest that profound congenital deafness comes mostly from disrupted cochlear development, while mild, progressive late-onset loss comes from impaired active cochlear mechanics. Preclinical gene therapy can restore connexin 26 expression in the cochlea, but it has not yet produced meaningful hearing recovery. The review sets out priorities for future work, including mutation-specific animal models, better gene delivery vectors and the search for genetic modifiers.

title: BASIN: Background-Anchored Signal Normalization with Integrated Quality Control for CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
synopsis: Comparing CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag samples is hard when a perturbation changes the global level of a chromatin mark: read-depth normalization hides such changes, and spike-ins add technical noise. BASIN instead uses recurrent peak-like background regions in IgG controls as an internal reference, since their share of reads rises as specific signal falls. It includes pipelines to define these anchor regions, compute scale factors and check whether the normalization's assumptions hold, plus a ready-made panel for Drosophila. BASIN stayed stable across a more than 100-fold range of cell input and detected global H3K36me3 loss in Set2 mutants that read-depth normalization concealed. It offers spike-in-free quantification of global chromatin changes.

title: Combining family history, polygenic scores, and childhood trauma to predict major depressive disorder
synopsis: This study asks whether combining family history, polygenic scores, childhood trauma and basic background factors predicts lifetime major depressive disorder better than any subset of them. It analysed about 14,000 participants from GLAD+ and about 111,000 from UK Biobank, using nested elastic net and XGBoost models within and across the two cohorts. The full model reached an AUC of 0.83 in GLAD+ and 0.74 in UK Biobank, and AUC stayed between 0.71 and 0.82 in external validation. Family history beat multi-trait polygenic scores in both cohorts. This matters because clinical and environmental information still adds substantially to genomic prediction of depression.

title: Cross- species developmental multiomics identifies RHOJ as a regulator of human-enriched cortical progenitor states
synopsis: What developmental changes underlie the expansion of outer radial glia, the progenitors linked to the enlarged primate cortex? The authors integrated time-resolved paired single-nucleus RNA and chromatin accessibility data from human, macaque and mouse fetal cortex and found two human-enriched progenitor programs. RHOJ, a conserved small GTPase gene, was enriched in outer radial glia and more highly expressed in human cortex. Expressing it in mouse fetal cortex increased progenitors and cells with oRG-like shape. An intronic RHOJ enhancer was more active with the human sequence, partly because of a human-specific change in an AP-1 motif. Deleting it in organoids lowered RHOJ expression and impaired growth, suggesting that conserved genes used differently contributed to human cortical evolution.

title: Fixed group shrinkage exposes the fairness accuracy Pareto frontier for cross ancestry polygenic risk scores
synopsis: Cross-ancestry polygenic risk scores predict unevenly across populations, and standard pipelines produce a single model without showing how accuracy trades against fairness. The authors propose cluster_fixed, a shrinkage framework that uses known ancestry labels to map the full Pareto frontier between overall accuracy and subgroup disparity. In 1000 Genomes simulations with mostly shared genetic effects, it cut worst-case disparity by 71.7% at the cost of a 57.8% drop in accuracy. When population-specific effects were large, fairness and accuracy improved together. The pattern replicated using Pan-UK Biobank height effects, where competing corrections fell short. The framework lets users choose a model under an explicit disparity limit instead of accepting one default.

title: From benchmarking to application: a scalable mitochondrial DNA analysis and variant identification framework for whole-genome sequencing
synopsis: Which tools call mitochondrial DNA variants most accurately from short-read whole-genome sequencing? The authors benchmarked MitoHPC, mtSwirl, mity and mtDNA-Server 2 on 1000 Genomes data and on simulations across diverse haplogroups, scoring homoplasmic and heteroplasmic variants. MitoHPC and mtSwirl performed best overall, especially in non-European populations. mity was strong for low-frequency SNVs but weaker for indels, and mtDNA-Server 2 had more false positives and missed variants in MT-RNR2. They built MARVel around MitoHPC, adding QC reporting, variant curation and a haplogroup principal component reference. In an ataxia cohort it recovered known pathogenic variants and flagged new candidates, giving practical guidance for large mtDNA studies.

title: Genetic analysis of non-familial early-onset Alzheimer's disease patients
synopsis: This study asks whether sporadic early-onset Alzheimer's disease has a different genetic architecture from late-onset disease. It compared 87 sporadic early-onset cases with 1,018 late-onset cases and more than 4,000 controls, using APOE genotyping, GWAS, SKAT, polygenic risk scores and rare-variant analysis. APOE e4 was enriched in early-onset cases compared with controls (52.2% vs 20.1%) but less common than in late-onset cases (64.5%). Polygenic risk in early-onset cases fell between controls and late-onset cases, and rare variants in APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2 were not enriched. Sporadic early-onset disease therefore looks closer to late-onset disease than to a high-burden form, and its missing risk may come from other sources.

title: Genomic foundation models and complementary variant-scoring strategies in LGMD-associated genes: architecture, adaptation, and sequence context
synopsis: This study compares how well six genomic foundation models classify variants in ten genes linked to limb-girdle muscular dystrophy. It used 6,960 ClinVar single-nucleotide variants and tested frozen embeddings at three context lengths, supervised fine-tuning, and gene-held-out classifiers, with GPN-Star and AlphaGenome scored natively. Frozen Evo2 performed best, and extending its context from 101 to 501 bp raised its MCC from 0.644 to 0.864. GPN-Star and AlphaGenome reached MCCs of 0.929 and 0.938, while fine-tuning helped only three of the six models. The results reflect aggregate ClinVar labels, which showed annotation-related structure, and clinical diagnostic usefulness remains untested.

title: Integrating CRISPRi perturbation responses and transcription-factor binding priors for regulatory network inference in triple-negative breast cancer
synopsis: This study asks whether perturbation data can improve gene regulatory network inference in triple-negative breast cancer, where co-expression-based methods produce many false discoveries. The authors combined single-cell CRISPRi Perturb-seq data from MDA-MB-231 cells (95,678 cells) with ENCODE ChIP-seq transcription factor binding at 819 mutation-associated enhancers. The resulting network ranked CTCF, EP300, JUND, MYC and FOS among its central drivers, linked to programs such as epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Against held-out CRISPRi ground truth it reached an AUPRC of 0.87, compared with 0.63 for GENIE3. Driver signatures also separated patients by survival in the METABRIC and TCGA cohorts, suggesting that interventional data can sharpen regulatory inference in cancer.

title: Meta-analysis of Sequencing Data Identifies Candidate Endometrial Cancer Susceptibility Genes
synopsis: This study looks for rare-variant contributions to endometrial cancer risk beyond the well-known mismatch repair genes. It meta-analysed 2,675 cases and 160,654 controls from UK Biobank and the 100,000 Genomes Project, running gene-level burden tests separately for protein-truncating variants and predicted-deleterious missense variants. The analysis recovered MSH6, MLH1 and MSH2 for truncating variants, with relative risks of 13 to 52, and PTEN for missense variants. A further 19 genes reached exome-wide significance in the truncating analysis, including PHKG2 (RR 29.8), along with eight more in the missense analysis. These candidate susceptibility genes still need replication.

title: NanoHIV-DR: a Nextflow workflow for consensus and read level HIV-1 drug resistance profiling from Oxford Nanopore sequencing
synopsis: Oxford Nanopore sequencing can genotype HIV-1 drug resistance quickly and portably, but analyzing the long reads takes many bioinformatics steps and few workflows exist. NanoHIV-DR is a Nextflow workflow that takes raw POD5 files through basecalling, demultiplexing, host-read removal, quality filtering, alignment and consensus generation. It then identifies resistance-associated mutations in two ways: consensus-based interpretation with Sierra, and read-level detection that can find and quantify mutations below the consensus level. The results are combined with clinical metadata into readable reports. The workflow aims to make Nanopore-based resistance testing reproducible and usable with less bioinformatics expertise and less manual processing.

title: Optimizing Exomiser to prioritize candidate genes underlying monogenic forms of common disease
synopsis: This study asks whether the variant prioritization tool Exomiser can find monogenic forms of a common disease, using kidney stone disease as the test case. In exome data from 701 cases and 200 controls, the authors benchmarked Exomiser settings on known gold-standard variants and then used the best pipeline to look for new genes. The optimized setup ranked 94% of known gene-participant pairs within its top five. It also nominated 62 new candidate genes, mostly involved in ion homeostasis, and independent rare-variant enrichment analyses supported ABCC6. The work shows how automated rare-variant prioritization can be adapted to common diseases with Mendelian subforms.

title: Quantification of Bias-Variance Tradeoffs in Genome-Wide Polygenic Indices: When 'Good' PGIs are Bad and 'Bad' PGIs are Good
synopsis: Polygenic indices predict less well in new samples than they could, because the GWAS they are built from contain estimation error. The authors correct for this error by running GWAS of the same trait in independent samples, and they show how to split existing summary statistics into synthetic independent halves when individual-level data are unavailable. They then compared clumping, LDpred2, SBayesR and PRS-CS in simulated and real data. Methods that shrink effects aggressively gave higher uncorrected accuracy but lower error-corrected accuracy. LDpred2-inf did the opposite and nearly recovered full SNP heritability. Aggressive shrinkage also distorted associations with other traits, so the choice of construction method involves a bias-variance tradeoff that is rarely recognized.

title: SpliceVarMech: A causal generative framework for mechanistic interpretation of non-canonical splicing variants
synopsis: This paper presents SpliceVarMech, a method for explaining how non-canonical splicing variants change splicing outcomes, not just scoring how disruptive they are. A dual-stream encoder compares wild-type and mutant sequences, discrete diffusion generates candidate splice outcomes, and Bayesian inference gives disruption probabilities with credible intervals. On 31 validated variants from male infertility genes, leave-one-out cross-validation gave an AUC of 1.000, compared with 0.619 for SpliceAI, the best of 16 existing tools. Fine-tuning on BRCA1 saturation editing data raised AUC from 0.722 to 0.840 on 203 held-out variants. The validation cohorts are small, and the authors note that held-out calibration still needs testing.

title: The IGVF Catalog Knowledge Graph
synopsis: This paper describes the IGVF Catalog, a knowledge graph that brings together the IGVF consortium's variant-to-function data. Version 1.3 has nearly 3 billion nodes and 8.6 billion edges, integrating 657 datasets from MPRA, CRISPR, Perturb-seq and coding-variant assays plus predictive models. These are linked to public resources such as GENCODE, dbSNP, GWAS, QTLs and protein interactions. Users can query it through a web portal, Python and R clients, an API and an MCP server for language-model agents. Case studies at type 2 diabetes, liver trait and coronary artery disease loci show how it supports mechanistic interpretation of variants.

title: The IGVF Data Portal: a repository for insights into genome function
synopsis: This paper describes the data portal built to store and share everything produced by the Impact of Genomic Variation on Function (IGVF) Consortium, which studies how genomic variation affects function using many assays and computational methods. The portal holds all consortium results and supplies the results integrated into the IGVF knowledge graph. As of November 2026 it held more than 240 terabytes of public data, available through a web browser, an API and agentic tools. The paper summarizes the available data and the portal's design, so it serves as a practical guide to a large resource on variant function.

title: EPIC2: integrating single-cell chromatin accessibility with human genetics to identify trait-relevant cell types
synopsis: This software note asks how to find the cell types through which genetic risk for a trait acts. The framework combines GWAS summary statistics with single-cell chromatin accessibility data. It tests whether GWAS association strength tracks cell-type-specific accessibility, and it accounts for linkage disequilibrium. Tests run at both the SNP and regulatory-peak level, and their P-values are merged with the Cauchy combination test. The method is available as an R package with vignettes and test data. It gives researchers a practical way to link GWAS signals to regulatory activity in specific cell types.

title: Read&Tag enables antibody-independent combinatorial and multifactorial chromatin profiling
synopsis: This paper introduces Read&Tag, a chromatin profiling method that fuses engineered chromatin reader domains or intrabodies directly to Tn5 transposase, so no antibodies are needed. It profiles active and repressive histone marks, DNA methylation and elongating RNA polymerase II, and it works in frozen tissue and low-input samples. Dual-specificity readers tag DNA only where H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 occur on the same fragment, so co-occurrence is measured directly rather than inferred from separate profiles. Barcoded complexes allow four chromatin features to be measured in a single reaction. This offers a modular way to study combinatorial chromatin states.

title: A Super-Enhancer-Like Element and a Positive Feedback Loop Drive Ultra-High Expression of CCS for Red Pepper Ripening
synopsis: This study asks why the pepper capsanthin-capsorubin synthase gene, which makes the red pigment, becomes one of the most highly expressed genes in ripe fruit. In its promoter the authors found a super-enhancer-like element made of 22 tandem repeats, split into groups by two transposable-element insertions. Small RNAs and DNA methylation tied to these insertions seem to keep the gene off before ripening, and demethylation releases it. During ripening, two MADS-box factors, RIN and TAGL1, activate the gene through repeated CArG motifs, with stronger activation at higher repeat copy number. The two factors also form a positive feedback loop, and RIN forms nuclear condensates at the promoter. Together these findings show how promoter structure, epigenetics and transcriptional circuits can produce extreme, tightly timed gene expression.

title: Both Endogenous Enhancer and Retrotransposon Inserted Nearby Are Required to Induce Ectopic Expression in Danforth's Short Tail Mutation
synopsis: In Danforth's short tail mice, an endogenous retrovirus inserted upstream of Ptf1a turns the gene on in the notochord and causes vertebral defects, but how this ectopic expression arises was unclear. The study edited the nearby Ptf1a auto-regulatory enhancer (ARE) and the retroviral insertion directly in the Sd genome. Deleting either the ARE or the retrovirus removed the vertebral defects, so both elements are needed. The half of the ARE closest to the insertion was the core element responsible, and ectopic expression still occurred in Ptf1a-deficient mice, so the PTF1 complex is not required. The work shows how a retroviral insertion can act together with a native enhancer to cause disease.

title: Enduring DNA Methylation Marks of Blast and Trauma Exposures in Warfighters
synopsis: This study asked whether DNA methylation records repeated blast and psychological trauma exposure in military personnel and whether it relates to cognitive performance. It analyzed blood from 190 breachers and 30 hand grenade operators, all male, using epigenetic clocks, epigenome-wide association with blast and trauma exposure factors, and methylation risk scores. Epigenetic age acceleration correlated with service length and with both exposure factors, and 12 regions were associated with blast and 22 with trauma. The risk scores had internal AUCs of 88% and 86% and external AUCs of 52% to 74%. The trauma score was linked to slower reaction time after blast exposure, suggesting methylation could serve as an objective exposure biomarker.

title: Genetic Dissection of the Mouse Class I Odorant Receptor Gene Cluster
synopsis: Mouse Class I odorant receptor genes sit in one large cluster on chromosome 7 and are controlled by a long-range enhancer called the J element, yet some of these genes stay expressed without it. To look for additional regulatory elements, the authors made targeted deletions on either side of the conserved beta-globin genes near the middle of the cluster. Deleting the centromeric part, which contains the J element, lowered expression of telomeric Class I genes, much like deleting the J element alone. Deleting the telomeric part instead increased expression of centromeric genes. The results confirm the J element as the main enhancer and suggest weaker secondary enhancers outside the centromeric region.

title: LACA: a cross-species single-cell resource for exploring longevity and aging-associated cellular and molecular programs
synopsis: Species differ greatly in maximum lifespan, but few resources link single-cell gene expression to lifespan across species. The Longevity & Aging Cell Atlas (LACA) brings together single-cell transcriptomic data from 134 species, covering more than 148 million cells and 190 annotated cell types, each paired with the species' maximum lifespan. It offers cross-species tools for comparing longevity genes and for correlating gene expression and cell composition with lifespan. It also includes a centenarian single-cell atlas, a human immune aging multi-omics atlas, a curated knowledge graph and a retrieval-augmented research agent. The resource lets researchers study conserved and species-specific longevity mechanisms without heavy computational work.

title: OMIGAT: Multi-Feature Enhanced Collaborative Attention and Graph Convolution Model for Cancer Driver Gene Identification
synopsis: Finding cancer driver genes from multi-omics data is difficult because the data are noisy and existing biological networks are incomplete. OMIGAT is a deep learning framework that combines genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic features with network topology to make gene representations more robust to noise. It learns along two parallel paths: a global path that builds a feature-similarity graph to find functional links missing from known networks, and a local path that encodes neighborhood structure within the biological network. An adaptive fusion step weighs the two paths when making predictions. On the PPNet dataset, OMIGAT reached an AUC of 87.46% for identifying known driver genes.

title: RNAcomp2D: a web tool to execute multiple methods and visually compare predictions of RNA secondary structure
synopsis: RNA secondary structure prediction methods are numerous, but each has its own interface, language and computing requirements, so it is hard to run several and compare their outputs. RNAcomp2D is a web tool where users enter an RNA sequence, or pick one from RNAcentral, and get predictions from several state-of-the-art methods at once. Classical thermodynamic methods and recent deep learning models are packaged in containers behind one website. All predictions, along with a reference structure when one exists, appear together in a single graphical view. The tool is built so new methods can be added, making side-by-side benchmarking of predictors much easier.

title: pyGENIE: A Python library for programmatic access and mutational analysis of AACR Project GENIE
synopsis: AACR Project GENIE now holds more than 268,000 samples from nearly 250,000 cancer patients, but analyzing it usually means writing custom code around complex flat files. pyGENIE is a Python package with a single API for loading GENIE data, running clinical and genomic queries, computing tumor mutational burden, and connecting to mutational signature tools such as SigProfiler and SigMA. All results come back as pandas DataFrames, so they plug directly into machine learning and plotting libraries. In a lung adenocarcinoma case study, it reproduced known mutation frequencies, co-mutation patterns and signatures with roughly ten times less code. This lowers the barrier to reproducible analysis of a widely used clinical genomics resource.

title: Multiancestry genome-wide association and integrative multiomics analyses implicate key pathways in endometriosis
synopsis: This study looks for the genetic basis of endometriosis, a common and painful condition with poorly understood mechanisms. It is a multiancestry genome-wide meta-analysis within the Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative, covering over one million participants (32% of non-European ancestry), and it uses new algorithms that identify procedure-confirmed cases. The authors found 58 associated regions, 27 of them new, including loci seen only in African and admixed American populations. Analyses of comorbidities, cell-context-specific expression and other omics implicated 314 genes in total. The results point to linked pathways across molecular, cellular and phenotypic levels and suggest several possible therapeutic targets.

title: Brain Cell-Type-Specific X-Chromosome Gene Regulation Reveals Sex-Biased Candidate Genes in Neurodegeneration
synopsis: This study asks how X-chromosome gene regulation in specific brain cell types might help explain sex differences in neurodegenerative disease. The authors mapped X-linked cis-eQTLs across seven brain cell types in 423 older individuals. They found 212 genetically regulated X-linked genes, mostly cell-type specific, and 10 of them showed regulation that differed by sex. They also found 101 sex-biased genes, mostly higher in females and especially in microglia, many of which escape X inactivation and are linked to Alzheimer's disease. Integration with X-chromosome association studies nominated 11 candidate causal genes for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and multiple system atrophy. This gives a resource for sex-aware study of neurodegeneration.

title: Brain-derived multi-omics prioritization of mitochondria-related genes in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depressive disorder
synopsis: This study asks which mitochondria-related genes might causally affect risk for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depression. The authors combined QTL data on brain DNA methylation, gene expression and protein abundance with GWAS results. They applied summary-data-based Mendelian randomization, HEIDI heterogeneity tests and colocalization, then ranked genes in a three-tier framework. ACADVL and SLC25A24 were top-tier candidates for schizophrenia, with COX11, DLST, ENDOG and PDF in lower tiers. ENDOG and PDF were also linked to the combined bipolar-schizophrenia phenotype, and ENDOG appeared to act through methylation. The work names genetically supported mitochondrial candidates for experimental follow-up in psychiatric disease.

title: CELL-X: A Single-Cell Transcriptomics Framework for Cell-Type and Disease-State Prioritization of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Genes
synopsis: GWAS have found hundreds of type 2 diabetes loci, but it is still hard to tell which genes are causal and which cell types they act in. CELL-X combines fine-mapped genetic evidence with a human pancreatic islet single-cell atlas of 245,878 cells, analysed without downsampling. It scores 37 candidate genes on a cell relevance score and a disease relevance score, which tracks expression shifts across normal, prediabetic and diabetic states. Beta cells come out as the main disease-relevant cell type, and known genes such as SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK and TCF7L2 rank highly. The method recovers targets well on a 30-gene benchmark and holds up against null models, giving a scalable way to generate cell-context hypotheses for GWAS genes.

title: One blood methylation profile stratifies ten-year risk across 21 common diseases
synopsis: This study asks whether a single blood DNA methylation profile can predict ten-year risk for many common diseases. The authors built methylation risk scores for 21 diseases in 12,785 adults from Generation Scotland and the Mass General Brigham Biobank. They used reproducible probes, null-calibrated feature selection and survival models, and evaluated everything on an untouched holdout set. Eight scores reached a holdout C-index of at least 0.80, including those for chronic kidney disease, heart failure, COPD and type 2 diabetes. Hazard ratios ranged from 2.6 to 4.1 per standard deviation, and the top tertile held 73 to 90% of events. Most of these scores beat published polygenic and methylation scores, which suggests methylation could be a broad tool for risk stratification.

title: Rare copy number variation in alcohol use disorder using whole-genome sequencing in the All of Us Research Program
synopsis: This study asks whether rare copy number variants contribute to alcohol use disorder, a heritable condition whose structural-variant component has been little studied. Using whole-genome sequencing from the All of Us Research Program, the authors tested rare CNVs in 56,062 participants, of whom 5,410 were cases defined from health records. Analyses were run within European-like, African-like and admixed American-like samples and then meta-analyzed. No genome-wide burden or individual large CNV region was significant. Duplications across many unrelated gene sets were associated with lower risk. A small deletion at the neuropsychiatric locus 16p12.1 was associated across ancestries (OR 2.93). Overall, CNVs detectable by short-read sequencing seem to contribute little to liability for the disorder at current sample sizes.

title: VEGABrain: a Visualizer of Enriched Gene Analysis for the developing human brain
synopsis: This paper presents a web tool for exploring gene expression in the developing human brain by region. The tool maps bulk RNA-seq data onto cortical and subcortical atlas surfaces across five developmental windows, from the first trimester to adulthood. Besides single-gene maps, it offers precomputed ssGSEA enrichment scores for about 19,000 gene sets from GO, Reactome, KEGG, BioCarta, HPO and the MSigDB hallmark collection, scored for each region and window. Users can also upload their own gene lists and get enrichment maps computed on demand. The tool is open source and needs no installation, so reused developmental transcriptome data become easy to inspect by region.

title: A new liability-based rare-variant burden test identifies a novel genetic association between HTRA3 and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
synopsis: Rare variants with modest effects often depend on a carrier's polygenic background to cause disease. Adding a polygenic risk score as a covariate improves rare-variant tests for quantitative traits but gives little or no gain for binary traits. The authors propose the liability threshold burden test (LTBT), which models rare variants and the polygenic score together under a liability threshold model. In simulations, LTBT kept false positives under control and was more sensitive than existing methods. Applied to sequencing data for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, it found and formally replicated a new association between rare predicted damaging missense variants in HTRA3 and the disease, showing how accounting for genetic background can aid gene discovery.

title: DGIdb in 2026: an interoperable resource for the druggable genome
synopsis: DGIdb is an open-access knowledgebase that standardizes and combines drug-gene interaction and gene annotation data from many therapeutic and biomedical sources. This update refreshes existing sources and adds three new ones: the Molecular Oncology Almanac, the PRISM Repurposing Dataset and the Broad Institute Drug Repurposing Hub. New Python and R clients, dgiPy and dgiR, give standardized programmatic access to the API. Versioned Docker images and a public repository of current and past releases in TSV and SQL formats support local deployment and reproducibility. Together these changes make drug-gene interaction data easier to use in computational workflows such as drug repurposing and target prioritization.

title: DIANA-miTED v2: an expanded microRNA tissue expression database with an integrated healthy-tissue reference atlas
synopsis: DIANA-miTED v2 is an updated database of human microRNA expression that gives a healthy-tissue reference for reading miRNA levels in disease or experimental settings. It grows from 15,183 to 49,630 uniformly processed small RNA-seq profiles drawn from GTEx V10, the Sequence Read Archive and TCGA. Together these cover 2,656 mature miRNAs across 96 tissues, 437 cell lines and 503 diseases. Healthy-donor profiles rise from 709 to 23,281, and tumour-adjacent normal samples are classified separately. The new interface supports tissue-centric and multi-miRNA queries, co-expression analysis with precomputed WGCNA modules, downloads and a REST API, making it a large baseline for miRNA studies.

title: GI-DB: a comprehensive variant database for exploring the extensive genetic diversity of the Indian population
synopsis: Indian populations are underrepresented in global genomic resources, which limits genomic medicine in South Asia. GI-DB is a public variant database built from about 10,000 genomes across 83 populations sequenced by the GenomeIndia initiative. It catalogs 136 million high-confidence variants, 44 million of which are absent from other global and South Asian databases. Allele frequencies are broken down by tribal versus non-tribal groups, biogeography and ethnolinguistic category. Variants are annotated with VEP and ClinVar and compared with 1000 Genomes, gnomAD and GenomeAsia. The resource can support interpretation of variants in rare disease, complex disorders and pharmacogenomics for Indian populations.

title: Integrating genetic and lung tissue proteomics data to identify susceptibility proteins for lung cancer
source: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
synopsis: This study asked which proteins in lung tissue influence lung cancer susceptibility and could be drug targets. The authors profiled the proteome and genome of 200 non-neoplastic lung tissue samples and built genetic models that predict protein abundance. They applied these models to GWAS data from 55,174 cases and 1,294,174 controls, then checked results with independent proteomic data, colocalization and Mendelian randomization. They identified 29 risk-associated proteins, several of them away from known risk loci. DSP, IL18 and TYMP showed both reproducible and potentially causal evidence and are targeted by six drugs that are approved or in phase III trials. These results point to new biology and candidate drug targets for lung cancer.

title: Dosage compensation is regulated by segregated chromatin modules during development in Drosophila
synopsis: This study asks how Drosophila dosage compensation of the male X chromosome adjusts to X-linked genes that differ in function and dosage sensitivity. The authors analysed epigenomic and 3D genome data from mostly sexed samples spanning embryos to adults. About 30% of X-linked genes are compensated only in particular stages or tissues. These genes tend to be developmentally regulated, carry more H3K27me3, and form long-range contacts with PionX elements and 1.6883F satellites that strengthen over development. Constitutively compensated housekeeping genes instead contact HAS elements and constitutive domain boundaries from the embryo onward. The results point to separate chromatin modules regulating dosage compensation for housekeeping versus developmental genes.

title: Optimizing phenotype scale improves genetic analyses in large-scale biobanks
synopsis: The scale on which a phenotype is measured can strongly affect genetic inference, yet biobank studies rarely question it. SIQReg learns a data-driven scale by minimizing heterogeneity across phenotype quantiles. Across 25 UK Biobank traits it rejects the default scale for 24, and the learned scales usually fall between the default and logarithmic. On the new scales, 97% of variance QTLs disappear, which suggests they are artefacts of the scale, while plausible nonadditive signals remain. Additive analyses gain power: GWAS loci rise by 11%, TWAS genes by 13% and polygenic prediction accuracy by 10%, with 50% more high-risk individuals identified. These gains replicate across ancestry groups, which makes scale choice a practical issue for biobank genetics.

title: Cellular reconfiguration of Alzheimer’s disease genetic susceptibility across aging and pathology
synopsis: This study asks how Alzheimer's disease genetic risk is spread across cell types during healthy ageing and disease progression. The authors developed scGIPA, which combines GWAS associations, brain regulatory evidence and hippocampal single-nucleus transcriptomes, and uses in silico perturbation to estimate each cell type's contribution. Six functional modules shifted their cellular makeup across stages, with lipid-clearance and amyloid-fibril contributions peaking in early pathology. Of 1,469 associated genes, 349 contributed to both ageing and pathology, and these were enriched in a microglial co-expression module. PVR and HBEGF pointed to endothelial ageing, while APOE and BIN1 changed their cellular roles across stages.

title: Functionally decoupled cis-regulatory signals at PCOLCE2 link fibroblast-lineage collagen maturation to pelvic organ prolapse
synopsis: This study asks which cell type and regulatory signal explain a suggestive, not genome-wide significant, GWAS association for pelvic organ prolapse at PCOLCE2, a regulator of procollagen processing. Using only public summary-level and single-cell data, it combines cis-Mendelian randomisation with fibroblast eQTLs, colocalisation, CAUSE, fine-mapping, plasma protein QTLs and single-cell analyses. The evidence supports a fibroblast-restricted cis-regulatory effect that raises prolapse risk (OR 1.28 per SD; PP4 = 0.954). A separate blood-restricted signal in the same haplotype block controls plasma protein levels but is unrelated to disease. All conclusions depend on independent replication of the index signal, and the mechanism remains a hypothesis.

title: MitoArc: A Reproducible Short-Read Workflow for Human Mitochondrial Genome Analysis with Circular-Coordinate and NUMT-Aware Evaluation
synopsis: Calling human mitochondrial variants from short reads is complicated by nuclear mitochondrial segments (NUMTs), the circular reference, sequencing depth and variant-caller settings. MitoArc is a Nextflow workflow that runs GATK Mutect2 and mutserve2 with standard and shifted coordinates. It reports quality metrics, NUMT evidence, haplogroups, contamination and annotations. It was evaluated on 18 synthetic datasets at depths from 100x to 5000x. Requiring confident mitochondrial mapping removed 33 NUMT-related false positives but lowered recall from 0.894 to 0.796. GATK recall rose from 0.741 to 0.917 with depth, and shifted-coordinate processing did not change results. The workflow keeps the evidence needed to interpret mitochondrial variants reproducibly.

title: PDAC BioPortal: An Integrated Web Resource for Multi-Scale Analysis of Pancreatic Cancer Transcriptomics
synopsis: Transcriptomic resources for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma are spread across separate datasets and data types. PDAC BioPortal is a web resource that brings together bulk TCGA-GTEx data from 349 samples, a 55-specimen treatment cohort, 224,988 single nuclei from 43 patients, and spatial data from five patients. It offers differential expression, enrichment, pseudobulk and spatial analyses, along with a natural-language interface grounded in the underlying data. In example analyses, primary tumors showed proliferative, inflammatory and EMT programs, while tumors after neoadjuvant treatment showed matrix-rich mesenchymal signatures. NRF2 redox genes were elevated in tumors and varied by cell type and by patient. A six-gene NRF2 signature was tentatively associated with shorter survival.

title: Sparrowhawk: harnessing WebAssembly for private microbial genomics, and beyond
synopsis: Many researchers cannot easily run new computational methods, and developers rarely have time to build interactive interfaces for them. Sparrowhawk is a framework that uses WebAssembly to turn algorithms into web applications that run entirely on the user's own machine, with no installation and no sensitive data sent over the internet. For genomic epidemiology, the authors built lightweight tools for genome assembly, antimicrobial resistance gene annotation and taxonomic identification. These outperformed earlier lightweight methods and reproduced or closely matched results from standard pipelines. They also ported algorithms from machine learning and physics to show that the framework is general. The approach could make advanced analyses more accessible for research, teaching and public engagement.

title: VPHYL: A Web Application for Converting Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s Nanopore 16S rRNA Abundance Tables into phyloseq and BIOM Objects
synopsis: Turning Oxford Nanopore 16S classifier outputs into standard phyloseq or BIOM objects usually requires scripting, because Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s produce files in different formats. VPHYL is an R Shiny web application that reads these outputs directly, splits taxonomic lineages into standard ranks, attaches sample metadata, and exports phyloseq or BIOM objects along with HTML reports of read statistics and diversity. Its output matched an independently written R script for all nine supported classifier-database combinations. Applied to a published respiratory microbiome dataset, it gave diversity and taxonomic profiles consistent with the original findings. The tool makes this conversion step accessible to researchers who do not program.

title: YAP1-induced super-enhancer rewiring mediates gene-environment-driven malignant reprogramming and metastatic ecosystem formation in head and neck cancer
synopsis: TP53 mutations are common in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma but cannot cause tumors on their own and are hard to drug, so this study asks which epigenetic mechanisms drive the cancer's evolution. Integrated multi-omics of mouse models and multiregional human tumor samples showed that global chromatin architecture stays largely stable as tumors progress, while YAP1 moves to newly formed super-enhancers marked by enhancer DNA hypomethylation. YAP1 sets up an IL6-dependent feedforward loop and works with stage-specific factors such as FOXM1, DeltaNp63 and PITX2. The YAP1-PITX2 axis promotes partial EMT, fibroblast activation and lymph node metastasis, which points to a possible therapeutic target.

title: nf-core/pairgenomealign: a scalable pipeline for pairwise whole-genome alignment
synopsis: Genome assemblies are accumulating rapidly, so reproducible and scalable whole-genome comparison is increasingly needed. nf-core/pairgenomealign is a Nextflow pipeline that automates pairwise genome alignment with the LAST suite across a wide range of evolutionary distances. It runs on local, cloud and HPC systems and exports alignments in MAF, BAM, BCF and CRAM formats. It can also pack many genomes aligned to one target into a single compact file that genome browsers display directly and from which multiple alignments of any region can be extracted. In benchmarks it is competitive with established aligners and allows tuning between speed and sensitivity, and the authors show uses in comparative genomics and assembly quality control.

title: Gene Burden Testing for Rare and Genetic Disease Studies: A Practical Beginner-Oriented Workflow
synopsis: This chapter is a beginner-oriented workflow for gene burden testing. Burden tests ask whether rare variants within a gene, transcript or defined variant set are jointly associated with disease. Most individual rare variants are too uncommon to reach adequate power alone, but aggregating them can increase detection power. The workflow covers study design, quality control, annotation, defining qualifying variants, choosing burden or kernel-based tests, covariate adjustment and interpreting results. It also discusses choices that affect reproducibility, such as ancestry matching and allele-frequency thresholds. It places burden testing alongside collapsing, weighted and variance-component methods and extensions to oligogenic or digenic disease, for Mendelian, complex-disease and unresolved exome studies.

title: Aging out of the blue: Region-specific epigenetic clock calibration for a blue zone with the DNAm SuperLearner
synopsis: Standard epigenetic clocks reflect average population trends, which may mislead when comparing biological aging in regions of exceptional longevity. Using DNA methylation from the Nicoya blue zone (n = 206) and other Costa Ricans (n = 875), the authors trained a SuperLearner ensemble on the reference population and built a calibrated test of epigenetic age acceleration. Without calibration, estimates for Nicoyans depended strongly on the clock: about three years younger with the SuperLearner, almost four years older with DNAmFitAge. Mean calibration gave a consistent advantage of about two years. After calibrating within age strata, only a small advantage of -0.35 years remained, mostly among the oldest participants. This shows that region-specific calibration matters.

title: GausSKAT: A Data-Adaptive Weighted Gaussian Kernel Procedure for Rare-Variant Association Testing Within the SKAT Framework
synopsis: The sequence kernel association test (SKAT) jointly tests rare variants in a region, and its power depends on how the kernel represents genetic similarity. The weighted Gaussian kernel is less used than the linear kernel, partly because its bandwidth hyperparameter is hard to choose, and no single value suits every genetic architecture. GausSKAT evaluates Gaussian SKAT over a phenotype-independent grid of hyperparameter values, with grid endpoints set from genetic distances, and combines the p-values with the aggregated Cauchy association test. In simulations it usually had more power than weighted-linear and identity-by-state SKAT, and the best hyperparameter differed across settings. Results in Dallas Heart Study triglyceride data varied by ANGPTL gene, so it complements standard SKAT rather than replacing it.

title: Population-Scale, Genotype-First Characterization of Monogenic Diabetes in 374,973 Individuals Across Ancestries in the NIH All of Us Research Program
synopsis: Most knowledge of maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) comes from phenotype-first studies in European-ancestry cohorts. This genotype-first study analyzed whole-genome sequencing and clinical data from 374,973 All of Us participants, 42% of non-European ancestry. Pathogenic variants in 10 MODY genes were found in 370 carriers (1 in 1,013), at similar rates in European and African ancestry participants. Penetrance was incomplete, at 43.5% by age 60, and highest for GCK. Carriers of variants in non-GCK/HNF genes had a modestly raised risk (HR 1.64). This was lower than the risk of noncarriers in the top 10% of type 2 diabetes polygenic risk (HR 1.91), and higher polygenic risk increased risk among carriers. The findings support MODY testing across ancestries.

title: Chromatin loci move coherently due to spatially correlated fluctuations
synopsis: This study builds a quantitative framework for how chromosomal loci move relative to each other, which matters for enhancer-promoter contact and DNA repair. Live imaging in Drosophila embryos and mouse stem cells showed that nearby loci diffuse relative to each other much more slowly than polymer models predict. The authors attribute this to spatially correlated fluctuations transmitted through the nucleoplasm. Polymer simulations reproduced the observed scaling only when driven by active flows, not equilibrium noise. Experiments showed that these fluctuations couple loci across chromosomes and depend on ATP-dependent activity and cohesin loop extrusion. They make encounters rarer but longer, which has direct consequences for gene regulation.

title: Regularized ensemble polygenic risk prediction with GWAS summary statistics
synopsis: Ensemble learning improves polygenic risk scores, but current ensemble methods need individual-level genotype data for training, which limits their use in non-European populations with few samples. This work introduces a statistical framework that builds a regularized ensemble from many candidate PRS models using only GWAS summary statistics. Across multiple traits and populations, the method consistently outperformed state-of-the-art PRS approaches, both within and across ancestries. Because new PRS models can be added to the ensemble alongside existing ones, the framework offers a scalable and general route to better risk prediction, especially in under-represented populations.

title: A Graded Immune-Cell-Resolved cis-eQTL Mendelian Randomisation Screen Across Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Related Immune Phenotypes
synopsis: Whole-blood eQTLs average over leukocytes, while systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) involves cell-specific immune processes. This study ran a Mendelian randomization screen using cis-eQTLs from 15 immune-cell types in DICE and eight FinnGen outcomes, after first auditing variant identities and allele orientation. Of 19,009 instruments, 6,525 passed the audit; among 48,958 tests, 1,186 reached FDR below 0.05, giving 288 independent signals. Signals for SLE were concentrated in the MHC, and most non-MHC signals involved rheumatoid arthritis and autoimmune hypothyroidism. Inflation correction substantially reduced significant results, and negative-control infection outcomes showed little signal. The authors present this as a graded, auditable screening framework rather than a definitive list of SLE genes.

title: AlphaGenome 2 predicts regulatory activity and variant effects across cell states
synopsis: Most trait- and disease-associated variants are non-coding and act in specific cell types or states, but single-cell atlases rarely include enough donors to map variant effects on expression directly. This work presents AlphaGenome 2, a sequence-to-function deep learning model trained on organism-wide human and mouse single-cell atlases and bulk functional genomics data. It takes a 1-Mb DNA sequence plus a condition specifying a tissue, cell type or cell state. Because the condition can be inferred from gene expression, the model works on unseen datasets without fine-tuning. It outperforms fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1 and specialized models, doubling recall of causal single-cell eQTLs at 90% precision. It also improves enhancer-gene linking and causal variant fine-mapping, and it yields an atlas of enhancer-gene links and effect scores for 7 million common variants.

title: Polygenic risk scores for sleep: from portability to clinical utility
synopsis: Single-author perspective on polygenic risk scores for sleep traits and disorders, covering how well they transfer across populations and whether they are clinically useful. No abstract is available, so this summary is based on the title only.

title: Integration of GWAS and Transcriptomic Data Links RMI1, ARHGEF15, TTC21B, and HAGH to Mitochondrial-Neuroinflammatory Coupling in Epilepsy
synopsis: This study asks which genes, cell types and molecular programs underlie epilepsy risk loci found by GWAS. The authors took GWAS summary statistics for eight epilepsy phenotypes and ran SuSiE fine-mapping, brain eQTL colocalization, SMR-HEIDI and transcriptome-wide association. They then checked the prioritized genes in 162 bulk RNA-seq samples, in CITE-seq data from 85,780 cells, and in network analyses. Four Tier 1 genes (RMI1, TVP23B, ARHGEF15, TTC21B) and four Tier 2 genes, including HAGH, were prioritized. The strongest coupling linked reduced oxidative phosphorylation with microglial activation (pooled rho = -0.52) and IL1 signaling (rho = -0.48). The results give genetically anchored hypotheses tying epilepsy risk to mitochondrial and neuroinflammatory pathways, but they do not show causal direction.

title: Joint Associations of Cardiovascular Health and Polygenic Risk with Incident Cardiovascular Disease across the CKM Syndrome Continuum: A Prospective Cohort Study
synopsis: This study asks whether ideal cardiovascular health protects against cardiovascular disease across all stages of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, and how polygenic risk modifies this. It followed 242,951 UK Biobank participants without baseline disease for a median of 15.2 years, scoring cardiovascular health with Life's Essential 8 and genetic risk with a polygenic score. Ideal versus poor cardiovascular health was linked to 53% lower disease risk (HR 0.47), and this protection held across all syndrome stages and genetic risk strata. The effect of polygenic risk grew stronger in more advanced stages. The authors argue that both measures should be used together for risk stratification.

title: A harmonized functional reference framework for GBA1
synopsis: Most rare GBA1 variants lack functional evidence, which makes them hard to interpret in Gaucher disease and Parkinson's disease. This study used a multiplexed assay of variant effect to measure lysosomal glucocerebrosidase activity for more than 10,400 variants, covering 97 percent of possible single-amino-acid substitutions. The resulting atlas matched known structural determinants and expert pathogenicity classifications. It found reduced activity in 94 of 186 variants of uncertain significance and showed that greater impairment tracks with Gaucher severity. Linked to data from a global Parkinson's genetics program, greater impairment was associated with earlier Parkinson's onset and higher odds ratios. The atlas gives a reference for clinical interpretation of GBA1 variants.

title: Computational and experimental strategies for functional validation of non-coding variants in pancreatic cancer
synopsis: This review covers how to identify and test non-coding variants that may drive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, where most research has focused on coding driver mutations. It describes computational approaches such as GWAS fine-mapping, colocalisation and machine-learning annotation, along with epigenomic profiling by ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq and CUT&RUN. It also discusses newer AI-based methods, including radiogenomics and imaging analysis, that link genetic variation to clinical and imaging features. Experimental validation methods covered include reporter assays, EMSA, chromatin conformation capture and CRISPR perturbation. Together these form a framework for connecting non-coding variation in this cancer to regulatory mechanisms.

title: Genetic regulation of ALK inhibitor response in diverse human cell types
synopsis: ALK inhibitors treat ALK-positive lung cancer but cause adverse events across many tissues, and genetic studies of these toxicities are limited by small patient numbers. The authors grew heterogeneous differentiating cultures containing multiple cell types from induced pluripotent stem cells of 49 individuals. They treated the cultures with five ALK inhibitors for 24 hours and profiled them by single-cell RNA sequencing. Drug responses included both cell-type-specific and shared transcriptional effects. Combining expression with genotypes, they identified 4,371 eQTLs across 21 cell types, including 2,137 response eQTLs whose effects differ between untreated and treated cells. These loci nominate candidate genetic modifiers of ALK inhibitor toxicity for follow-up.

title: LAMP sheds light on how sequence to function models learn variant effects during post-training
synopsis: Sequence-to-function models underestimate the effects of causal variants, and fine-tuning them on personal genomes has not improved expression prediction for held-out genes and people. To find out why, the authors introduce LAMP, which inserts artificial SNVs with large, consistent effects on transcription factor motifs into personal genome datasets. Even with these easy-to-learn signals, fine-tuned Enformer still underperformed on held-out data. The authors trace this to pre-trained priors that downweight distal elements, making it hard to learn enhancer-gene links, and to sequence differences between motif instances at different loci. They suggest that existing human variation is too limited for simple fine-tuning, and they propose data augmentation strategies that help.

title: Joint Analysis of Common Regulatory and Rare Coding Variants for Improved Power in Kernel Association Tests
synopsis: Gene-based rare-variant tests usually treat rare coding variants independently of the common regulatory variants around them, even though regulatory context can change their penetrance. PrediXSKAT addresses this by estimating each person's cis-regulated gene expression with PrediXcan and embedding that prediction in the SKAT kernel through similarity weighting. In simulations where variants have small, mixed-direction effects, it gained power over standard kernel tests across sample sizes and causal architectures while controlling type I error. Applied to whole-genome sequencing from the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project, it recovered known loci and strengthened signals at new candidate genes without broadly inflating results. The framework extends to any kernel set test and to pathway-level analyses.

title: Projected clinical utility of polygenic risk score-stratified cancer screening: a systematic review
synopsis: This systematic review asks whether using polygenic risk scores to stratify cancer screening improves outcomes compared with uniform screening. It included 25 studies, mostly decision-analytic models, covering breast, colorectal, prostate, lung and gastric cancer, and found no eligible studies for cervical cancer. Stratified strategies were projected to improve QALYs for most cancers and to reduce mortality for colorectal, gastric and lung cancer. For prostate cancer, the main projected benefit was less overdiagnosis rather than lower mortality. Gains over standard screening were modest, harms rose in intensified high-risk groups, and certainty of evidence was very low throughout. The authors conclude that PRS-stratified screening should remain investigational until prospective trials in diverse populations test it.

title: How inherited variation shapes human disease trajectories
synopsis: Inherited variation is fixed at birth, but its effects on disease change with age and differ between common and rare variants. Mendelnoulli is a longitudinal model that jointly captures age-dependent polygenic and monogenic effects on health records. It separates each person's overall disease burden from their specific disease susceptibilities. Applied to 348 diseases across three biobanks, it showed that polygenic effects change significantly with age.
