It improved one-year prediction for all 28 diseases tested (mean AUC gain 0.023) and identified 8.6 more of every 100 new cases among people with no prior diagnoses. It also recovered known gene-disease timing, such as earlier breast cancer effects for BRCA1 than for BRCA2.

title: In Silico Prioritization of GWAS-Derived 3' UTR MicroRNA-Binding Variants at Colorectal Cancer Risk Loci Detected in Hispanic Patients from the All of Us Research Program
synopsis: Colorectal cancer genetics has focused on European-ancestry individuals, leaving Hispanic populations underrepresented. This study looked for 3' UTR risk variants that alter microRNA binding at colorectal cancer loci in Hispanic individuals. Variants from the GWAS Catalog were checked in 453 Hispanic All of Us participants, expanded using Admixed American linkage disequilibrium, and scored with TargetScan and RNAhybrid. Of 38 candidate SNPs, 19 altered miRNA binding across nine genes. Three loci, DCBLD2, GREM1 and SMC1B, met all criteria: the risk allele disrupts a strong binding site and the gene is overexpressed in tumors without evidence of methylation or chromatin-driven regulation. This points to loss of miRNA repression as a likely mechanism and gives candidates for functional validation.

title: A multi-tissue atlas of age-associated differential transcript usage in mouse reveals predominantly regulatory isoform switching across brain, liver, and adipose
synopsis: Alternative splicing is increasingly linked to aging, but its tissue-specific patterns and functional consequences are not well described. This study mapped differential transcript usage and isoform switching in mouse brain, liver and adipose tissue during natural aging and in Ercc1 mutant mice, adding functional annotation and structural modeling. Across tissues, 36.5-42.6% of switches changed the predicted coding sequence, while many others affected non-coding regions or left the protein unchanged. 3' UTRs tended to lengthen in brain and shorten in adipose, and one Ighm switch recurred across seven tissue samples. Structural modeling was feasible for only a minority of switches. The results suggest that age-related isoform changes act mainly through regulation, with structural effects confined to tissue-specific events.

title: Hyperglycemia-responsive circRNA drives diabetic neuropathic pain by competing for PUM2 binding and promoting proNT3/CCL2 in DRG neurons
synopsis: Diabetic neuropathic pain is common and poorly treated, and its disease-specific mechanisms are unclear. This study identified a conserved circular RNA, cRps6kb1, that is upregulated in dorsal root ganglion neurons in mouse models of type 1 and type 2 diabetes and in human donors with the condition. Blocking its upregulation reduced neurotrophin-3, proNT3 and CCL2 levels and relieved pain hypersensitivity. Mimicking the upregulation caused pain-like symptoms in healthy mice, and high glucose induced the circRNA in cultured mouse and human neurons. Mechanistically, cRps6kb1 competes with the Nt3 3' UTR for the repressor PUM2, which increases Nt3 translation and stability. This makes cRps6kb1 a candidate therapeutic target.

title: Inferring chromatin looping interactions from microscopy-based measurements: opportunities and pitfalls
synopsis: Live-cell microscopy is often used to study chromatin loop dynamics, but looping events have to be inferred from noisy 3D distance trajectories. Using polymer simulations with known ground truth, the authors show that the common approach of thresholding on 3D distance can badly misestimate looping probability, lifetime and search time at realistic localization precision. Simple statistical arguments show that threshold-based inference stops working once localization error is comparable to the size of the interaction being studied. The authors then show that noise-aware methods recover looping parameters more accurately in these regimes. The work offers practical guidance for interpreting live-imaging studies of genome organization.

title: The Gata2 3'-distal region is essential for IL-3 responsiveness in basophil and mast cell progenitors
synopsis: This study asks how GATA2 expression is maintained during mast cell and basophil development in mice. The authors identified an enhancer 53 kb downstream of Gata2 that is highly acetylated, bound by GATA2 in mast cells and basophils, and partly conserved in humans. Deleting this enhancer impaired IL-3-dependent mast cell differentiation and basophil expansion. It also blunted the rise in GATA2 at the progenitor stage and lowered expression of the IL-3 receptor beta-chain genes Csf2rb and Csf2rb2. The results show how a single distal enhancer can sustain lineage-specific transcription by setting how strongly progenitors respond to a cytokine.

title: Excluded causal variants produce false discoveries in genetic fine-mapping
synopsis: This study asks whether fine-mapping becomes unreliable when GWAS and QTL pipelines drop rare variants and indels before analysis. Comparing filtered and unfiltered fine-mapping at 499 All of Us loci, the authors found that 20% of high-confidence calls after a 1% MAF filter, and 32% when indels were also removed, lacked support in the unfiltered analysis. Errors were concentrated where tested variants tagged an omitted causal variant, so its signal was assigned to a proxy. Modeling infinitesimal effects did not reliably prevent these errors. Imputing the omitted variants, or using the new SuSiE-OUT method, prevented most of them. The findings point to a widespread source of false causal-variant claims.

title: Efficient count-based models improve power and robustness for large-scale single-cell eQTL mapping
synopsis: This paper introduces jaxQTL, a fast pseudobulk framework that uses count-based models to map single-cell eQTLs at population scale. In simulations, a negative binomial model gave calibrated inference and outperformed linear models. In the OneK1K data it found 16% more eGenes than linear models and ran much faster than single-cell Poisson mixed models. Compared with bulk eQTLs, fine-mapped single-cell eQTLs lay farther from transcription start sites and were more enriched in cell-type-specific enhancers. Across 16 blood and immune traits they explained more SNP-heritability than bulk eQTLs (9.90% versus 6.10%). They also prioritized disease genes such as IL6ST, narrowing but not closing the gap between GWAS hits and eQTLs.

title: Genetic susceptibility and risk of cardiometabolic diseases after traumatic brain injury
synopsis: This study asks whether traumatic brain injury independently raises long-term cardiometabolic risk, or whether the link mainly reflects shared inherited susceptibility. In 487,252 UK Biobank participants, 4,309 of whom had incident TBI, Cox models treated TBI as a time-varying exposure for coronary artery disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hypercholesterolemia, and tested interactions with polygenic risk scores. TBI was independently associated with higher risk of all four outcomes, and its joint effects with polygenic risk were largely additive. A composite meta-PRS predicted post-TBI cardiometabolic risk in UK Biobank (HR 1.19) and replicated in the Mass General Brigham Biobank (HR 1.15). This suggests genetics could help stratify risk after brain injury.

title: ATP8B1-TMEM30B flippase activity maintains stereocilia lipid asymmetry required for hearing
synopsis: The core hearing proteins TMC1 and TMC2 also scramble membrane lipids, so the authors asked whether an opposing flippase keeps lipids asymmetric in hair-cell membranes. In mice, they found that the lipid flippase ATP8B1 and its chaperone TMEM30B are selectively expressed in outer hair cells, enriched in stereocilia, and upregulated once hearing begins. Losing either protein raised auditory brainstem response thresholds, exposed phosphatidylserine on the outer membrane surface, and caused rapid hair-cell degeneration. The work shows that lipid homeostasis is essential for outer hair cell survival and identifies TMEM30B as a new deafness gene.

title: Genomic and multi-omic insights into the heterogeneity of diabetic kidney disease
synopsis: This review argues that diabetic kidney disease is a biologically and clinically varied condition rather than a single microvascular complication of high blood sugar. It stresses the need to distinguish diabetic from non-diabetic kidney disease in people with diabetes. It describes interacting drivers including hyperglycaemia, haemodynamic stress, dyslipidaemia, obesity, inflammation and ancestry-specific genetic risk. The authors summarize how genomic, epigenomic, proteomic and metabolomic signatures, combined with polygenic scores, data-driven clustering and single-cell kidney atlases, are starting to define disease subtypes that classification by filtration rate or albuminuria misses. They also cover remaining challenges in validation, equitable representation and clinical implementation of precision approaches.

title: Overlapping enhancer activity robustly regulates rax expression during ocular development in zebrafish
synopsis: This study asks which noncoding regulatory elements control rax, an early eye field transcription factor needed for optic vesicle formation. In zebrafish, the author identified five new ocular enhancers that drive expression patterns resembling rax at three key stages of eye development. Two of them were characterized in depth and largely overlapped endogenous rax expression. Enhancer deletion lines showed that rax regulation is mostly robust to removing enhancers singly or in combination. Some perturbations, however, produced microphthalmia or anophthalmia. The findings show how redundant enhancers buffer developmental gene expression and suggest noncoding causes of unexplained congenital eye disease.

title: SPACE-Tag Enables High-Throughput Spatial Chromatin Profiling With CUT&Tag
synopsis: This paper presents SPACE-Tag, a spatial CUT&Tag method that converts DNA carrying histone marks into polyadenylated RNA by T7 amplification. This lets chromatin profiling run on standard spatial transcriptomics platforms. In mouse brain, it resolved activating and repressive chromatin states, recovered region-specific regulatory programs, and correlated well with bulk and single-cell reference data. The authors built an aging brain atlas covering five histone modifications plus the transcriptome across the adult lifespan. Fiber tracts showed broad transcriptional decline, often without nearby chromatin changes. The isocortex showed coordinated changes, including an age-increasing H3K4me1 module at super-enhancers linked to genes that regulate neuronal plasticity.

title: Optogenetic induction of TAD boundary pairing promotes gene activity
synopsis: This study asks whether the physical pairing of topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries directly affects transcription of genes inside the domain. The authors built OptoTet, an optogenetic tool that uses light to induce chromatin contacts quickly and in a controlled way, with no mutations or protein depletion needed. Applied to the TADs containing ERRFI1 and MYC, light-induced boundary pairing increased transcriptional bursting of ERRFI1 but had no effect on MYC. It also partly rescued ERRFI1 expression after cohesin depletion. The results suggest that TAD boundary dynamics can regulate genes, but the effect depends on the gene.

title: Robust fine-mapping in the presence of linkage disequilibrium mismatch
synopsis: Fine-mapping from GWAS summary statistics depends on an external linkage disequilibrium reference panel, and a mismatch between that panel and the study population can lower accuracy. The authors developed RSparsePro, a probabilistic graphical model fit by efficient variational inference, to fine-map robustly when such LD mismatch is present. In simulations with different levels of mismatch, it gave credible sets with higher power and coverage than existing methods. In cis-pQTL and complex trait loci, its credible sets were more enriched for likely functional variants and replicated better across studies and reference panels. Applications pointed to relevant variants in drug target genes and possible regulatory mechanisms for LDL cholesterol.

title: Efficient and accurate mixed model association tool for single-cell eQTL analysis
synopsis: Genetic effects on gene expression often differ between cell types, but current single-cell eQTL methods aggregate cells, rely on Gaussian models that fit read counts poorly, or do not scale. SAIGE-QTL is a Poisson mixed model that works directly on single-cell read counts. It adjusts for donor-level and cell-level covariates and for unequal numbers of cells per donor. In simulations and three datasets it was well calibrated, more statistically efficient than pseudobulk approaches, and much cheaper to run than existing single-cell models. In 1.2 million immune cells it found 48.8% more eGenes than pseudobulk analysis. It also supports genome-wide trans-eQTL mapping and rare-variant set tests.

title: Metabolic syndrome, genetic susceptibility, and risk of cardiovascular disease: a prospective study in the UK Biobank
synopsis: This prospective study asks how metabolic syndrome and polygenic risk together relate to cardiovascular disease, using 385,036 UK Biobank participants who had no CVD at recruitment and were followed for a median of 13.6 years. In Cox models, metabolic syndrome was associated with incident CVD (HR 1.39), coronary heart disease (HR 1.64), stroke, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.54) and all-cause mortality (HR 1.25). Risk rose as more syndrome components were present, and associations were stronger in women. Polygenic scores were associated with CVD and coronary heart disease but not heart failure. The gene-by-syndrome interaction findings were exploratory and need validation.

title: Translation of a small upstream open reading frame functions as a rheostat for the regulation of lin-41 by the Let-7 microRNA in Caenorhabditis elegans
synopsis: This study examines how microRNA repression works together with other mechanisms to set the level of a dosage-sensitive developmental target, LIN-41, which the Let-7 microRNA represses in C. elegans. The authors identify a second, independent layer of translational repression in somatic cells, carried by a 5' regulatory exon that contains a seven-amino-acid upstream open reading frame and conserved sequence elements. Genome editing showed that the uORF's amino acid sequence is not required. Instead, translation of the uORF and the structure of the 5'UTR seem to limit initiation at the main lin-41 start codon. Together with Let-7, this multi-tiered control keeps LIN-41 at levels compatible with normal development.

title: Leveraging short and long-read sequencing to comprehensively characterize alternatively polyadenylated and alternatively spliced transcripts
synopsis: This study asks how alternative splicing and alternative polyadenylation diversify transcripts in mantle cell lymphoma, combining short-read and long-read sequencing. The disease-relevant genes SOX11 and ATM expressed transcripts with short 3'UTRs, but short-read data did not show widespread global 3'UTR shortening. Both canonical and non-canonical polyadenylation signals were used, and selected sites were confirmed experimentally. The combined sequencing data allowed splicing events to be classified and splice variants to be identified in genes including PTEN and EZH2. GLS1 expression was validated at the protein level and with GLS1 inhibitors. The work offers an approach for cataloguing transcript isoforms in disease.

title: PRISM-AD quantifies clinical and genetic contributions to cognitive risk prediction
synopsis: This study asks how clinical measures and inherited Alzheimer's disease risk each contribute to individual forecasts of cognitive decline. PRISM-AD combines nonlinear clinical functions with a polygenic risk score term and was developed in 4,435 European-ancestry participants. It was internally validated for progression from cognitively normal to mild cognitive impairment (908 participants) and from MCI to dementia (714) over three and five years. For normal-to-MCI progression, average precision was 0.30 at three years and 0.41 at five years, close to logistic regression, and the polygenic term did not significantly improve prediction. Higher genetic contributions were associated with later AD at similar modeled cognitive risk, a finding that needs independent validation.

title: Reference-Guided De Novo Retrieval of 3D Chromatin Organizational Features with Representation Learning
synopsis: Standard chromatin contact-map callers detect predefined features, so they offer little help when researchers have examples of a pattern but no dedicated method to find it. C-Fetch is a reference-guided retrieval framework that takes example and contrasting patches and ranks candidate Hi-C or Micro-C regions using a representation learned by a weakly KL-regularized 3D autoencoder trained without feature labels. Polycomb-guided queries retrieved contacts enriched for PRC2-associated signals. Loop-guided retrieval improved focal enrichment over full Mustache call sets and selected loops that were more sensitive to cohesin depletion. The approach extended to Region Capture Micro-C and HiChIP and remained stable across replicates and lower sequencing depths.

title: Single-nucleus chromatin accessibility time course of excisional wound repair in rat skin
synopsis: This is a resource paper describing chromatin accessibility across cell types during skin wound healing in rats. Single-nucleus ATAC-seq was performed on unwounded skin and on full-thickness excisional wounds at 1, 2, 5, 10 and 19 days after injury, spanning the inflammatory, proliferative and remodeling phases. Nuclei were isolated with a two-step dissociation protocol, libraries prepared with a DNBelab single-nucleus ATAC kit, and sequencing done on the MGI DNBSEQ-T1. After quality filtering, 37,555 nuclei were retained and assigned to 23 cell types, including fibroblast subpopulations, keratinocytes, vascular endothelial cells, immune cells and skin appendage cells. The dataset supports study of regulatory dynamics in repair and comparison with other wound healing systems.

title: NAD Metabolism Drives CTCF-Cohesin Chromatin Regulation in EBV-Transformed B-Cells
synopsis: This work asks how cellular metabolism sustains the chromatin architecture that Epstein-Barr virus depends on in transformed B cells. EBV-positive B cells show elevated PARP1 activity, which consumes NAD+ and supports the PARP1-CTCF interaction that stabilizes viral chromatin organization and latent gene expression. Using pharmacologic inhibition of NAMPT, the rate-limiting enzyme of the NAD salvage pathway, the authors show that blocking NAD+ production disrupts CTCF-cohesin chromatin folding and loop extrusion, phenocopying PARP1 inhibition, and that efficient infection and transformation require this pathway. NAMPT inhibition also reduced tumor burden in EBV-positive xenografts. The results tie NAD+ homeostasis to three-dimensional genome organization and point to a therapeutic vulnerability in EBV-associated cancers.

title: OmicsNCyc: An Integrated Pipeline for Fast Analysis of Nitrogen Cycle Functional Genes With a Curated Database
synopsis: Profiling microbial nitrogen-cycle genes from sequencing data usually takes several analysis steps with complicated parameters. OmicsNCyc runs the whole process with a single command, from raw metagenomic or metatranscriptomic reads to statistical summaries and plots. It can also analyze individual pathways such as nitrification or denitrification. It relies on NCycTaxDB, a manually curated database of 71 annotated genes in six functional modules. When the tool was applied across diverse environments, read-based profiling picked up many low-abundance genes that assembly-based methods missed. This gives environmental microbiologists an easier and more complete way to study how microbes drive nitrogen cycling.

title: Proteome- and phenome-wide studies identify circulating protein drivers of kidney diseases
synopsis: This study asks which circulating proteins causally influence chronic kidney disease and which could be drug targets. It ran proteome-wide Mendelian randomization using cis-pQTLs for 2807 proteins from four proteogenomic cohorts, tested against four kidney outcomes in up to 464,631 Million Veteran Program participants, with colocalization, replication, nine CKD subtypes, 1020 phecodes, and druggability annotation. Of 93 significant proteins, twelve held up across all sensitivity tests, including UMOD, ANGPTL3 and INHBC. Forty-seven mapped to specific CKD subtypes, seven showed kidney-restricted effects, and 34 were drug targets. This gives a prioritized list of druggable proteins for different causes of CKD.

title: Acceleration of the GrimAge2 epigenetic clock is associated with atherogenic inflammageing and independently predicts acute coronary syndrome incremental to SCORE2-OP and PREVENT
synopsis: This study tested whether epigenetic age acceleration adds predictive value for cardiovascular events in older adults beyond existing risk calculators. Participants aged 60 to 99 were sampled by frailty status from a cohort of 1,400 community-living older adults; five epigenetic clocks were derived from MethylationEPIC blood DNA data, and serum lipoproteins, lipids and glycosylated acetyls were profiled by proton NMR. Among 535 individuals, GrimAge2 acceleration was most strongly linked to cardiometabolic comorbidity and atherogenic inflammageing. Over 4.6 years of follow-up, each additional year of GrimAge2 acceleration raised the hazard of cardiovascular hospitalization by 6% and acute coronary syndrome hospitalization by 11%, and adding it improved the concordance index of SCORE2-OP from 0.693 to 0.734 and of PREVENT from 0.682 to 0.725. It was not associated with all-cause mortality. Methylation-based aging measures may therefore sharpen risk stratification where current calculators perform poorly.

title: The RNA and protein landscapes of mouse brain organoids
synopsis: This study characterizes how closely mouse brain organoids resemble the developing brain in vivo, since they mature faster than human organoids but have been poorly defined molecularly. The authors profiled the transcriptome and proteome of organoids grown for three weeks and compared them with mouse brain tissue. Both layers of data were close to those of a neonatal mouse brain, and the organoids reproduced most of the alternative splicing and alternative polyadenylation events that distinguish neural identity in vivo. Proteomics showed that most mRNA expression changes were reflected at the protein level, and the three-week organoids already contained a complex synaptic protein network including ionotropic and metabotropic glutamate and GABA receptors. This supports their use as a scalable model for neurodevelopmental screening.

title: Association Between Saturated Fat Intake and Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Across the Genetic Spectrum
synopsis: This analysis asks whether inherited susceptibility to high LDL cholesterol modifies the effect of dietary saturated fat. Among 20,940 genotyped Women's Health Initiative participants, saturated fat intake was estimated from food frequency questionnaires and combined with a polygenic score for LDL-C, with LDL-C as the primary outcome and incident atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease as the secondary outcome, assessed by linear and Cox regression with interaction terms and restricted cubic splines. The polygenic score modified the saturated fat-LDL-C association (interaction P = 0.01), with effect sizes rising nonlinearly at the upper end of the score distribution. Among 16,835 women without prevalent disease, 1,582 developed ASCVD over a median 10 years; a 5% isocaloric increase in saturated fat was associated with higher risk only in the top polygenic score quartile (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.08-1.47) versus no association in the lower three quartiles (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.89-1.12; interaction P = 0.006). Dietary advice on saturated fat may matter most for those genetically predisposed to high LDL-C.

title: Chromatin compartment shifting is recurrent and associated with epigenetic reprogramming in prostate cancer
synopsis: This study asks whether large-scale chromatin compartment organization is reorganized during prostate cancer progression. Hi-C, ATAC-seq and transcriptomic data were integrated from 18 clinical samples spanning benign prostatic hyperplasia, primary prostate cancer and castration-resistant prostate cancer, using a computational framework that accounts for copy number variation and tumor purity so that A/B compartments can be called in aneuploid tumors. Recurrent shifts from inactive B to active A compartments were found in both primary and castration-resistant disease, indicating shared reorganization across stages. The switched regions were enriched for prostate cancer-associated expression including the biomarker PCA3, for active histone marks, and for accessible chromatin bound by AR, FOXA1 and HOXB13. Higher-order genome folding thus accompanies the transcriptional and epigenetic rewiring of prostate carcinogenesis.

title: Machine Learning-Based Classification of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Using a Polygenic Risk Score and DNA Methylation
synopsis: This study asks whether combining genetic and epigenetic information improves machine-learning classification of prevalent type 2 diabetes. Models were trained on the Korean Ansan/Ansung cohort (n = 1,318) and validated in an independent Health Examinee cohort (n = 358), using a polygenic risk score computed from external GWAS summary statistics and methylation beta values at diabetes-related CpG sites. Three feature sets were compared: a clinical base set, base plus polygenic score, and base plus score plus methylation. Performance improved stepwise across algorithms, with a linear support vector machine on the full feature set reaching AUROC 0.896 and AUPRC 0.801, and decision curve analysis showing greater net benefit across clinically relevant thresholds. SHAP attributed the largest single-feature contribution to the polygenic score and the largest group-level contribution to methylation, suggesting the two data types carry complementary information.

title: Long-range chromatin interactions nominate candidate susceptibility genes at non-coding PDAC risk loci
synopsis: This study tries to connect non-coding pancreatic cancer risk loci to the genes they act on, which have largely remained unidentified. Starting from 31 significant or suggestive GWAS signals across 26 loci, the authors fine-mapped 1,414 variants and used GWAS Capture-C chromosome conformation capture to find promoters those variants physically contact. The analysis nominated 2,108 transcripts corresponding to 273 unique candidate target genes at 25 loci, with 1,078 fine-mapped variants interacting with 259 genes over a wide range of distances, including contacts exceeding 1 Mb with KRT gene promoters at 17q21.2 and an approximately 280 kb interaction with SOX9 at 17q24.3. At 7p14.1 they found an eQTL for INHBA (rs12701838, NES = 0.22, P = 1.5x10-5) and an approximately 900 kb promoter interaction, and CRISPR inhibition of four fine-mapped variants reduced INHBA expression, indicating a distal enhancer; lower INHBA levels in pancreatic duct epithelial cells were associated with inflammation-related pathways. The work provides a prioritized gene list for functional follow-up of pancreatic cancer risk.

title: Population-scale single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of skeletal muscle reveals extensive context-specific genetic regulation
synopsis: This study asks how genetic variation shapes gene regulation in the individual cell types of human skeletal muscle, a tissue central to metabolic traits and diseases. Using genetic multiplexing, the authors generated single-nucleus chromatin accessibility and RNA profiles from 287 frozen muscle biopsies, identifying 13 cell types. They mapped more than 7,000 eQTLs and more than 100,000 chromatin accessibility QTLs, including many with cell-type-specific effects. Nearly 3,500 GWAS signals across 38 traits colocalized with these QTLs, mostly in a cell-specific way and more often with chromatin accessibility than with expression. This suggests population-scale chromatin profiling is important for interpreting GWAS loci.

title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
synopsis: This study asks how common and rare genetic variants affect gene expression in individual immune cell types. It combines single-cell RNA sequencing of more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types with whole-genome sequencing from 1,925 individuals. A method that models single cells directly, rather than pseudobulk counts, gives extra power. Common regulatory variants were found for 83% of 21,404 tested genes, and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47%. About half of the effects appeared in only one or a few cell types. Linking these results to disease associations suggests molecular mechanisms and extends single-cell eQTL mapping to rare variation.

title: Fine-tuning of polygenic score to local data improves risk prediction and clinical implementation
synopsis: Polygenic risk scores often transfer poorly across populations and cohorts, which limits their clinical use. This study proposes a simple post hoc framework that combines several published scores for a disease and reweights them with machine learning to fit a local target cohort. Applied to coronary artery disease, breast cancer and prostate cancer in the MGB Biobank, local optimization raised C-statistics by an average of 19.8%, 8.3% and 9.4%, respectively. It also identified more cases in the high-risk group than the best single published score, for example 27.7% versus 17.8% for coronary disease. The approach requires no new GWAS and could help health systems adopt polygenic scores more fairly.

title: Genome-wide LD scores enable robust heritability and genetic correlation estimation from summary statistics across genetic ancestries
synopsis: Estimating heritability and genetic correlation from GWAS summary statistics is difficult in structured and admixed populations, partly because long-range linkage disequilibrium is hard to model. The authors present SUMMIT, which combines genome-wide LD scores, estimated efficiently with random projections, with summary statistics. In UK Biobank simulations of European, South Asian and admixed African-European cohorts, SUMMIT was more accurate and less biased than earlier methods, with the largest gains outside Europeans. Across 40 traits its heritability estimates were broadly consistent across ancestries and closer to sequencing-based estimates. It found more significant genetic correlations in non-European groups, and these generally matched European patterns, suggesting pleiotropy is largely shared across ancestries.

title: Functional architecture of rare protein coding variation across 786,871 exomes
synopsis: This study asks how well protein structural features and predicted functional scores explain the effects of rare coding variants on complex traits. The authors introduce the Kernel Allelic Series Model, which combines 35 annotations to describe how allelic effects covary within a gene. They apply it to exomes from 786,871 UK Biobank and All of Us participants across 26 traits. Rare missense heritability is estimated at 1.27% to 1.83%, above loss-of-function heritability (0.87%) and well above earlier missense burden estimates. AlphaMissense was the most enriched single predictor, but a composite score doubled its enrichment. Residues that are close in 3D structure but distant in sequence showed correlated effects, pointing to testable functional hypotheses.

title: Hidden Monogenic Diagnoses in Young-Onset Dialysis After Exclusion of Clinically Apparent Polycystic Kidney Disease
synopsis: This study asks whether genome sequencing finds missed monogenic diagnoses in people who started dialysis by age 50, after those with clinically apparent polycystic kidney disease were excluded. Among Japanese dialysis patients, 108 volunteers underwent whole-genome sequencing covering 465 candidate genes, mitochondrial DNA and structural variants. Diagnoses were found in 10 of 108 (9.3%), nine supported by pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants. They spanned renal and systemic or metabolic disorders and appeared across labels such as diabetic kidney disease and nephrosclerosis. Because enrollment was nonrandom and sequencing coverage varied, the results may not generalize, but they suggest clinical labels often hide genetic causes.

title: Genomic foundation models do not yet boost common variant discovery beyond standard functional annotations
synopsis: This study tests whether annotations derived from genomic foundation models improve the discovery of common-variant GWAS loci. Using a functionally informed false discovery rate framework across 27 UK Biobank traits, the authors compared standard baselineLD annotations with annotations from AlphaGenome, Borzoi and the language model GPN-Star. GPN-Star reduced locus discovery compared with a standard GWAS. AlphaGenome and Borzoi increased discovery (medians 1.8% and 3.8%), but by less than baselineLD (5.1%). Adding the model-based annotations to baselineLD gave essentially no further gain. This suggests current foundation models mostly capture information already in standard annotations for common-variant discovery.

title: Sequence-based variant-effect predictions reveal trait-specific regulatory-layer profiles of complex-trait heritability
synopsis: This study asks whether the regulatory layer most informative for a trait's heritability differs between traits within the same tissue. Measured annotations for different layers usually come from different samples, which makes direct comparison hard. The authors instead used AlphaGenome predictions, grouped into 12 lineages and six regulatory layers, and partitioned the heritability of 11 traits with stratified LD score regression. The most informative layer differed between traits. Predicted chromatin accessibility was most informative for height and bone density, while predicted transcription initiation was most informative for Alzheimer's disease, brain traits and cholesterol. These patterns held in sensitivity analyses and in pre-specified related traits, offering hypotheses about the regulatory basis of complex traits.

title: The landscape of polygenic score prediction accuracy and transportability across the phenome in ancestrally diverse populations
synopsis: This study asks how well existing polygenic scores predict traits across the phenome and how well they transfer between ancestry groups. The authors evaluated 3,994 published scores in the ancestrally diverse CCPM biobank and found many trait-specific and cross-trait associations. Predictive effects often differed between ancestry groups, which raises equity concerns for applying the scores. Accuracy and portability also depended on whether a score was used as a continuous value or a threshold. Hierarchical mixed models identified score-development, genomic and cohort factors linked to better performance, which could guide the design of more portable scores for research and clinical use.

title: A common germline 3' UTR variant controls DDIT4 translation efficiency and stress responses in cancer cells
synopsis: This study asks how common germline variants can change protein output by altering how efficiently mRNAs are translated, a class of effects that existing variant screens rarely capture. The authors built and validated a pipeline that compares total and polysome-bound mRNA to find translation-associated SNPs, meaning variants enriched on ribosomes in an allele-specific way without any change in mRNA levels. They focused on rs1053639 in the 3' UTR of DDIT4, a negative regulator of mTORC1. The two alleles bind the RNA-binding protein RBMX differently, which changes where the mRNA sits in the cell, how well it is translated, mTORC1 repression under stress, autophagy, cell fitness and drug response. Genotype at this variant was also associated with clinical outcome in colorectal cancer.

title: Impact of selection bias on the association of kidney function polygenic scores with CKD progression in populations with CKD
source: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association
synopsis: This study asks whether polygenic scores for low eGFR predict CKD progression the same way in the general population as in people who already have CKD. Using a FinnGen-derived score, the authors analyzed 107,536 UK Biobank participants and 6,846 participants from the SHARP, CRIC and EMPA-KIDNEY cohorts. In UK Biobank, a high score predicted lower eGFR, faster decline and higher progression risk (HR 1.36). In the CKD cohorts, the same score was linked to lower progression risk (HR 0.76), a reversal consistent with collider bias. Applying polygenic scores in groups selected for having a disease can therefore give misleading conclusions.

title: Kidzoi Enables Cell-Type-Specific Regulatory Activity and Variant Effect Prediction in Kidney
synopsis: Sequence-to-function deep learning models predict regulatory activity from DNA, but each is limited to the cell types it was trained on, and training a new one from scratch is costly. This work builds Kidzoi by fine-tuning the pretrained Borzoi model on single-nucleus chromatin accessibility data from human kidney. Kidzoi predicts accessibility for specific kidney cell types and improves regulatory variant effect prediction in proximal tubule cells by up to 23% in AUROC over existing models. It also prioritizes fine-mapped GWAS variants for eGFR and indicates which cell types they act in. Ablation experiments show that 32–64 kbp of local sequence context captures most of the predictive signal, and a multi-task model matches the single-task models at much lower computational cost.

title: A heritability-optimized method for functional prioritization of rare coding variants in complex traits
synopsis: Sequencing studies have found millions of rare missense variants, but it remains hard to tell which ones affect complex traits. This paper introduces RovHer, which scores each rare variant by its probability of being functional, defined as its contribution to trait heritability. The scores are learned from exome-wide association statistics on about 4.9 million rare variants, using multivariate adaptive regression splines to combine 75 variant- and gene-level features. Across 21 UK Biobank traits, the top 1% of prioritized missense variants explained on average 16.1% of rare-variant heritability, about ten times the share captured by seven alternative methods. The scores do not depend on allele frequency, replicate in a multi-ancestry sample, and identify high-risk carriers for 17 monogenic gene-trait pairs.

title: Evolution, application and clinical significance of profiling chromatin interactions at a genome-wide scale
synopsis: This review follows how methods for mapping where proteins bind chromatin have developed, from classical biochemical footprinting to single-cell multi-omic integration. It argues that specific chromatin-protein interactions may act as key anchors organizing three-dimensional genome architecture. The authors describe how pairing single-cell multi-omics with functional perturbation can move beyond correlation. This can establish causal links between chromatin architecture, epigenetic marks and transcriptional output. They also propose a framework they call Sentinel Genomics, which would use these layered chromatin data to predict disease course and treatment response before symptoms appear. The review is mainly useful as an overview of the field's methods.

title: vartracker: an end-to-end tool for pathogen longitudinal variant analysis and visualization
synopsis: Longitudinal sequencing of pathogens during acute and chronic infections can show within-host evolution, but putting ordered samples into a coherent framework is tedious and error-prone. vartracker accepts raw reads, aligned BAM files or VCF files with coverage, and processes reads and BAM files through an integrated Snakemake workflow. It normalizes and annotates variants and tracks them across timepoints. Each variant is classified as original or newly emerging and as transient or persistent. Outputs include a documented results table, provenance metadata, static figures and an interactive heatmap, and SARS-CoV-2 mutations are linked to published literature. The tool comes with SARS-CoV-2 reference files but works for any pathogen given suitable reference data, as shown with SARS-CoV-2 and RSV-A datasets.

title: GeneSIS: enhancing transferability of polygenic scores with variant-level gene-by-sex interaction effects
synopsis: Polygenic scores often lose accuracy when applied to ancestry groups other than the one they were trained in. This study asks whether modeling context-dependent effects, here gene-by-sex interactions, can help. GeneSIS jointly models additive and sex-interaction effects of individual variants from individual-level data, applied to 406,659 UK Biobank participants, including admixed individuals, with 1.3 million variants and 99 traits. About 8% of selected variables captured gene-by-sex effects, which sex-stratified analyses confirmed. Including these effects improved prediction for 32 traits in non-European individuals, including a 3.7-fold gain for hip circumference in Africans. The models also suggest biological hypotheses, such as sex-dependent pleiotropic effects of a GCKR variant on body measurements and menopause.

title: All of Us diversity and scale yield context-dependent improvements in polygenic prediction
synopsis: This study asks how the diversity and scale of the All of Us program affect polygenic risk score accuracy across ancestries. Using 245,388 whole genomes from All of Us together with UK Biobank data, the authors built multi-ancestry scores for 32 traits and examined how ancestry, method and genetic architecture shape their performance. The added diversity improved accuracy for several traits, especially in under-represented groups. However, combining both biobanks to maximize sample size was not always best: for less polygenic traits, training on All of Us alone performed best in participants of African ancestry. Accuracy fell linearly as individuals' ancestry diverged from the discovery GWAS, and multi-ancestry training reduced this decline.

title: SPLENDID incorporates continuous genetic ancestry in biobank-scale data to improve polygenic risk prediction across diverse populations
synopsis: Multi-ancestry polygenic risk methods usually require each individual to be assigned to an ancestry group, which is awkward in clinical settings and fits admixed people poorly. SPLENDID is a penalized regression framework for biobank-scale individual-level data that treats genetic ancestry as a continuum and produces a single prediction model without ancestry labels. In simulations and in data from All of Us (224,364 participants) and UK Biobank (340,140), it predicted more accurately than existing methods, with the largest gains in non-European and admixed individuals. This offers a practical route to polygenic risk prediction that works more equitably across diverse populations.

title: Coding, modifier, and regulatory effects shape circulating APOL1 levels
synopsis: This study asks how APOL1 genotypes and regulatory variants shape circulating APOL1 protein levels, which may link the kidney-risk variants G1 and G2 to disease. It analyzed Olink APOL1 measurements in 43,587 UK Biobank participants, focusing on people with recent sub-Saharan African ancestry, and mapped protein QTLs and cis-acting variants across the locus. G1, G2 and E150K changed APOL1 levels in a dose-dependent way, with G2 having the largest effect. Levels stayed higher in Black participants after accounting for genotype, and several independent cis-regulatory variants also contributed. The results show that G1 and G2 have distinct molecular effects and that regulatory variation may explain differences between ancestry groups.

title: Beyond exons: Linking noncoding heritability and polygenicity across complex human traits and disorders
synopsis: This study asks how a trait's polygenicity relates to where its SNP heritability lies across functional regions of the genome. Using a MiXeR-based framework, the authors partitioned heritability across 74 annotations for 34 complex traits and introduced a likelihood-based score for each annotation's contribution. Exons explained a minority of heritability, falling from an average of 22% in less polygenic diseases and biomarkers to 13% in highly polygenic psychiatric and cognitive traits. Intergenic shares showed the opposite trend, while intronic shares stayed stable. Highly polygenic traits drew more on conservation and variant-effect annotations, whereas less polygenic traits drew more on promoter, transcription and chromatin annotations, suggesting a shift from gene-proximal to dispersed regulatory architectures.

title: Systematic benchmarking of multi-ancestry fine-mapping under variant heterogeneity and LD mismatch
synopsis: Multi-ancestry GWAS can sharpen fine-mapping by exploiting differences in linkage disequilibrium between populations, but effect heterogeneity, population-specific variants and LD mismatch complicate this. This study benchmarks nine methods, including joint models of cross-ancestry LD and effect sharing as well as approaches that combine ancestry-specific results afterward. It uses realistic simulations based on UK Biobank genotypes and validation in All of Us. Joint models gave better power and resolution for causal variants shared across populations, while post-hoc integration recovered population-specific variants more reliably. All methods lost power when GWAS summary statistics and LD references were mismatched. The authors propose a decision strategy that chooses a method locus by locus, based on evidence of ancestry-specific variants.

title: Whole-exome sequencing in individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder and chronic tic disorders identifies 36 large-effect risk genes
lab: the Tourette International Collaborative Genetics (TIC Genetics)
synopsis: This study asks which rare coding mutations confer large risk for obsessive-compulsive disorder and chronic tic disorders, where only four high-confidence genes were previously known. Whole-exome sequencing of 3,964 affected individuals, including 2,418 trios, showed an excess of de novo and rare protein-damaging mutations in cases and identified 36 high-confidence risk genes at FDR below 0.1. Four of these overlap OCD GWAS loci, and many are shared with other neurodevelopmental conditions. Expression and network analyses point to convergence in the cerebellum, cortex and striatum, which gives a starting point for work on mechanisms and treatment targets.

title: Efficient genome-wide mapping of reproducible, context-dependent eQTLs at single-cell resolution
synopsis: Most single-cell eQTL studies pseudobulk cells, which can hide regulatory effects that change with cell state. The authors present Dynema, which fits a Poisson model with cluster-robust variance estimators to account for correlation among cells from the same individual, mapping context-dependent and context-independent eQTLs genome-wide at true single-cell resolution. The method is statistically calibrated and fast enough for large datasets. In two independent T cell datasets it found reproducible cell-state-dependent eQTLs, some missed by pseudobulking and many independent of lead eQTLs. TSPAN32 and other autoimmune loci colocalized with these dynamic effects, linking disease alleles to specific cell states.

title: Deciphering the mechanisms of transcriptome remodeling in residual HCC recurrence post-radiofrequency ablation via long-read sequencing
synopsis: This study asks how residual hepatocellular carcinoma survives and recurs after insufficient radiofrequency ablation. Nanopore long-read RNA sequencing was applied to paired tumor and adjacent tissue from five patients, before and after ablation, to assess gene expression, differential transcript usage and alternative polyadenylation. Residual tumor cells kept high expression of proliferation and anti-apoptosis genes such as CDK1 and BIRC5, showed isoform switching in DNA repair genes, and had a reshaped polyadenylation landscape, with 3'UTR changes in oncogenes such as SAE1 and SPINK1. Together these suggest coordinated transcriptome adaptation behind recurrence and give candidate targets, though the small cohort means functional validation is still needed.

title: Cell-type-specific eQTLs underlie the genetic architecture of complex traits
synopsis: Known eQTLs explain surprisingly little of complex trait heritability, and this study tests whether cell-type-specific eQTLs help close that gap. A variance component model was applied to population-scale single-cell RNA-seq of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from the OneK1K cohort. Cell-type-specific eQTLs, but not shared ones, were enriched for complex trait heritability, and specificity tracked with selective constraint, enhancer complexity and network connectivity. About 60% of trans eQTLs were cell-type-specific, compared with about 30% of cis eQTLs. The findings replicated in a second dataset and were consistent across ancestries, which supports cell-type specificity as a key missing layer between variants and traits.

title: Methylation profile scores in child and adolescent health: a practical guide
synopsis: This review is a practical guide to methylation profile scores, which combine many DNA methylation sites into one value per individual, with a focus on children and adolescents, who have been little studied. It covers five uses: proxies for hard-to-measure exposures such as prenatal smoking, proxies for physiological processes such as inflammation, risk stratification, diagnosis of rare Mendelian syndromes and paediatric brain tumours, and treatment monitoring. It explains why developmental context makes paediatric scores differ from adult ones and gives criteria for judging studies critically. The authors conclude that, with a few exceptions, these scores are still early-stage research tools rather than clinical ones.

title: Mapping the NFYA 3'UTR landscape identifies alternative polyadenylation as a targetable vulnerability in prostate cancer
source: Journal of experimental & clinical cancer research : CR
synopsis: This study asks whether alternative polyadenylation of NFYA, the regulatory subunit of the oncogenic transcription factor NF-Y, drives prostate cancer. Bulk, single-cell and 3'-end RNA-seq from cell lines and patients identified four functional 3'UTR isoforms and widespread 3'UTR shortening in tumors, which correlated with grade, metastasis, higher NF-YA protein and faster proliferation. Longer 3'UTRs lowered NF-YA through reduced mRNA stability and translation and through nuclear retention, not through microRNA repression. Forcing lengthening with CRISPR deletion or antisense oligonucleotides reduced aggressive traits in vitro and in vivo. This offers proof of concept for gene-specific therapies that target polyadenylation.

title: Novel prediabetes subtypes and genetic variants predict differential risk of progression to type 2 diabetes: a data-driven cohort analysis
synopsis: This study asks whether data-driven subtypes of prediabetes, combined with genetics, predict progression to type 2 diabetes. In 1,016 individuals with prediabetes, k-prototypes clustering on clinical and metabolic variables found four subtypes, ranging from low-risk to metabolic syndrome. Compared with controls, the metabolic syndrome cluster had about 24-fold higher hazard (58.1 cases per 1,000 person-years) and the low-risk cluster about 3.35-fold. Variants in THADA, CDKN2B, VPS26A and SLC30A8 showed cluster-specific effects, and a polygenic risk score refined prediction, especially within the low-risk cluster. The results support prevention tailored to combined phenotypic and genetic risk.

title: Integrated Analysis of Skeletal Muscle Transcriptional Networks Characterizes Dysregulation in Pathways and Trait-Associated Regulatory Regions in Type 2 Diabetes
synopsis: This study asks how skeletal muscle gene regulation is disrupted in type 2 diabetes and what drives these changes. Co-expression network analysis of 301 muscle biopsies from people with and without diabetes found 56 modules, annotated using single-nucleus RNA-seq cell type signatures and pathway enrichment. Dysregulated pathways included mitochondrial function and mRNA processing in muscle fibers, vascularization in endothelial cells, and inflammation in immune cells. Hub gene and transcription factor analyses nominated drivers such as SIRT1, ATF2, CLEC14A and IRF8. Integration with single-nucleus ATAC-seq connected muscle fiber and endothelial modules to diabetes and related trait GWAS signals.

title: Risk factor control and type 2 diabetes event risks in people with high genetic susceptibility to diabetes
synopsis: This study asks whether controlling modifiable risk factors can offset the excess type 2 diabetes risk carried by people with high genetic susceptibility, and whether prediabetes weakens that benefit. Using 382,313 UK Biobank participants, the authors split people by the median of a T2D polygenic risk score and used Cox models to relate diabetes onset to how many of six factors were well controlled: not smoking, physical activity, diet, sleep, BMI and blood pressure. Among high-genetic-risk participants, those who controlled all six had lower incidence than low-genetic-risk participants (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.68-0.92). People with prediabetes, however, stayed at higher risk even with all six controlled. Lifestyle can therefore compensate for genetic risk but not fully for existing dysglycemia.

title: Genetic determinants of serum creatinine and cystatin C independent of kidney function generate bias in filtration markers
synopsis: This study asks how much genetic variation affects serum creatinine and cystatin C through routes unrelated to kidney filtration, which would bias estimated GFR. Using GWAS in about 470,000 UK Biobank participants, the authors applied strict criteria plus colocalization to separate biomarker-specific loci from GFR loci, then built polygenic scores to measure the resulting bias. They found 52 creatinine-specific and 48 cystatin C-specific loci, pointing to muscle and energy metabolism for creatinine and to inflammation and immune pathways for cystatin C. Mean individual genetic bias was 3.8 mL/min/1.73m2 for creatinine-based eGFR and 0.6 for cystatin C-based eGFR, and this bias was linked to measured-GFR discrepancies in two independent cohorts. The work quantifies a hidden genetic source of error in kidney function estimates.

title: Leukocyte DNA methylation-based signatures for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk prediction in the Million Veteran Program
synopsis: This study tests whether leukocyte DNA methylation adds to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease prediction beyond standard clinical risk factors. In 44,674 Million Veteran Program participants, an epigenome-wide association study in people who already had ASCVD guided CpG selection. Elastic net methylation risk scores were then trained and tested in 17,114 people free of disease, of whom 2,789 developed ASCVD over a median 7.4 years. Each of three scores carried a hazard ratio of roughly 2 per standard deviation. They gave modest discrimination gains (concordance gain about 0.013-0.016) and improved reclassification, mainly by correctly moving non-cases to lower risk, while staying calibrated. Methylation therefore offers a small but real increment for ASCVD risk assessment.

title: Scalable context-dependent single-cell eQTL mapping reveals disease-relevant regulatory variation beyond static models
synopsis: Standard eQTL mapping explains only part of GWAS loci, possibly because regulatory effects change with cell state and environment. The authors present CASTIE, a Poisson mixed model fitted directly to sparse single-cell counts that tests genotype-by-context interactions genome-wide without first requiring a static eQTL. In 1.2 million blood cells from 982 OneK1K donors, it found 3,155 context-dependent eQTLs, including 2,022 eGenes with no detectable static effect. These produced 374 colocalizations across 94 traits at 270 loci, and static eQTLs missed 197 of those loci. In stimulated adipose-derived stem cells, CASTIE found 36-92% more eGenes. Modeling cellular context thus links more disease loci to specific genes and cell states.

title: SuSiNE: Genetic fine-mapping with signed functional priors and multi-basin ensembling
synopsis: This work examines where the widely used SuSiE fine-mapping method fails and proposes SuSiNE, an extension that adds signed functional annotations, such as AI sequence-model predictions, as a prior mean on effects. Conjugacy, credible sets and summary-statistic use are preserved. The authors show that the routine purity-filtering step often discards real signal, and they pair the model with grid-based ensembling across several variational optima. In simulations calibrated to AlphaGenome eQTL benchmarks, AUPRC for the largest causal variants rose from 0.247 to 0.313, and recall at 75% precision rose from 11.9% to 19.3%. Gains held across annotation quality levels but reversed under strong spurious alignment. In a GTEx lung case study using reference LD, SuSiNE changed which variants received high posterior inclusion probability at 7 of 20 loci.

title: The CTCF Paralog BORIS Contributes to the Ovarian Cancer Transcriptional Program by Relaxing CTCF-mediated 3D Genome Organization
synopsis: This study asks how BORIS (CTCFL), a germ cell-specific paralog of CTCF that is aberrantly switched on in cancers, reshapes chromatin in ovarian cancer cells. By removing BORIS chromatin binding and profiling transcription, CTCF and cohesin occupancy, histone marks, accessibility and 3D genome contacts, the authors show that BORIS maintains its own transcriptional program. That program acts on long-range clusters of neighboring genes, including hormonally regulated gene families. Losing BORIS increases TAD insulation, sharpens A/B compartment separation, strengthens chromatin loops and compacts chromatin. BORIS therefore appears to drive transcriptional reprogramming by weakening CTCF-mediated insulation, which makes it a candidate biomarker and therapeutic target in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.

title: Polygenic risk-informed white matter integrity improves deep learning-based prediction of youth depression
synopsis: This study asks whether combining genetic risk with brain imaging improves prediction of youth depression. Polygenic risk scores were used to pretrain a 3D convolutional neural network on white matter diffusion maps (track-weighted fractional anisotropy) from 4,741 children aged 9-10 in the ABCD Study. The network was then fine-tuned on held-out data for prediction at baseline and two years later. It predicted depression and suicidality with AUCs of 0.61-0.66, beating genetics-only and imaging-only models, and its most informative features were tracts such as the superior longitudinal fasciculus, cingulum and corpus callosum. It reached an AUC of 0.67 in an independent Korean youth sample, which supports cross-ancestry use of combined genetic and imaging models, though accuracy remains modest.

title: Stress-Related Methylation Risk Scores Predict Coronary Heart Disease
synopsis: This study asks whether DNA methylation helps explain the link between psychosocial stress and coronary heart disease in postmenopausal women. An epigenome-wide association study of stressful life events in 3,857 Women's Health Initiative participants found 841 FDR-significant CpGs, 13 of them Bonferroni-significant, including sites near TNF and ALDH2. Methylation risk scores built from these sites predicted incident CHD (HR 1.33-1.37) and mediated about 17% of the stress-CHD association. In the Jackson Heart Study and MESA, the 13-site score replicated (HR 1.34), while the 841-site score was only suggestive. Cell-type deconvolution placed most predictive sites in monocytes, pointing to monocyte epigenetic regulation as a possible mechanism.

title: Uromodulin T62P variant causes kidney tubular stress and injury modulated by age and polygenic risk
synopsis: This study asks why a relatively common UMOD missense variant, T62P, shows variable penetrance for kidney disease, testing age and polygenic risk as modifiers. Genotype and phenotype data from 882,306 individuals in UK Biobank, with validation in All of Us and MyCode, were combined with experiments in kidney tubular cells expressing wild-type or mutant uromodulin. T62P was reproducibly associated with age-dependent CKD risk, caused defective uromodulin maturation with endoplasmic reticulum retention and stress, and interacted with a genome-wide polygenic score, with carriers in the top quintile having an odds ratio of 5.17 versus the population average. The results show how background polygenic risk shapes the penetrance of an intermediate-effect variant.

title: External validation of four breast cancer risk prediction models for personalized screening in a prospective Dutch screening cohort
synopsis: This study externally validates four breast cancer risk models (Gail, BCSC, BOADICEA, IBIS) for use in risk-based screening. Five-year risk was predicted for 38,767 women in a prospective Dutch screening cohort using questionnaire data and mammographic density without genetic information, with cancers ascertained through registry linkage. Among 609 cancers over a median 4.3 years, Gail performed poorly (C-index 0.56), while the other three models had modest discrimination (C-index 0.60-0.61). BCSC and BOADICEA were well calibrated, and IBIS overpredicted risk. These results suggest that non-genetic traditional models are not accurate enough for nationwide personalized screening and that better models are needed.

title: ELF3 links kidney function GWAS loci to maladaptive epithelial inflammation
synopsis: This work identifies the effector gene behind a kidney function GWAS locus and its disease mechanism. Using mouse injury models, human CKD tissue, conditional knockout mice and spatial transcriptomics, it shows that ELF3 is induced in injured proximal tubule cells, where it marks transitional states enriched for inflammatory programs. Deleting Elf3 after injury reduced the accumulation of injured tubule cells, cytokine production and immune recruitment. ELF3 directly activated noncanonical NF-κB pathway genes and was needed for NFκB2 nuclear translocation. In human kidneys, ELF3 expression tracked epithelial inflammation and loss of kidney function, linking GWAS signal to mechanism and nominating ELF3 as a therapeutic target in CKD.

title: Impact of African-enriched GATM regulatory variants on creatinine-derived estimated glomerular filtration rate
synopsis: This study asks whether African-enriched variation at GATM, which encodes the rate-limiting enzyme of creatine synthesis, biases creatinine-based estimates of kidney function. It combines whole-genome sequencing from Ugandan and South African cohorts with eQTL, metabolomic and iohexol-measured GFR data, plus African American participants from the Million Veteran Program. Variants at about 50% frequency in Africans explained 1.0-1.7% of eGFRCr variance and lowered eGFRCr by about 2 ml/min/1.73 m2 per allele by increasing creatine synthesis. They showed no association with measured GFR or cystatin C-based eGFR. In African Americans they raised the odds of a creatinine-based CKD diagnosis but not of end-stage disease, indicating biomarker bias rather than true kidney dysfunction.

title: PRANA: A Deep Learning Method for Adapting Polygenic Risk Scores to Diverse Ethnic Groups
synopsis: This work tackles the reduced accuracy of European-derived polygenic risk scores in other ancestries when large target-population GWAS are not available. It introduces PRANA, a deep learning framework that adapts pre-trained European PRS models using modestly sized cohorts from the target population. Across seven complex traits in South Asian, East Asian and Ashkenazi Jewish populations, including small East Asian subpopulations, PRANA mostly improved baseline effect sizes and Nagelkerke R2 by 5-20%. In most cases it also outperformed existing cross-ancestry multi-PRS methods. This offers a practical route to more equitable genomic risk prediction for underrepresented groups.

title: Scalable penalized regression boosts accuracy and computational efficiency for single- and cross-ancestry polygenic prediction
synopsis: This paper addresses the trade-off between adaptive shrinkage and computational cost in polygenic scores, along with the poor transfer of scores beyond European ancestry. It proposes SSL, a spike-and-slab LASSO ensemble for single-ancestry prediction, and pSSL, which adds European GWAS priors for cross-ancestry prediction. Across simulations and 32 traits in UK Biobank and the East Asian Dongfeng-Tongji cohort, SSL was best for 90.6% and 84.4% of traits, with average R2 gains of 7.8% and 10.4% over PRS-CS. pSSL ranked first for 71.9% of traits, with a 12.3% gain over PRS-CSx. Both methods ran in under a third of the time of Bayesian approaches, making accurate scores more practical for diverse populations.

title: A Cross-Species Systems Genetics Framework Identifies Causal Genes in Diabetic Nephropathy
synopsis: This study looks for genes that control susceptibility to diabetic nephropathy, whose genetic architecture remains poorly understood. Using a mouse model, the authors mapped QTLs for albuminuria, glomerulosclerosis and macrophage infiltration, and prioritized candidates with eQTL and pQTL mapping guided by single-cell transcriptomics and with cell-type-specific co-expression networks. They identified 192 candidate genes for albuminuria; 27% had prior genetic associations and 40% were validated in a human diabetic cohort. Twelve genes fell in a podocyte network enriched for human GWAS signals, and knockdown in Drosophila confirmed roles for DCAF6 and ZNRF2. Combining species in this way can reveal new targets for risk prediction and treatment.

title: Improved heritability partitioning and enrichment analyses using summary statistics with graphREML
synopsis: This paper seeks a more powerful alternative to stratified LD score regression for partitioning heritability across functional annotations using GWAS summary statistics. It introduces graphREML, a likelihood-based method that becomes computationally tractable through sparse linkage disequilibrium graphical models. In simulations and many real traits, its enrichment estimates agreed with S-LDSC on average, suggesting both are unbiased. However, graphREML detected 2.5 times more significant trait-annotation enrichments. It also flexibly models how annotations relate to per-SNP heritability and gives well-calibrated estimates, improving functional interpretation of genetic architecture.

title: Multiple instance fine-mapping: Predicting causal regulatory variants with a deep sequence model
synopsis: This study addresses the lack of ground-truth labels for training models that predict causal regulatory variants. It proposes Multiple Instance Fine-mapping (MIFM), a multiple instance learning objective that groups putatively causal variants by LD scores so a deep classifier can be trained on DNA sequence using over 13,000 aggregated GWAS. Polygenic risk scores built from variants prioritized by MIFM transferred better across ancestries. The method also helped separate effect sizes of highly correlated variants for GWAS fine-mapping. This shows how weak supervision from GWAS can train sequence models for causal variant prioritization.

title: Blood DNA methylation and breast cancer risk: a prospective nested case-control study
synopsis: This study asks whether DNA methylation in whole blood, measured before diagnosis, can predict later breast cancer risk. Within Sweden's mammography screening programme, it profiled blood methylation with the EPIC array in 377 women who later developed breast cancer and 378 age-matched controls. CpG sites were discovered in Stockholm and validated in Skåne. Of 87 sites found in Stockholm, 22 validated, and the sites were combined into a methylation risk score. The signature was significantly associated with breast cancer risk and looked most useful for 3-5-year risk. Blood methylation could add to existing risk models, but it needs further validation and testing for clinical use.

title: Atlas of glomerular disease-specific genetic effects on blood transcriptome
synopsis: This study asks how genetic variants affect the blood transcriptome in five primary glomerular diseases. It combined whole-genome sequencing with blood RNA sequencing in 1,822 CureGN participants and mapped expression, splicing and RNA-editing QTLs within each disease and across all of them. It found 16,068 eGenes, 4,644 sGenes and 4,611 edQTLs. About 90% of signals were shared between at least two diseases and 5-10% were disease-specific. The cross-disease maps found thousands of signals absent from GTEx, along with QTLs modified by age or disease severity. Combining the maps with GWAS nominated new candidate genes for each disease, making this a resource for kidney disease gene discovery.

title: Live imaging and multimodal profiling reveal transdifferentiation of a cochlear supporting cell subpopulation upon Notch inhibition
synopsis: This study asks why cochlear supporting cells rarely turn into hair cells, a limit that makes hair cell loss and hearing loss permanent. It combined live imaging with single-cell multiomics in neonatal mouse cochlear explants treated with a Notch inhibitor. Notch inhibition broadly silenced supporting cell genes, but only a rare subpopulation of Deiters' cells began turning into hair cells. These cells remodelled their transcription and enhancers together, linking epigenetic priming to changes in cell shape. Other supporting cells did not respond, even though Notch targets went down robustly. The work defines an early transitional state and points to which cells could be targeted for regeneration.

title: Population-scale genomics reveals divergent pathogenicity of variant classes across paralogous collagen IV genes
synopsis: This study asks whether the same classes of variants are equally harmful in COL4A3 and COL4A4, two paralogous collagen IV genes. It used whole-genome sequencing from about 500,000 UK Biobank participants, with replication in about 414,000 from All of Us. Variant-level, gene-collapsing and phenome-wide analyses covered haematuria, proteinuria and chronic kidney disease. It found 64 COL4A3 and 92 COL4A4 rare variants associated with haematuria or proteinuria. Glycine substitutions carried similar risk in both genes, but truncating and NC1-domain missense variants were much less harmful in COL4A3. The results argue that variant interpretation and genetic counselling should take the specific gene into account.

title: Distinct and shared genetics of kidney filtration function versus albuminuria revealed by multi-trait GWAS
synopsis: This study asks how far the genetics of kidney filtration function (eGFR) and albuminuria (UACR) overlap, since both define chronic kidney disease. A multi-trait GWAS of about one million individuals found 812 signals, and multi-trait fine-mapping narrowed down likely causal variants. Of 333 signals classified as filtration or albuminuria signals, only 11 overlapped. The shared signals had concordant effects that were driven mainly by eGFR and were independent of HbA1c and blood pressure. They pointed to filtration area and sodium-related intraglomerular pressure. Variants linked to fluid intake affected UACR without causing albumin leakage. Overall, the two traits have largely separate genetic architectures.

title: MIXPRS enables multi-population and multi-method polygenic risk scores using summary statistics
synopsis: Many methods build polygenic risk scores across ancestries, but none is best in every setting, and combining them usually needs individual-level tuning data. This paper presents MIXPRS, which combines several multi-population PRS methods using only GWAS summary statistics, based on the data fission approach. It prunes SNPs to reduce linkage disequilibrium mismatch and estimates combination weights with non-negative least squares. In simulations and real data covering up to 26 traits, MIXPRS consistently predicted better than existing methods. An extension, MIXPRS+, adds functional annotations and clinical PRSs and gives further gains in non-European populations. This could improve risk prediction for underrepresented groups.

title: Cell-type-resolved genetic variation shapes inflammatory bowel disease risk
synopsis: Most risk variants for inflammatory bowel disease lie in non-coding regions, which makes it hard to tell which genes and cell types they act through. This study mapped cis-eQTLs across 2.2 million single cells from intestinal biopsies and blood of 421 individuals, including 125 with IBD. Compared with tissue-level eQTLs, cell-type eQTLs were more often distal, enriched in enhancers, and less likely to regulate the nearest gene. They were also more than 3.5 times as likely to colocalize with IBD GWAS loci. The study nominated effector genes at more than half of known IBD loci. These implicate reduced Notch signalling in myeloid cells and Wnt-regulated genes in epithelial stem cells.

title: DiscoDivas: Leveraging genetic-ancestry continuum information to interpolate PRS for admixed populations
synopsis: Polygenic risk scores perform poorly in admixed populations because those groups are underrepresented in both GWAS summary statistics and the individual-level cohorts used to fine-tune scores. Building on evidence that the best PRS model for a sample changes linearly along a continuous ancestry space, this method combines several PRS models, each fine-tuned in a mostly single-ancestry sample, and weights them by genetic distance to produce one harmonized score. It treats ancestry as continuous and needs no matched fine-tuning cohort. It performed as well as or better than conventional ancestry-matched fine-tuning, with the largest gains in admixed individuals. This offers a practical route to fairer PRS when matched data are lacking.

title: MetaSTAARlite: an all-in-one tool for biobank-scale whole-genome sequencing meta-analysis
synopsis: This paper addresses how to meta-analyse rare variants across biobanks when individual-level data cannot be pooled. It introduces MetaSTAARlite, a pipeline that runs functionally informed rare-variant association meta-analysis from summary statistics in both coding and noncoding regions. Applied to sequencing data from the UK Biobank and All of Us, its computation time, memory use and storage grew linearly with sample size. Its results closely matched those of a pooled analysis of individual-level data. The tool makes large multi-biobank whole-genome rare-variant studies practical despite data-sharing restrictions.

title: A large-scale single cell map of primary and conditional regulatory variation in the human brain
synopsis: Many GWAS loci do not colocalize with primary eQTLs, which suggests that some regulatory signals are being missed. This study built a single-cell resource from single-nucleus RNA-seq of 956 postmortem brains (4.8 million nuclei, seven major cell types) with matched whole-genome sequencing. In 763 individuals of European ancestry, it mapped sc-eQTLs for 32,189 eGenes, and stepwise conditional analysis found 6,174 additional independent signals. These conditional signals were more cell-type-specific, lay farther from transcription start sites, were less enriched in annotated promoters and enhancers, and were linked to genes under lower constraint. Several schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease loci colocalized better with conditional than with primary sc-eQTLs, showing that secondary signals can reveal disease mechanisms.

title: Evaluating confounding in rare variant genome wide association studies
synopsis: Confounding in rare variant association studies has been a theoretical concern but had not been tested empirically. Using 306,991 UK Biobank exomes, this study shows that common and rare variant principal components capture recent demography poorly, and that accounting for haplotype sharing does not remove false-positive rare variant associations with non-heritable, spatially structured traits. Re-analysis of 155 phenotypes in siblings found more bias in effect estimates for traits that are unevenly distributed in space, while bias for height appeared to come mainly from assortative mating. The authors also examine false discoveries arising from family-private variants and from linkage with common causal variants, and argue that family-based designs allow useful sensitivity analyses.

title: Mapping Genetic Risk Associations to Cellular Contexts via Deep Learning and Biological Ontologies
synopsis: Linking GWAS signals to the cell types and tissues where they act is hard because the regulatory code is complex and associated variants are in linkage disequilibrium. This framework aggregates deep-learning predictions of how noncoding variants affect transcriptional regulatory elements across GWAS loci and tests their statistical significance empirically. It then organizes the aggregated signals within biological ontologies, which allows statistically calibrated interpretation of which cell-type and tissue contexts are relevant to each trait. The approach offers a principled way to move from association signals to the cellular contexts where they likely act, across a range of human traits.

title: New mechanistic insights from alignment of accessible chromatin and renal lineage factor DNA-binding with genetics of kidney function
synopsis: GWAS of kidney function have found hundreds of noncoding signals, but their target genes and mechanisms are mostly unknown. This study aligned variants credibly associated with estimated glomerular filtration rate with accessible chromatin across 29 human tissues and found substantial overlap with regulatory elements in kidney and liver. The variants were enriched in elements bound by the lineage transcription factor HNF-1β in renal tubules, which helped assign several signals to likely target genes. One example was a polymorphic NDRG1 enhancer that interacted differently with HNF-1β depending on allele and regulated growth and migration of human tubule cells. The work shows the value of combining genetics with tissue-specific transcription factor binding.

title: The Biobank Rare Variant consortium powers the discovery of rare genetic associations through global collaboration
synopsis: Discovering rare coding variants that affect disease is limited by sample size, especially for uncommon diseases. The BRaVa consortium combines sequencing and linked health records from ten biobanks and cohorts, covering over 1.2 million individuals of diverse ancestries, and ran gene-based meta-analyses across 33 clinical endpoints and 11 quantitative traits.
