It found 514 gene-trait associations, 31 of them previously unreported. Of the gene-level associations, 36.1% were not detectable in any single biobank and 91 appeared only in cross-ancestry meta-analysis, and effect sizes agreed across ancestries. Examples include ANKRD12 in asthma and COPD and NAA15 in type 2 diabetes. The public summary statistics provide a reference map for gene discovery and target prioritization.

title: Paediatric DNA methylation profile scores: a systematic review and open-source atlas
synopsis: Methylation profile scores combine many DNA methylation sites into one score per person to index exposures, biological states, or disease risk, and they are increasingly applied to children even though most were built in adults. This systematic review covers 119 early-life studies and 828 scores. It finds substantial heterogeneity in study design and reporting. Scores were often applied in samples that differ from their training data in age group, tissue, array or platform, or ancestry, which may affect how well they work. To help researchers choose suitable scores, the authors release DEMETRA, a searchable open-source atlas of early-life methylation profile scores.

title: An efficient LASSO framework for admixture-aware polygenic scores
synopsis: Polygenic scores trained mostly on European cohorts transfer poorly to other populations, and existing cross-population methods do not properly handle people with recent admixture. This work introduces HAUDI, which recasts an earlier local-ancestry-aware method, GAUDI, as a standard LASSO problem. That lets it estimate ancestry-specific effects much faster and extend to admixture among more than two ancestries. In simulations HAUDI matched or beat GAUDI with far less computation. In real data it outperformed GAUDI across all 18 clinical phenotypes tested and beat ancestry-agnostic scores for white blood cell count and chronic kidney disease. It was also faster and more accurate than SDPR_admix.

title: FastGxC: Fast and powerful context-specific eQTL mapping in bulk and single-cell data
synopsis: Context-specific eQTLs help explain how genetic variants influence complex disease, but existing methods for mapping them are slow and underpowered. FastGxC uses the correlation structure in multi-tissue bulk and single-cell RNA-seq data to map these eQTLs efficiently. In simulations it was nine times more powerful and 106 times faster than existing approaches. Applied to bulk multi-tissue data (n = 698) and PBMC single-cell data (n = 1,218), it produced eQTLs with 4-fold enrichment in context-matched open chromatin, twice the enrichment of standard context-specific eQTLs. It also improved precision in identifying trait-relevant contexts 3-fold and expanded candidate causal genes by 25% in cell types and 6% in tissues.

title: DNA methylation signatures associated with bipolar disorder in peripheral blood improve prediction models
synopsis: This epigenome-wide association study of bipolar disorder, the largest to date, asks whether blood DNA methylation marks the disease and adds predictive value beyond polygenic scores. It meta-analyzed 1729 cases and 1747 controls from twelve cohorts. The analysis found 47 differentially methylated CpG sites and 90 differentially methylated regions overall, with genes enriched for immune and phosphorylation pathways and neurotransmission genes such as GABBR1 and CACNA2D4. A polymethylation score explained 2% of case-control variance and raised the variance explained by the polygenic score from 7.9% to 8.5%, and from 15.9% to 18.5% for bipolar I disorder. Blood methylation may therefore capture disease biology that genetics alone misses.

title: Systematic common and rare variant association testing in 392,030 whole genomes in All of Us
synopsis: This study runs common and rare variant association tests across the phenome in the All of Us v8 release, using whole genomes from 392,030 participants. A unified framework tested 3,602 phenotypes and found 49,863 roughly independent, high-quality single-variant and gene-level associations. Meta-analysis with UK Biobank, reaching up to 786,871 participants, found 193 predicted loss-of-function gene-phenotype associations that neither cohort detected alone, 22 of them not highlighted before. The results are available through a public interactive browser and a Featured Workspace, and the pipeline is built to rerun on future releases. That makes it a large, reusable source of summary statistics from a diverse cohort.

title: Empirically determined baseline masking strategies and other considerations for gene-level burden tests
synopsis: Gene-level burden tests depend on masks, the rules for which coding variants are filtered and aggregated, yet these choices vary widely between studies. A review of 234 studies cataloged 664 masks and found that masking strategies rarely repeat and are rarely justified. Applying every strategy to 54 traits in 189,947 UK Biobank exomes gave anywhere from 58 to 2,523 significant associations. This variation helps explain why separate published analyses of the same data overlap by less than 30%. The authors determine high-power baseline strategies from the data and use them to study other factors affecting burden tests, offering a default that should improve power and replicability.

title: Enrichment of Rare Mitochondrial DNA Variants Among Individuals With Kidney Disease Reveals Undiagnosed Mitochondrial Disease
synopsis: This study asks how much pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variants contribute to kidney disease, since the mitochondrial genome is often left out of genetic studies. It analyzed mtDNA from exome sequencing of 27,747 participants in an ancestrally diverse biobank linked to health records. Of 3935 people with kidney disease, 45 carried clinically associated mtDNA variants, and 42 of them had no mitochondrial diagnosis. Carrying such a variant was linked to higher odds of kidney involvement (OR 1.72), and the m.1630A>G variant in MT-TV was especially enriched (OR 5.56). Adding mtDNA analysis to kidney disease evaluation could reveal mitochondrial disease that has gone unrecognized.

title: KDM1A regulates nephron progenitor programs and is associated with human kidney disease risk
source: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association
synopsis: This study tests whether KDM1A, a chromatin regulator prioritized from fine-mapped kidney function GWAS of 2.27 million people, is a causal gene. The authors deleted Kdm1a in mouse nephron progenitors or in mature tubular cells and examined kidneys at baseline and after injury; they also blocked KDM1A with a drug in embryonic kidney cultures. Loss in progenitors caused nephron loss, cysts and fibrosis, with Notch and Wnt signaling switched back on, while loss in mature tubules had no effect. Drug inhibition reproduced the developmental defects. KDM1A is therefore essential for nephron development, which argues against broad KDM1A inhibition as a treatment.

title: Admixture-informed polygenic risk reporting using the ePRS framework
lab: the Consortium Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine
synopsis: Polygenic risk scores shift with ancestry because allele frequencies and linkage disequilibrium differ between populations, which complicates interpreting them across diverse groups. This work defines the expected polygenic risk score (ePRS), the score expected given a person's global or local admixture, and the residual score (rPRS), the deviation from that expectation, which serves as an ancestry-agnostic measure of liability. Simulations show that adjusting for ePRS alone gives nearly unbiased score-outcome associations without principal components. In TOPMed and All of Us, rPRS effect estimates closely matched those from scores adjusted for principal components. The framework guards against population stratification and gives a fairer way to report genetic risk.

title: Integrating common and rare variants improves polygenic risk prediction across diverse populations
synopsis: Most polygenic risk scores use only common variants and ignore rare variants that may carry missing heritability. RICE builds two separate scores: an ensemble of methods for common variants, and gene-level testing with functional annotations plus penalized regression for rare variants. It was evaluated in simulations and in UK Biobank and All of Us sequencing data covering up to 740 million variants, 361,939 individuals of diverse ancestry and 11 traits. RICE improved prediction for traits with distinct rare variant architectures, especially lipids and height. For lipids, adding rare variants raised R2 by up to about 11.2% in Europeans and 60.7% in people of African ancestry, with signal extending beyond known high-penetrance genes.

title: Leveraging cell-type specificity and similarity improves single-cell eQTL fine-mapping
synopsis: Mapping eQTL separately for each cell type limits both power and accuracy in single-cell studies. CASE is a Bayesian fine-mapping framework that analyzes multiple cell types jointly, capturing shared and cell-type-specific effects while accounting for linkage disequilibrium. In simulations it outperformed the single-trait method SuSiE and the multi-trait method mvSuSiE. Applied to the OneK1K single-cell data, CASE found more regulatory associations, captured cell-type specificity better, and gave eQTL with stronger functional enrichment and more disease associations. The approach can also be applied to multi-tissue and multi-trait genetic studies.

title: Rare variant optimized GWAS with functional validation identifies causal architecture of kidney function in East Asian population
synopsis: This study maps genetic variants affecting kidney function in an East Asian population. It performed a GWAS of estimated glomerular filtration rate in 72,298 Korean individuals using a Korean-specific genotyping array and a matched imputation panel, which allowed rare variants to be detected. The analysis found 30 independent signals, including an East Asian-specific rare variant. Fine-mapping and epigenomic annotation suggested that rs9895661 changes TBX5 binding and thereby TBX2 expression, and experiments confirmed allele-specific enhancer activity. The work shows the value of population-specific genetic resources and of linking GWAS hits to mechanisms through functional follow-up.

title: Analysis of rare coding variants in schizophrenia-associated genes and generalised cognition in the UK Biobank
synopsis: This study asks whether cognitive impairment in schizophrenia reflects biology shared with the disorder or is a consequence of having it. It analyzed exome data from 76,783 UK Biobank participants without schizophrenia, testing very rare variants in schizophrenia-associated genes for association with general cognition (g). Protein-truncating and damaging missense variants in loss-of-function-intolerant genes were linked to lower g. Effects were stronger for protein-truncating variants in genes implicated by rare-variant schizophrenia studies and for missense variants in likely causal genes at common-variant loci. The results suggest that impaired cognition and schizophrenia partly share underlying biology.

title: A non-coding 2p24.2 variant confers susceptibility to non-syndromic orofacial cleft via FOXP2 condensate-mediated transcriptional regulation of MYCN
source: Journal of genetics and genomics = Yi chuan xue bao
synopsis: The 2p24.2 locus is a major risk locus for non-syndromic cleft lip and palate, but its causal variant and mechanism were unknown. Targeted sequencing and replication in 2,437 Chinese patients and 2,391 controls identified the common non-coding variant rs4263114 as the functional regulatory variant. It lies in an enhancer that loops to the MYCN promoter. The risk allele reduces FOXP2 binding at the enhancer and disrupts transcriptional activity linked to FOXP2 phase separation. This lowers MYCN activation and impairs differentiation of cranial neural crest cells. Promoting FOXP2 phase separation partly restored MYCN expression in cells with two risk alleles. The work offers a mechanistic model for how a non-coding variant raises risk of a complex trait.

title: Damaging missense variants in innate immunity genes are associated with earlier age of breast cancer onset in BRCA1 185delAG carriers
synopsis: Breast cancer risk and age at onset vary widely among women carrying the same BRCA1 pathogenic variant, and polygenic risk scores built from common variants explain less than 10% of this variability. To look for further modifiers, the study used whole-exome sequencing in 321 Israeli women carrying the BRCA1 185delAG founder variant. Carrying additional putatively damaging missense variants in innate immunity genes was associated with earlier breast cancer onset. For genes in the natural killer cell activation set, the hazard ratio was 3.62 (95% CI 1.96 to 6.67). This points to innate immune pathways as possible modifiers of BRCA1 penetrance and could help refine personalised risk prediction.

title: Genome-wide fine-mapping improves identification of causal variants
synopsis: Fine-mapping usually works one locus at a time and ignores the genome-wide genetic architecture. This work develops methods for genome-wide fine-mapping that use functional annotations and compares them with existing approaches in simulations and real data. Genome-wide fine-mapping improved error control, power, resolution, precision, replication and trans-ancestry prediction. Across 48 complex traits, its credible sets explained on average 18% of SNP-based heritability, and 30% of them lay outside genome-wide significant loci. Based on the estimated architecture, fine-mapping over half of SNP-based heritability would need about 2 million samples on average. The approach recovered the known FTO variant for body mass index and found new missense causal variants for schizophrenia and Crohn's disease.

title: Rare coding and noncoding variants map 1,342 diseases and biomarkers in 490,549 whole genomes
synopsis: Rare variants, especially noncoding ones, are thought to contribute substantially to heritability but remain understudied in large biobanks. This study analyzed whole-genome sequencing from up to 490,549 UK Biobank participants across 1,342 phenotypes, including 944 diseases, 76 clinical biomarkers and 322 metabolomic traits. Using a new scalable framework for phenome-wide rare variant testing, STAARpipelinePheWAS, it identified 49,121 genome-wide significant gene-trait pairs. Many were missed by earlier exome- or array-based studies and were enriched in drug targets and coherent biological pathways. The results are available in a public interactive portal, which provides a broad map of rare coding and noncoding associations for follow-up and translational work.

title: Systematic assessment of machine learning-based variant annotation methods for rare variant association testing
synopsis: Machine learning scores are widely used to judge variant pathogenicity, but it is unclear how well they select variants for gene-level rare variant association tests. This study benchmarked CADD v1.6, CADD v1.7, AlphaMissense, ESM-1b and GPN-MSA across several gene-based and aggregation tests for 14 quantitative traits in up to 350,377 UK Biobank participants. It also introduced a Wasserstein distance framework to measure calibration and power. CADD gave the best signal separation, and AlphaMissense-based tests were systematically less well calibrated. Significant genes from all methods were enriched 1.8 to 5.8-fold for loss-of-function intolerant genes, with GPN-MSA showing the highest enrichment. The work offers practical guidance on choosing annotations for rare variant studies.

title: A meta-analysis of single-nucleus expression quantitative trait loci linking genetic risk to brain disorders
synopsis: Most genetic risk variants for neurological diseases are noncoding and likely act by changing gene expression. However, bulk tissue eQTL studies miss the brain's many cell types. This meta-analysis combined single-nucleus RNA-seq and genotype data from four cohorts, totaling 5.8 million nuclei from 983 individuals of European ancestry. It mapped cis- and trans-eQTLs across brain cell types and subtypes, including disease-specific and sex-specific effects, and used colocalization and Mendelian randomization to link genes to disease risk. The study found up to tenfold more cis-eQTLs than before and identified cell-type-specific genes tied to neurological disease. The resulting resource, SingleBrain, can help explain how risk variants act in specific brain cells.

title: Biobank-Scale Polygenic Prediction in Admixed Populations Using Local Ancestry via the Group Lasso
synopsis: Polygenic risk models often transfer poorly across ancestries, and ancestry-specific models do not work for admixed individuals, whose ancestry varies along the genome. This work presents Combine, a sparse regression method that adds local ancestry dosages to genotype features and fits them jointly with a variant-level group lasso. In 99,298 admixed All of Us participants, it clearly outperformed multi-ancestry summary-statistic methods, including a 144% relative improvement over PRS-CSx for white blood cell count. It matched or beat optimized individual-level models for seven of nine traits while offering locus-level interpretability. An extension, Combine-S, identifies ancestry-dependent effect sizes, and adding external GWAS evidence improved LDL cholesterol prediction.

title: Massive-scale single-nucleus multi-omics identifies novel rare noncoding drivers of Parkinson’s disease
synopsis: Rare noncoding variants may explain a substantial part of the heritability of complex diseases, but their functional effects are hard to predict at scale. This study generated single-nucleus multi-omic data from more than 3.3 million nuclei across five brain regions in 80 people with Parkinson's disease and 21 controls, all with 30x whole-genome sequencing. The data were used to characterize cell-type-specific disease features, map chromatin accessibility and expression QTLs, and train models that predict how variants affect gene regulation. The analysis identified rare noncoding variants associated with sporadic Parkinson's disease and proposed candidate drivers in familial cases without a known genetic cause. The approach could be applied to other complex diseases.

title: Scalable and accurate rare-variant association tests for whole genome sequencing time-to-event analysis in large biobanks
source: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
synopsis: Biobank whole-genome sequencing makes it possible to study how rare variants affect time-to-event outcomes such as age at diagnosis, disease progression and lifespan. Such analyses are complicated by heavy censoring, cryptic relatedness and population structure. This work introduces GATE-STAAR, a frailty-model framework for rare variant tests that accounts for these issues and uses functional annotations to improve power. It also uses a saddlepoint approximation to handle heavy censoring. Simulations showed good power and proper type I error control. Applied to about 400,000 UK Biobank participants and validated in European-ancestry All of Us participants, it found rare variant associations with age at diagnosis for a range of diseases.

title: Polygenic risk scores and HLA class II variants are biomarkers of corticosteroid response in childhood nephrotic syndrome
synopsis: Children with nephrotic syndrome are classified as steroid-sensitive or steroid-resistant, but no reliable predictor of steroid response exists at first presentation. This study ran genome-wide association analyses, built polygenic risk scores and typed classical HLA alleles in 1,997 previously unstudied children, split into discovery and replication cohorts, plus 3,558 ancestry-matched controls. Steroid-sensitive disease, but not steroid-resistant disease, was associated with HLA-DQB1, HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQA1 variants and with CLEC16A. One HLA haplotype carried about four times the risk. A model combining haplotype, polygenic score and age at onset reached an AUC of 0.68-0.70. These results support steroid-sensitive disease as an immune-mediated disorder and point toward genetic biomarkers for choosing treatment.

title: Practical utility of sequence-to-omics models for improving the reproducibility of genetic fine-mapping
synopsis: This study asks whether deep learning models that predict molecular phenotypes from DNA sequence can make eQTL fine-mapping more reproducible. The authors evaluate AlphaGenome, Borzoi, Enformer and Sei on eQTL datasets from GTEx, TOPMed and MAGE, and propose a framework that combines statistical posterior inclusion probabilities with sequence-model scores to produce functionally informed PIPs. Purely statistical fine-mapping often had high replication failure rates, and adding model predictions substantially reduced them and better prioritized variants that replicated in other consortia, with newer models such as AlphaGenome and Borzoi performing best. This gives a practical, scalable way to make causal variant prioritization more robust.

title: Advancing regulatory variant effect prediction with AlphaGenome
synopsis: This paper introduces AlphaGenome, a deep learning model that addresses the trade-off between input length and output resolution in sequence-based prediction of functional genomic measurements. It takes 1 Mb of DNA sequence and predicts thousands of tracks, up to single-base resolution, across gene expression, transcription initiation, chromatin accessibility, histone marks, transcription factor binding, chromatin contacts and splicing, after training on human and mouse genomes. AlphaGenome matched or exceeded the strongest external models in 25 of 26 variant effect prediction evaluations and recapitulated the mechanisms of clinically relevant variants near TAL1. Released tools make it broadly usable for interpreting regulatory variants.

title: CoEVFold suite: User friendly pipelines to visually represent protein coevolution
synopsis: Coevolution is the main signal behind sequence-based structure and interaction prediction, yet few user-friendly tools exist to find and visualize it. CoEVFold computes direct couplings with GREMLIN (with CCMpred and plmc as options) from MMseqs2 alignments and maps them onto single proteins, oligomers, complexes and protein networks. Across 18 heteromeric complexes, top-ranked inter-protein couplings found interface contacts with precision of 0.8 or higher in seven. Network rankings agreed with STRING for an E. coli cell-wall synthesis network (ROC AUC 0.72-0.74). For homo-oligomers, 25-47% of top pairs not explained by the monomer structure were protomer contacts, compared with 2% or less expected by chance. This makes coevolution analysis practical for researchers studying protein-protein interactions.

title: Comprehensive benchmarking single and multi ancestry polygenic score methods with the PGS-hub platform
synopsis: This study benchmarks 13 single- and multi-ancestry polygenic score methods within one framework, across 36 traits in European and African UK Biobank samples. It assesses prediction accuracy, computational cost, number of variants and the effect of LD reference panel size. LDpred2 performed best overall among single-ancestry methods, and LDpred2-multi outperformed PRS-CSx and X-Wing, which performed comparably to each other. Larger LD reference panels clearly improved performance when the panel had fewer than 1,000 samples, with gains leveling off above 5,000. The authors also release PGS-hub, an online platform that runs all of these methods with ancestry-stratified LD panels, which lowers the technical barrier to using them.

title: A novel age-informative polygenic score improves predictive ability for kidney function and kidney function decline
synopsis: This work asks whether accounting for age-dependent genetic effects improves polygenic prediction of kidney function (eGFR) and its decline. The authors build an age-informative score from main and age-interaction effects at 282 kidney function SNPs and test it in UK Biobank and in independent cohorts aged 25 to 98. Ignoring age mis-specified genetic effects, and the age-informative score explained more eGFR variance in both young (6.3% versus 5.9%) and old individuals (2.3% versus 1.8%). It also better captured eGFR decline, with differences between the top and bottom quintiles similar to those for diabetes or obesity, although individual-level prediction remained difficult.

title: Federated single-cell QTL meta-analysis reveals novel disease mechanisms
synopsis: This study uses federated single-cell eQTL meta-analysis to resolve cell type-specific genetic regulation that bulk analyses miss. It combines 12 PBMC datasets covering 2,032 individuals and 2.5 million cells. Across six immune cell types, it identified cis-eQTLs for 6,592 genes and fine-mapped 14,985 loci, and the 42% of eQTLs not detected in a large whole blood study showed stronger enrichment for disease GWAS loci. Integration with bulk trans-eQTLs anchored 6,382 trans-eGenes to upstream regulators, for example a hemorrhoidal disease variant acting through BACH1 in CD4+ T cells. The work shows how single-cell QTL meta-analysis can help interpret disease genetics.

title: Improving polygenic score prediction for underrepresented groups through transfer learning
synopsis: This paper addresses the weaker performance of polygenic scores in non-European ancestries, which follows from most training data being European. It presents GPTL, an R package with three transfer learning approaches: gradient descent with early stopping, penalized regression that shrinks effects toward prior values, and a Bayesian finite-mixture method that can combine several prior sources. In simulations and in UK Biobank and All of Us data, transfer learning scores consistently outperformed single-ancestry scores and often matched or exceeded multi-ancestry ensemble scores. The software works with individual-level data or GWAS summary statistics, making it widely applicable.

title: Cross-Ancestry Polygenic Prediction: Comparing Methods and Assessing Transferability Across Traits
synopsis: This study compares seven cross-ancestry polygenic prediction methods for five traits in UK Biobank: BMI, height and three cholesterol measures. GBLUP and PRS-CSx performed best for highly polygenic traits such as height and BMI. PRSice and PolyPred did best for less polygenic cholesterol traits, with PRS-CSx comparable at larger sample sizes. Restricting to SNPs whose effects point the same direction across ancestries improved cross-ancestry accuracy, and how well scores transferred varied by trait. These results help guide the choice of method and inform development of fairer polygenic prediction.

title: Blood-based DNA methylation captures variance in adult height
synopsis: This study asks how much of the variation in adult height can be captured by blood DNA methylation, a trait previously thought to show little methylation signal. Using EPIC array data from 7,654 unrelated Generation Scotland participants and Bayesian penalized regression, methylation captured 25.0% of height variance conditional on genetic effects. Methylation and genetics together captured 80.3%, compared with 56.3% for genetics alone. A methylation profile score correlated only weakly with height in independent cohorts (0.14 to 0.26). The authors caution against calling traits methylation-null based only on association scans and recommend whole-genome variance methods.

title: Integrative kidney multi-omics traces genetic drivers of chronic kidney disease to targets within the renal epigenome, transcriptome and proteome
synopsis: This study asks which genes and molecular mechanisms underlie genetic risk for chronic kidney disease. Genome-wide association meta-analyses of four CKD-defining traits in up to 890,000 individuals found 508 loci, 237 of them linked to more than one trait. Colocalization with kidney mRNA, protein and methylation data prioritized 651 kidney genes, 330 of them new candidates. Genes shared across several traits were more relevant to kidney biology. The results also point to genetic control of developmental DNA methylation. Follow-up of a rare syndrome involving CA12 linked loss of this gene to hyperuricemia and reduced kidney function, which points to possible adverse effects of CA12 inhibitors such as acetazolamide.

title: A multiscale framework for hypothesis generation from sex-stratified X-linked gene networks
synopsis: This paper presents a reproducible framework for comparing gene co-expression networks across biological groups. It addresses unbalanced cohorts, unstable networks, dependence on the correlation method, and multiple testing. The pipeline combines cohort balancing, bootstrap consensus networks, topology statistics, paired label permutations and multiplicity control. The authors demonstrate it on sex-stratified networks of X-linked genes, grouped by X-inactivation escape status, across 15 TCGA cancer cohorts (90 networks). None of the 315 permutation tests survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Exploratory graphlet profiles still showed cancer- and gene-class-specific patterns worth replicating. The work shows how to separate nominal or visually striking network differences from evidence that holds up after correction for multiple testing.

title: SurvSTAAR: A Powerful Statistical Framework for Rare Variant Analysis of Time-to-Event Traits in Large-Scale Whole-Genome Sequencing Studies
synopsis: Most rare-variant association methods for whole-genome sequencing handle quantitative or binary traits and ignore censored time-to-event information such as age of onset. This paper introduces SurvSTAAR, a scalable framework for testing rare coding and noncoding variants against time-to-event traits. It accounts for sample relatedness, population structure and heavy censoring, and it uses functional annotations to gain power. Applied to Alzheimer's disease in 458,773 related UK Biobank WGS samples, it found putatively novel coding and noncoding associations. The authors examined how these variants might affect disease progression through amino acid changes, structural changes and domain disruption. The method makes biobank-scale rare-variant analysis of disease onset and progression practical.

title: Patient and provider experiences with genomic risk result return: Case-based insights from eMERGE IV
synopsis: This study examines how patients and providers experienced the return of genome-informed risk results in eMERGE IV. In that network, polygenic risk scores, monogenic findings, family history and clinical factors for 11 common conditions were returned to nearly 24,000 people at 10 sites. Researchers who disclosed results were surveyed about their cases, and content analysis was applied to the 24 eligible cases out of 64 submitted. The cases fell into four categories: PRS-driven outcomes, challenges in returning results, interactions with primary care providers, and monogenic or mosaic findings. The authors recommend educational materials or genetic counselors, care coordination for patients with multiple results, and study of how multiple genetic risk factors combine.

title: Integrated Genetic Risk Stratifies Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer in Two Independent Cohorts
synopsis: Age-based colorectal cancer screening treats all adults under 50 alike. This study tested whether an integrated inherited risk measure, combining a polygenic risk score, family history and Lynch syndrome variants, stratifies early-onset colorectal cancer risk. The authors followed adults under 50 in the UK Biobank and a US health-system biobank until age 50, using Cox models and Kaplan-Meier estimates. Among 102,797 UK Biobank participants, 109 developed early-onset cancer. Compared with the low-risk group, hazard ratios were 5.95 for the high-risk group and 28.41 for the very-high-risk group. Cumulative incidence by age 50 rose from 0.08% in the low-risk group to 2.06% in the very-high-risk group. The results support evaluating genomics-informed, risk-based screening.

title: Nephrotic syndrome genomic discovery in the Mass General Brigham Biobank identifies monoallelic MEFV variants as a risk factor for focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
synopsis: This study tested whether a health-system biobank can support genetic discovery in nephrotic syndrome. Among 130,000 Mass General Brigham Biobank members, reviewing pathology reports was the best way to find FSGS or minimal change disease cases. Of 319 exome-sequenced cases, 9.7% carried Mendelian variants and 7.5% had high-risk APOL1 genotypes, and both groups had higher odds of kidney failure. Many genetic cases had biopsies read as secondary FSGS. Monoallelic pathogenic MEFV variants appeared in six FSGS patients with collapsing and thrombotic microangiopathy features. Cases from Genomics England and a case-control study (odds ratio 3.8) supported the finding. MEFV may be an underrecognized susceptibility gene for steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, even without Familial Mediterranean Fever.

title: cellSTAAR: incorporating single-cell-sequencing-based functional data to boost power in rare variant association testing of noncoding regions
lab: the NHLBI Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine (TOPMed) Consortium
synopsis: Rare noncoding variants are hard to interpret because regulatory effects often depend on cell type. cellSTAAR integrates whole-genome sequencing with single-cell ATAC-seq to build cell-type-specific functional annotations and regulatory elements. It uses a comprehensive strategy to account for uncertainty in linking regulatory elements to their target genes. The authors applied it to about 60,000 TOPMed participants and replicated findings in about 190,000 UK Biobank participants. Across four lipid traits, cellSTAAR detected more biologically meaningful associations and made results easier to interpret. The work shows that cell-type-aware annotation can increase power in rare-variant association studies of noncoding regions.

title: Integrating polygenic and methylation risk scores for pleural mesothelioma risk stratification
synopsis: Asbestos causes most pleural mesothelioma, but not everyone exposed develops it, which points to other risk factors. This study built polygenic and DNA methylation risk scores in a retrospective case-control study of 749 participants. The scores were then evaluated in 268 participants from a nested case-control study within the prospective EPIC cohort, where cases were sampled before diagnosis. Adding the scores raised the AUC from 0.66 to 0.85 in the held-out test set and from 0.51 to 0.62 in the prospective samples. The polygenic score worked best at low asbestos exposure, while the methylation score was stable across exposure levels, and combining them improved discrimination. Multi-omic biomarkers may help target early detection in exposed groups.

title: Limited Generalizability of Epigenetic Clocks and Scores Across Pediatric Tissues and Age Ranges
synopsis: This study asks whether epigenetic clocks and scores, mostly trained in adult blood, work in children and in saliva, which is how DNA methylation is often collected in pediatric research. Using matched blood and saliva methylation profiles from 291 children aged 3-12, more than half of whom were exposed to early-life adversity, the authors computed 22 common epigenetic measures and compared them with measured age, BMI, CRP, IQ and telomere length. Performance varied widely. Only nine measures tracked their phenotype equally well in both tissues, and age acceleration correlated only weakly to moderately between blood and saliva. Scores for lower cognition and higher inflammation were associated with adversity and low socioeconomic status. The authors urge caution when applying these measures across tissues and age ranges, and they release CpG-level blood-saliva correlations as a resource.

title: The landscape of allele-specific expression in human kidneys
synopsis: This study asks how allele-specific expression, the preferential expression of one gene copy, behaves in human kidney disease. Using paired whole-genome sequencing and RNA-seq from microdissected glomerular and tubulointerstitial tissue of patients with proteinuric kidney disease, the authors built a genome-wide map of allele-specific expression. Most common events appeared deterministic and driven by sequence. Compared with controls, diseased kidneys showed more allele-specific expression in glomeruli than in tubules, and this glomerular excess was linked to better kidney outcomes. Differential expression analysis pointed to a protective transcriptional response, including upregulation of ribosome and ATP synthesis genes. The work suggests glomerular allele-specific expression marks adaptive rather than pathogenic regulation.

title: Methylome-wide association studies and epigenetic biomarker development for 133 mass spectrometry-assessed circulating proteins in 14,671 Generation Scotland participants
synopsis: This study examines how blood DNA methylation relates to 133 highly abundant serum proteins measured by high-throughput mass spectrometry in 14,671 Generation Scotland participants. Epigenome-wide association models adjusted for common confounders found 15,855 significant CpG-protein associations across 125 proteins. The authors then trained methylation-based predictors (EpiScores) for each protein, and 112 of them correlated significantly with the measured protein in a held-out test set. Sixteen protein EpiScores were associated with incident cardiovascular disease, compared with only one directly measured protein. Because methylation may reflect longer-term exposure than a single protein measurement, protein EpiScores could serve as useful biomarkers alongside measured proteins for predicting disease risk.

title: High cell-type specificity of eQTLs revealed by single-nucleus analyses of brain and blood
synopsis: This study asks how cell-type-specific the genetic effects on gene expression in the brain are, a key question for interpreting GWAS signals. The authors built scMetaBrain, a single-nucleus RNA-seq resource of 3.9 million transcriptomes from 785 individuals across 10 brain datasets, and identified 19,371 eGenes across major cell types, most of them in excitatory neurons. About 31% of eQTLs were highly cell-type-specific. Differences in effect sizes between brain cell types were often as large as differences between brain and non-brain bulk tissues, and effects agreed best between functionally similar cell types, including across brain and blood. Colocalization prioritized 662 genes for 11 brain traits, which suggests that bulk tissue analyses overstate how much eQTLs are shared across cell types.

title: Recessive variants in the intergenic NOS1AP-C1orf226 locus cause monogenic kidney disease responsive to anti-proteinuric treatment
synopsis: Variants in NOS1AP were already known to cause monogenic nephrotic syndrome. This study shows that the main kidney isoform in mammals is an intergenic splice product joining NOS1AP and the neighboring C1orf226 gene, and that this product cannot bind nitric oxide synthase 1. Mice with a knockout that disrupts only the intergenic product developed nephrotic syndrome features. In two patients, causative NOS1AP splice variants were found, including one first classified as benign because it was judged against the canonical transcript. By changing genetic background, the authors produced a mouse model that responds to anti-proteinuric treatment. The work shows that annotating isoforms correctly matters for variant interpretation and for testing therapies.

title: Population-scale multiome immune cell atlas reveals complex disease drivers
synopsis: This study asks how non-coding disease variants act through chromatin and gene expression in immune cells. The authors generated paired single-nucleus ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data from 10 million blood mononuclear cells across 1,108 Finnish individuals. They mapped 51,083 eQTLs, 338,100 chromatin accessibility QTLs, about 119,000 fine-mapped variants and nearly 500,000 enhancer-gene links. Variants whose effects run all the way from chromatin to expression colocalized with disease about twice as often as variants with chromatin-only effects. In constrained genes, chromatin effects were transmitted to expression only weakly, which helps explain why eQTLs appear depleted at these genes. Base editing validated causal variants at Finnish-enriched loci, and the resource offers mechanistic hypotheses for over half of immune disease associations.

title: S4-multi: Enhancing polygenic score prediction in ancestrally diverse populations
synopsis: Polygenic scores predict disease less accurately in non-European populations. This study extends S4, a Bayesian model that selects and shrinks variant effects from summary statistics, into a multi-ancestry version called S4-Multi. The method was benchmarked in simulations and on several biobanks, including UK Biobank, FinnGen, Biobank Japan and All of Us, for type 2 diabetes, breast and colorectal cancer, asthma and stroke. In simulations, S4-Multi was more than 1.6 times as accurate as single-ancestry S4 in non-European groups and matched or beat leading methods. In real biobank data, it performed on par with the best methods while using 9-77% fewer variants, which may make it practical where genomic data are limited.

title: Chronic kidney disease
synopsis: This review summarizes the current state of chronic kidney disease, which affects about 850 million people worldwide, with about 4 million needing kidney replacement therapy. It is projected to become the fifth leading cause of death by 2050. The review notes that the disease can be screened for, diagnosed and staged with simple laboratory tests. Most patients die or become disabled from cardiovascular disease before they ever reach kidney failure. Large trials since 2019 have identified treatments that both slow kidney function decline and lower cardiovascular risk. The authors argue that earlier detection and timely treatment across clinical specialties could substantially reduce the global burden of the disease.

title: Scalable and accurate rare variant meta-analysis with Meta-SAIGE
synopsis: Meta-analyzing rare variants across cohorts increases power, but existing methods can fail to control false positives for low-prevalence binary traits and are computationally expensive. This paper introduces Meta-SAIGE, which estimates the null distribution accurately and reuses linkage disequilibrium matrices across phenotypes to make phenome-wide analyses efficient. Simulations based on UK Biobank exome data showed controlled type I error and power comparable to pooled individual-level analysis with SAIGE-GENE+. Applied to 83 low-prevalence phenotypes across UK Biobank and All of Us exomes, it found 237 gene-trait associations, 80 of which were not significant in either dataset alone.

title: PRISM: ancestry-aware integration of tissue-specific genomic annotations enhances the transferability of polygenic scores
synopsis: Polygenic scores transfer poorly across ancestries, partly because functional annotations and other reference resources are sparse for underrepresented populations. This paper presents PRISM, a transfer learning approach that combines multi-ancestry training, fine-mapping and ancestry-aware weighting of tissue-specific genomic annotations. Applied to 7,352 fine-mapped variants, 414 ENCODE annotations and 406,659 UK Biobank participants, PRISM gave its largest gains in African-ancestry individuals, an average 13.1% improvement over annotation-agnostic multi-ancestry scores. The best model used 102-fold fewer annotations than non-specific models. The approach offers a way to improve prediction equity now, using the best biologically matched resources already available.

title: Computationally efficient meta-analysis of gene-based tests using summary statistics in large-scale genetic studies
synopsis: Meta-analysis of gene-based rare-variant tests usually requires each study to share a variant covariance matrix for every trait, which becomes impractical when there are many phenotypes. This paper presents REMETA, a tool that uses one sparse covariance reference file per study and rescales it for each phenotype using single-variant summary statistics. The authors also develop methods for binary traits with case-control imbalance and for estimating allele frequencies, genotype counts and burden-test effect sizes. They demonstrate it on five traits in 469,376 UK Biobank samples. The open-source software should make it easier to combine large exome-sequencing studies.

title: Estimation and mapping of the missing heritability of human phenotypes
synopsis: This study asks how much of the heritability of complex traits whole-genome sequencing can capture, especially from rare non-coding variants. It uses WGS data from 347,630 UK Biobank individuals of European ancestry and about 40 million variants to partition heritability for 34 traits and diseases. On average, WGS captures about 88% of pedigree-based narrow-sense heritability, with 20% from rare and 68% from common variants. Non-coding variants account for 79% of rare-variant heritability. For 15 traits, WGS-based and pedigree-based estimates did not differ significantly. Association analyses found 11,243 common-variant and 886 rare-variant associations. These results suggest much of the missing heritability can be found and mapped with sequencing.

title: Rare genetic variants confer a high risk of ADHD and implicate neuronal biology
synopsis: This study asks how rare coding variants contribute to ADHD, which so far has mostly been studied through common variants. It analyzes exome-sequencing data from 8,895 individuals with ADHD and 53,780 controls. Three genes, MAP1A, ANO8 and ANK2, are implicated, with odds ratios of 5.55 to 15.13. Their interaction networks are enriched for risk genes of other neurodevelopmental disorders and for cytoskeleton, synapse and RNA-processing genes. Top risk genes are expressed across brain development and in GABAergic and dopaminergic neurons. Each rare deleterious variant was associated with a 2.25-point lower IQ. Comorbidities appear to reflect variants in specific gene sets rather than a general burden across constrained genes.

title: Flexibly Modeling Rare Variant Pathogenicity Improves Gene Discovery for Complex Traits
synopsis: Rare-variant burden tests are limited by how well they separate functional from benign alleles. This paper introduces FlexRV, which models nonlinear relationships between functional annotations and phenotype in gene-based aggregation tests. Across 62 quantitative and 44 disease traits in the UK Biobank, FlexRV outperformed DeepRVAT, STAAR and Regenie, finding 51% more quantitative and 102% more disease associations than Regenie. Its associations replicated more often in All of Us and were more enriched at genes nominated by GWAS. Missense and loss-of-function variants contributed nearly equally to burden heritability. FlexRV weights also improved rare-variant polygenic scores for identifying people with extreme phenotypes.

title: Specificity, length and luck drive gene rankings in association studies
synopsis: This study examines why GWAS and rare-variant burden tests, though conceptually similar, rank different genes as top hits. Analyzing 209 quantitative traits in the UK Biobank, the authors propose two criteria for prioritizing genes: trait importance and trait specificity relative to other traits. They find that burden tests favor trait-specific genes, while GWAS favor genes near trait-specific variants. Because non-coding variants can act in specific contexts, GWAS can also highlight highly pleiotropic genes. Both designs are also shaped by trait-irrelevant factors such as gene length and chance. The results clarify what each approach reveals about trait biology and how to interpret their gene rankings.

title: Transcriptome-wide association studies at cell-state level using single-cell eQTL data
synopsis: Transcriptome-wide association studies usually test gene-disease links at the bulk-tissue or cell-type pseudobulk level, which ignores variation within a cell type. This paper presents TWiST, a method that uses single-cell eQTL data to run TWAS at the level of cell states. It represents cell state with pseudotime and models the effect of gene expression on a trait as a continuous curve, which allows tests of global, dynamic and nonlinear associations. In simulations and real data, it had more power than pseudobulk methods. Applied to OneK1K, it identified hundreds of genes whose effects on autoimmune diseases change along immune cell differentiation.

title: A machine-learning framework to characterize functional disease architectures and prioritize disease variants
synopsis: This work introduces V2D, a machine-learning framework that models disease effect sizes from genome-wide fine-mapping posteriors and functional annotations. The goal is to characterize disease functional architecture and to build priors for variant prioritization. Simulations and real data show it gives reliable estimates of heritability enrichment. Applied with linear trees to 15 UK Biobank traits, it found nonlinear interactions between constraint and regulatory annotations, with constrained regulatory variants showing 17.3-fold enrichment across 79 GWAS. Neural-network V2D scores were 20.6-fold enriched in the top 1% and outperformed existing prioritization scores. They also transferred to gene expression and non-European data and improved fine-mapping.

title: Exome-Wide Analysis Identifies a Rare EXD3 Missense Variant Associated With Diabetic Kidney Disease
synopsis: This study asks whether low-frequency and rare coding variants contribute to diabetic kidney disease. It ran an exome-wide meta-analysis of up to 10,312 individuals with type 1 diabetes across 10 definitions of kidney disease, with single-variant and gene-level tests. Besides the known COL4A3 variant, it found a rare missense variant in EXD3 (MAF 0.4%) associated with the disease (OR 8.7, P = 4.5e-9). Knocking down EXD3 in podocytes reduced nephrin expression, and UK Biobank data supported a link with albuminuria. Gene-level tests implicated seven genes, including MUC5B. The findings point to a role for EXD3 in podocyte integrity.

title: Modeling heterogeneity in single-cell perturbation states enhances detection of response eQTLs
synopsis: This study asks whether modeling each cell's individual response to a perturbation, rather than treating perturbation as a simple on/off condition, improves detection of response eQTLs. Single-cell expression data from cells exposed to influenza A virus, Candida albicans, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were analyzed with a per-cell perturbation-state model. Accounting for heterogeneity found on average 36.9% more reQTLs than the standard discrete model. Examples include a weaker eQTL effect for PXK under influenza infection. About 25% of reQTLs had cell-type-specific effects, such as a stronger RPS26 effect in B cells. The approach offers a general way to find context-dependent genetic regulation more accurately.

title: Human Kidney Alternative Splicing Information Illuminates Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Risk
synopsis: This study maps alternative splicing in 404 human kidney cortex samples spanning a range of disease severity to see how transcript-level regulation contributes to kidney and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic traits. Splicing and expression QTL analyses found 1,948 genes with significant splicing QTLs. Colocalization and Mendelian randomization against GWAS data identified 30 splice variants that share genetic signals with these traits. Six genes, including MANBA, GSTA1 and GSTA2, had concordant splicing, expression and protein QTL evidence, and a CLCNK splice variant was implicated in blood pressure. Long-read RNA sequencing found novel isoforms and confirmed the short-read estimates. The results show that isoform-resolved analysis can identify candidate mediators of complex kidney disease risk.

title: A single-cell genetic colocalization test improves power and resolves disease-mediating cell types
synopsis: Colocalization with bulk-tissue eQTLs fails to explain most GWAS loci, and single-cell analyses that rely on pseudobulk clusters can lose power when clustering is imperfect. This work introduces scJLIM, a cluster-free colocalization test that models eQTL interactions with continuous cell states such as principal components and estimates colocalization in individual cells. In simulations it was more powerful than pseudobulk methods. Applied to blood and brain scRNA-seq paired with autoimmune and neurological GWAS, it found nearly twice as many colocalizations. Highlighted results include ETS2 for inflammatory bowel disease in a myeloid subset and TRPV2 for Parkinson's disease. The method helps pin down the cell states through which disease variants may act.

title: Genetic screens of imaging-derived kidney volumes identify genes linked to kidney function
synopsis: This study asks whether genetic studies of kidney structure can reveal chronic kidney disease genes that are missed by studies of kidney function markers like eGFR. A neural network derived total kidney volume and cortex, medulla and sinus volumes from MRIs of 38,816 UK Biobank participants of European ancestry, and each volume was analyzed by GWAS. The scans found 34 loci for total volume, 26 for cortex, 24 for medulla and 71 for sinus, compared with 32 for eGFR. Prioritized genes were enriched for kidney development and hypoxia pathways. Some loci, such as PKHD1 and BICC1, were linked to volume but not eGFR, and rare loss-of-function BICC1 variants were associated with CKD and dialysis risk. This shows that imaging traits can uncover new CKD risk genes.

title: From GWAS to Translational Insights: Comprehensive Genetic Analysis of Nephrotic Syndrome from Multiple Populations
synopsis: To clarify the genetic architecture of nephrotic syndrome, this study ran a multi-ancestry genome-wide association study linked to electronic health records, with 5,214 cases and over 1.6 million controls. It found 37 loci, including new associations at JAML and STPG2, and confirmed known signals at PLA2R1, HMCN1 and APOL1. MHC fine-mapping found the strongest European-ancestry signal at an HLA-DRB1 allele (OR 2.01), with nominal ancestry-specific HLA associations in other populations. Transcriptome-wide analysis found 484 gene-tissue associations, including C4A in kidney cortex. Adult and pediatric disease showed substantial genetic correlation (Rg 0.63). Mendelian randomization implicated APOM expression. The findings suggest therapeutic targets informed by ancestry.

title: Mono-allelic pathogenic variants in JAG1 cause autosomal dominant tubulo-interstitial kidney disease (ADTKD-JAG1)
synopsis: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease remains genetically unexplained in 25-50% of families after screening the known genes. This study examined 203 ADTKD families plus sporadic and end-stage kidney disease cases from the 100,000 Genomes Project, along with expression and ER stress assays in patient-derived urinary epithelial cells. Pathogenic JAG1 variants, previously known from Alagille syndrome, were found in three large unsolved families and in some sporadic cases. None of the 23 affected adults showed liver, heart, eye or skeletal features. Functional data pointed to haploinsufficiency rather than toxicity from an abnormal protein. The authors propose ADTKD-JAG1 as a new subtype, which expands genetic testing for this disease.

title: MACHINE: a robust and scalable multi-ancestry fine-mapping method using a continuous global-local shrinkage prior
synopsis: Multi-ancestry fine-mapping can sharpen the search for causal variants, but most existing methods use discrete priors, assume causal variants are shared across ancestries, or need sharing probabilities set in advance. MACHINE is a Bayesian method with a continuous global-local shrinkage prior that models both shared and ancestry-specific effects without these assumptions. It adds false discovery rate control for analyses based on summary statistics with out-of-sample LD, and it can use functional annotations through generalized LD score regression. In simulations it was robust and controlled FDR better than existing methods. Applied to four lipid traits and schizophrenia, it identified previously unknown causal variants and described how genetic architecture differs across ancestries.

title: Quantifying APOL1, Human Leukocyte Antigen, and Other Genetic Contributions to Unexplained Kidney Failure
source: American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation
synopsis: About 15% of people needing kidney replacement therapy have no known cause for their kidney failure. This study used whole-genome sequencing of 218 such patients with onset before age 50 from the 100,000 Genomes Project. Candidate variant review, gene-based and structural variant tests, APOL1 genotyping, polygenic scores and HLA analyses were compared against 26,373 controls. A monogenic diagnosis was made in 17% of patients, less often in those aged 36 or older, and the case-control analyses solved no additional cases. High-risk APOL1 genotypes were much more common in cases of recent African ancestry than in controls (52% vs 8.4%). The results suggest a genetic architecture distinct from common chronic kidney disease.

title: Dissecting the Predictive Accuracy of Polygenic Indexes for Behavioral Phenotypes Across Genetic Ancestries
synopsis: Polygenic indexes trained mostly in European-ancestry samples predict poorly in other ancestries, but this loss of accuracy is less well studied for behavioral and social traits. Using UK Biobank and Health and Retirement Study data, this study measured how well genome-wide polygenic indexes transfer across ancestries for 52 traits, accounting for heritability differences and comparing standard with family-based GWAS. Relative accuracy was 24% in African, 37% in East Asian and 51% in South Asian ancestries, and biologically proximal traits transferred better than social ones. Differences in LD and allele frequencies explained 82% of the loss in African ancestries but much less in Asian ancestries. Family-based GWAS modestly improved transfer for some traits.

title: Diagnostic Yield of Whole-Genome Sequencing in Patients With Kidney Failure of Undetermined Etiology at Age 50 Years or Younger
synopsis: This cross-sectional study asked how often a genetic cause can be found in patients who reached kidney failure of undetermined cause by age 50. Of 124 patients first screened with SNP arrays and MUC1 testing, 114 without a diagnosis underwent whole-genome sequencing, analyzed in stages by gene panel, family and cohort reanalysis. Sequencing found a genetic cause in 23%, giving a combined yield of 29%. Six genes, including the COL4A genes, MUC1, NPHP1 and INF2, accounted for nearly 70% of diagnoses. Family history was the only predictor, although 18% of patients without a family history still had genetic disease. TMEM126B is proposed as a new cause of adult-onset disease.

title: fSuSiE enables fine-mapping of QTLs from genome-scale molecular profiles
synopsis: Molecular QTL studies of traits like DNA methylation and histone marks usually test each variant and each site separately. This ignores LD and the spatial correlation of effects between nearby sites. fSuSiE combines wavelet-based functional regression with the Sum of Single Effects framework to jointly fine-map causal variants and identify the sites they affect. In simulations it outperformed methods that ignore spatial structure. In ROSMAP prefrontal cortex methylation and H3K9ac data, it gave much higher resolution, for example 6,355 single-variant methylation credible sets versus 328 from an existing approach. At Alzheimer's disease risk loci, it found candidate causal variants colocalizing with GWAS signals near CASS4 and CR1/CR2, suggesting possible regulatory mechanisms.

title: The proteogenomic landscape of the human kidney and implications for cardio-kidney-metabolic health
synopsis: Cardio-kidney-metabolic diseases affect about a third of people worldwide, but their molecular mechanisms are poorly understood. This study combined whole-genome sequencing, RNA sequencing and tissue proteomics from 337 human kidney samples and released the data as a public database. Colocalization and Mendelian randomization of kidney protein QTLs against 36 GWAS prioritized 89 proteins for these traits. Highlights include a possible role for kidney ANGPTL3 in serum lipids and kidney function, and for CHMP1A in kidney function and hypertension. Kidney tissue proteomics added information that neither tissue gene expression nor blood proteomics captured. The study points to targetable mechanisms that may link these related conditions.

title: Noncoding rare variant associations with blood traits in 166,740 UK Biobank genomes
synopsis: This study asks how to pick noncoding rare variants for association tests when whole-genome data cover almost the entire genome. Using knowledge of blood gene regulation and deleteriousness scores, it selected noncoding variants and ran collapsing tests on 42 blood cell count and biomarker traits in 166,740 UK Biobank genomes. The tests found hundreds of gene-trait associations involving noncoding variants. However, most of these repeated known associations or were driven by linkage disequilibrium between nearby common and rare variants. The work shows how hard noncoding rare variant analysis still is and argues for caution when interpreting such results.

title: Whole-genome sequencing of 490,640 UK Biobank participants
lab: the UK Biobank Whole-Genome Sequencing Consortium
synopsis: This paper describes whole-genome sequencing of 490,640 UK Biobank participants, adding to the cohort's earlier array genotyping. The sequences were linked to the biobank's detailed phenotype data to run genetic association studies within and across ancestry groups. Most disease associations were found in participants of European ancestry, but strong or new signals also appeared in participants of African and Asian ancestry. Because whole-genome sequencing genotypes structural variants and coding and UTR variation more accurately, it confirmed and extended results from earlier whole-exome analyses. The dataset is a major open resource for variant discovery, drug target work and precision medicine research.

title: Whole-exome sequencing analysis identifies risk genes for schizophrenia
synopsis: To find more genes in which rare coding variants affect schizophrenia risk, this study sequenced the exomes of 4,650 new cases and 5,719 controls. It combined them with published data, for a total of 28,898 cases, 103,041 controls and 3,444 proband-parent trios. STAG1 and ZNF136 reached exome-wide significance, and six more genes, including SLC6A1, PCLO and KLC1, were associated at a 5% false discovery rate. Several of these genes are also enriched for rare variants in other developmental and psychiatric disorders, and STAG1 and KLC1 also have fine-mapped common variant signals. The results add support for disrupted chromatin organisation as a cause of schizophrenia.

title: Epigenetic biomarkers predict macrovascular events in individuals with type 2 diabetes
synopsis: This study looks for blood DNA methylation markers that predict major cardiovascular events (heart attack, stroke and similar) in people newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. In 752 patients, 102 of whom had such an event during follow-up, 461 methylation sites were associated with events. A methylation risk score built from 87 sites reached an AUC of 0.81, or 0.84 when combined with clinical risk factors. Standard clinical and polygenic risk scores reached AUCs of only 0.54 to 0.62. Sites were partly validated in two independent cohorts, where a methylation score reached an AUC of 0.80. These epigenetic markers could improve cardiovascular risk stratification in diabetes care.

title: Rare-variant association studies: When are aggregation tests more powerful than single-variant tests?
synopsis: This paper asks when aggregation tests, which pool rare variants within a gene, are more powerful than testing each variant on its own. Using analytic calculations, released as an online tool, and simulations based on 378,215 UK Biobank participants, it shows that power depends on sample size times region heritability, the number of causal variants and the total number of variants. Aggregation tests win only when a large share of the pooled variants are causal. For example, pooling protein-truncating and deleterious missense variants is more powerful for over 55% of genes under plausible causal probabilities with 100,000 participants. The results help researchers choose a test for large rare-variant studies.

title: Towards improved fine-mapping of candidate causal variants
synopsis: This review covers statistical fine-mapping, which tries to identify likely causal variants among highly correlated candidates at genome-wide association loci. It explains that most methods use a multiple regression framework with different assumptions about effect sizes and different inference algorithms, and that most are Bayesian. It then surveys recent advances: refined modelling assumptions, use of functional and other external information, methods that work from summary statistics, and scalable algorithms. Together these have improved fine-mapping resolution and efficiency. The review is a useful overview of a key step in turning association signals into biological mechanisms.

title: Improved multiancestry fine-mapping identifies cis-regulatory variants underlying molecular traits and disease risk
synopsis: This paper presents SuShiE, a multiancestry fine-mapping model that uses differences in linkage disequilibrium between ancestries to better locate causal variants that affect gene expression and protein levels (cis-molQTLs). It also estimates how well effects correlate across ancestries and builds ancestry-specific prediction weights. In simulations it outperformed existing methods. Applied to 36,907 expression and protein phenotypes from TOPMed-MESA and GENOA, it fine-mapped 18.2% more genes, with smaller candidate sets and stronger functional enrichment. Effects were mostly shared across ancestries but differed at genes intolerant to loss of function. Transcriptome- and proteome-wide association studies on white blood cell traits in All of Us found 25.4% more genes.

title: Leveraging global genetics resources to enhance polygenic prediction across ancestrally diverse populations
synopsis: This study compares ways to build polygenic scores from GWAS summary statistics of several ancestries when no individual-level tuning data are available. It evaluated many single-source and multi-source methods for 10 traits in African, East Asian and European populations, using data from Uganda, Biobank Japan, UK Biobank and the Million Veteran Program. In African and East Asian populations, scores that combined ancestry-matched and European GWAS beat single-source scores. Linear combinations of separately optimized scores consistently outperformed jointly optimized multi-source methods and needed much less computation. A new use of the LEOPARD method tuned these combinations from summary statistics alone, matching tuning with individual-level data. All analyses are available in the open-source GenoPred pipeline.

title: DNA Methylation Signatures of Cardiovascular Health Provide Insights Into Diseases
synopsis: This study asks how overall cardiovascular health, measured by the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 score, relates to DNA methylation. Epigenome-wide association studies across five diverse cohorts identified 609 CpGs linked to the score, which were combined into a cardiovascular health methylation score. Mendelian randomization found 261 CpG-phenotype pairs involving 141 CpGs, including a locus near MIR33B and SREBF1 associated with lower stroke risk. Each standard deviation increase in the methylation score was associated with a 19-32% lower risk of incident cardiovascular disease and 27-45% lower all-cause mortality. The results point to epigenetic pathways that may connect cardiovascular health to clinical outcomes.

title: Borzoi-informed fine mapping improves causal variant prioritization in complex trait GWAS
synopsis: Statistical fine mapping often cannot resolve causal variants because of linkage disequilibrium and limited sample sizes. Functional priors help, but annotation overlap is only an indirect measure of variant impact. This work presents Sniff, which adds variant effects predicted by the long-context sequence model Borzoi to broad functional annotations within PolyFun to set prior causal probabilities. Across 15 UK Biobank traits, Sniff found 9.45% more variants with posterior inclusion probability above 0.8 than PolyFun-Baseline. Prioritized variants showed allele-specific activity in reporter assays, and the genes they nominated scored higher under PoPS for most traits. Attribution analysis of Borzoi predictions also suggests mechanistic hypotheses for GWAS associations.

title: Cross-omics risk scores of inflammation markers are associated with all-cause mortality: The Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
synopsis: This study asks whether omics-based scores capture inflammation burden beyond circulating biomarkers. Polygenic, metabolomic, and epigenetic risk scores for CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α were built and combined into multi-omics scores, then tested for prediction of all-cause mortality in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. Multi-omics scores generally outperformed single-omics scores. With circulating IL-6 in the same model, an IL-6 metabolomic-epigenetic score had a hazard ratio of 2.20 per SD, compared with 0.94 for measured IL-6. Modest associations replicated in older participants of three US cohorts. Combined omics scores may therefore improve how chronic inflammation is measured in aging and mortality research.

title: Leveraging local ancestry and cross-ancestry genetic architecture to improve genetic prediction of complex traits in admixed populations
synopsis: Polygenic risk scores transfer poorly beyond Europeans, and most cross-ancestry methods ignore admixed individuals, whose genomes mix local ancestries. This work introduces SDPR_admix, which models each variant's effects in two ancestries as jointly null, enriched in one ancestry, or shared with correlation. The method outperformed alternatives in simulations and improved prediction in European-African admixed UK Biobank participants when trained on PAGE (N = 13,000). Training on All of Us (N = 52,000) raised accuracy about five-fold on average at manageable computational cost. Both ancestry-enriched and shared effects contributed to the gains, and the method also performed best in admixed Americans with European and Indigenous American ancestry.

title: Transcriptional programs of cell identity and p53-induced stress responses are associated with distinctive features of spatial genome organization
synopsis: Most studies of 3D genome organization compare tissues or differentiation stages, where transcription is extensively reprogrammed. This study compares that setting with the narrower transcriptional response to stress, using p53 activation as a model. Micro-C, RNA-seq, and p53 ChIP-seq were profiled in 10 cell lines before and after p53 induction. Across cell types, gene expression tracked spatial organization, with hundreds of active enhancer-promoter loops tied to cell-type marker genes. Within a cell type, p53-induced expression changes showed no such link, even at p53-bound enhancers and promoters. These results suggest that identity-defining and stress-induced chromatin contacts differ, and they support a contact-independent model of enhancer-promoter communication.

title: Genome-Wide Association Study of Quantitative Kidney Function in 52,531 Individuals with Diabetes Identifies Five Diabetes-Specific Loci
source: Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN
synopsis: This study looks for genetic factors that affect kidney function specifically in diabetes. GWAS meta-analyses of eGFR were run in 52,531 individuals with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, accounting for kidney disease status, diabetes duration and subtype, BMI, HbA1c, and albuminuria. Thirteen loci reached genome-wide significance. Five of them, near HIPK3, TRIM5, RORA, ERBB4, and BCL6/LPP, were not associated with eGFR in the general population or acted in the opposite direction. Kidney expression and methylation QTL data supported several candidates, including a BCL6/LPP variant within a kidney enhancer. The findings point to diabetes-specific genetic mechanisms of diabetic kidney disease.

title: Applying blood-derived epigenetic algorithms to saliva: cross-tissue similarity of DNA-methylation indices of aging, physiology, and cognition
synopsis: Most epigenetic clocks and methylation profile scores were developed in blood, but saliva is easier to collect. This study pooled three public datasets with paired blood and saliva methylation from 107 people aged 5-74, corrected for cell composition, and computed cross-tissue intraclass correlations. Second- and third-generation measures showed moderate agreement: PCGrimAge 0.76, PCPhenoAge 0.72, Epigenetic-g 0.69, and DunedinPACE 0.68. Agreement was poor for first-generation clocks, at 0.19-0.25. Blood-trained scores may therefore be usable in saliva for some research, but not reliably for clinical or commercial use, and paired samples are needed to validate or build saliva-specific scores.

title: Using LDpred2 to adapt polygenic risk score techniques for methylation score creation
synopsis: This study tests whether LDpred2, a polygenic risk score tool, can be adapted to build methylation scores from methylome-wide association summary statistics. Because linkage disequilibrium does not apply to methylation, it replaced the LD prior with co-methylated regions, topologically associating domains, or genomic sliding windows. Models were evaluated on schizophrenia cases and controls (N = 1,227). Domain-based and sliding-window models matched existing methods, explaining about 3.6% of phenotypic variance, while the co-methylated region model underperformed. A random-cluster null model performed similarly to the domain-based one. LDpred2 can therefore be applied to methylation data, but it offers little improvement, and the choice of structural prior matters little.

title: Characterization of Monogenic Kidney Disease in Older Patients With CKD
synopsis: Monogenic causes explain about 10% of adult chronic kidney disease, but they are poorly characterized in people aged 60 or older. This study analyzed 265 older adults from 202 families referred to an Irish registry for suspected monogenic disease. Diagnostic variants were found in 60.4% of families, including 39% of families with noncystic disease. Variants linked to later-onset phenotypes, such as those in IFT140, ALG5, DNAJB11, monoallelic COL4A3 and UMOD p.Thr62Pro, were enriched in patients with onset at 60 or later and were associated with delayed kidney failure. Family history and a prior cystic disease diagnosis predicted a positive result. Genetic findings changed management in 24% of diagnosed patients.

title: Influence of race, ethnicity, and sex on the performance of epigenetic predictors of phenotypic traits
synopsis: This study asks whether DNA methylation-based predictors of traits work equally well across racial, ethnic, and sex groups, given that most were trained on samples with little diversity. Using a diverse sample of adult NHANES participants from 1999-2002, the authors tested epigenetic clocks and predictors of telomere length, cell proportions, and plasma proteins. They measured accuracy with correlations and median absolute errors and compared groups using bootstrapping and regression. Every predictor was associated with its target trait overall. However, each one showed at least one significant performance gap, most often lower correlation in Mexican American and non-Hispanic Black participants, and these gaps remained after adjusting for cell composition and socioeconomic factors. The findings raise concerns about using these biomarkers across diverse populations.

title: An atlas of single-cell eQTLs dissects autoimmune disease genes and identifies novel drug classes for treatment
synopsis: Many GWAS risk loci do not colocalize with expression QTLs, possibly because eQTL studies have limited power or because effects are specific to certain cell types. This work introduces JOBS, which models bulk-tissue eQTL effects as a weighted sum of cell-type-specific single-cell eQTL effects. This lets large bulk datasets boost the power of smaller single-cell studies. Applied to OneK1K and eQTLGen, JOBS found 586% more eQTLs, roughly the power of a single-cell study four times larger. Combining these eQTLs with GWAS for 14 immune-mediated diseases colocalized about 30% more loci than either data type alone. An extension of the method was used for drug repurposing and identified candidate drugs supported by real-world data.

title: Fine-mapping in admixed populations using CARMA-X, with applications to Latin American studies
synopsis: Statistical fine-mapping is difficult even in a single homogeneous population, and there are few methods for admixed populations such as those in Latin America and the Caribbean. This paper presents CARMA-X, a Bayesian fine-mapping method for admixed individuals. It estimates linkage disequilibrium in a way that accounts for small reference panels, differences between populations, and cross-ancestry LD, and it adds a hypothesis test that keeps results robust when LD comes from external panels. In simulations, CARMA-X had higher power than recent multi-ancestry methods while controlling false discoveries, especially when using out-of-sample LD. Applications to a Dominican Alzheimer's family study and the Mexican Biobank prioritized candidate causal variants, including findings driven by African- and Native American-specific effects.

title: CR1 variants contribute to FSGS susceptibility across multiple populations
synopsis: This study asks which rare genetic variants raise the risk of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome, across ancestries. The authors sequenced about 2,500 genes expressed in podocytes in 726 FSGS cases and 13,994 controls from diverse ethnic backgrounds and ran rare-variant association tests. The tests confirmed known risk genes and found a new association with the complement receptor gene CR1. The implicated variant, rs17047661 (the Sl1/Sl2, R1601G allele), was previously linked to protection against cerebral malaria. This points to a trade-off between resistance to infection and susceptibility to kidney disease, and to a role for immune pathways in FSGS that could be targeted by treatment.

title: Polygenic risk scores for eGFR are associated with age at kidney failure
synopsis: This study tests whether polygenic risk scores for traits related to chronic kidney disease predict the age at which patients reach kidney failure.
