Using genome-wide genotypes from 10,586 patients with kidney failure in 12 cohorts, the authors built scores for hypertension, albuminuria, rapid eGFR decline, reduced kidney volume and reduced eGFR from published GWAS weights. They then related each score to age at kidney failure, both overall and within each primary kidney disease. People in the top 10% of the reduced-eGFR score reached kidney failure about two years earlier. Each standard deviation increase in that score modestly raised the odds of kidney failure before age 60 (OR 1.05). The results suggest that common polygenic background shapes when kidney failure develops, not only whether it does.

title: Haploinsufficiency of ITSN1 is associated with a substantial increased risk of Parkinson's disease
synopsis: Parkinson's disease is substantially heritable, but much of its genetic basis remains unexplained. Using whole-genome sequencing of 3,809 cases and 247,101 controls in the UK Biobank, this study found that protein-truncating variants in ITSN1 raise Parkinson's risk about tenfold (odds ratio 10.5). The association replicated in three independent datasets with 8,407 cases, reaching a combined p of 4.5 × 10^-12. In fruit flies, losing the ITSN1 counterpart made α-synuclein-induced neuronal toxicity and motor problems worse, and lab assays suggested ITSN1 physically interacts with α-synuclein. ITSN1 loss has also been linked to autism. The results establish ITSN1 as a large-effect Parkinson's risk gene and point to vesicle trafficking as part of the disease mechanism.

title: Whole-genome sequencing analysis identifies rare, large-effect noncoding variants and regulatory regions associated with circulating protein levels
synopsis: Little is known about how rare noncoding genetic variants affect common traits, partly because large whole-genome sequencing datasets have only recently become available and noncoding variants are hard to group. This study used whole-genome sequences from about 50,000 UK Biobank participants to test 1.1 billion variants and 123 million noncoding aggregate tests against levels of 2,907 circulating proteins, focusing on variants near each protein's gene. It found 604 independent rare noncoding single-variant associations. Unlike rare coding variants, these were almost as likely to raise protein levels as to lower them. Aggregate tests found 357 independent associated regions, 21% of which single-variant tests missed. This shows the value of grouping noncoding variants when testing for rare-variant effects.

title: Benchmarking DNA Sequence Models for Causal Regulatory Variant Prediction in Human Genetics
synopsis: Predicting which noncoding variants cause traits is a central problem, but the field has lacked well-curated labeled datasets to compare machine learning models fairly. This work introduces TraitGym, a set of causal or strong-candidate regulatory variants for 113 Mendelian and 83 complex traits, paired with carefully matched control variants. The authors tested supervised sequence-to-function models, self-supervised DNA language models, annotation-based models, and ensembles on a binary classification task. Alignment-based models CADD and GPN-MSA did best for Mendelian and complex disease traits, while Enformer and Borzoi did better for complex non-disease traits. Evo2 improved with scale but still trailed alignment-based models, especially on enhancer variants. The benchmark is publicly available.

title: Kidney multiome-based genetic scorecard reveals convergent coding and regulatory variants
synopsis: This study aims to clarify the genetic architecture of kidney function and to prioritize causal genes. A multi-ancestry genome-wide association study of 2.2 million individuals identified 1,026 independent loci, 97 of them new. Ancestry-specific analyses showed that new common-variant signals are weaker in European-ancestry populations, which highlights the value of diverse cohorts for further discovery. The authors mapped allele-specific expression and regulatory circuits in more than 700 human kidneys and 237,000 single cells. They found 1,363 coding variants in 782 genes, with coding and regulatory variants converging on 161 genes. Combining 32 types of genetic evidence, they built a Kidney Disease Genetic Scorecard that ranks candidate causal genes, cell types and druggable targets.

title: A novel framework to build saliva-based DNA methylation biomarkers: Quantifying systemic chronic inflammation as a case study
synopsis: Saliva is easier to collect than blood, but most DNA methylation biomarkers of ageing and disease risk were built from blood. This work presents a framework for building saliva-based methylation biomarkers by using a dataset with replicate samples across tissues to carry blood-derived methylation proxies of proteins (EpiScores) over to saliva. The authors used it to build InflammAge, an epigenetic clock that measures systemic chronic inflammation. In Generation Scotland, a cohort of over 18,000 people with linked health records, InflammAge was associated with all-cause mortality, disease outcomes, lifestyle factors, and immune ageing, often outperforming C-reactive protein. The framework could support non-invasive monitoring of ageing and of interventions aimed at slowing it.

title: Blood-based epigenome-wide association study and prediction of alcohol consumption
synopsis: Self-reported alcohol intake is prone to recall error, so this study asks whether blood DNA methylation can measure drinking more objectively. In Generation Scotland, the authors trained an elastic net methylation score (EpiScore) for weekly alcohol units on 16,717 people, also testing CpG pre-filtering, sex differences, and recent versus typical drinking. In four external cohorts totaling over 10,000 people, the score's correlation with self-reported intake reached 0.41 to 0.53. In the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936, higher scores were linked to worse global brain imaging measures, while self-reported drinking was not. A Bayesian epigenome-wide association study also found two new CpG sites associated with alcohol intake.

title: Cell state-dependent allelic effects and contextual Mendelian randomization analysis for human brain phenotypes
synopsis: This study asks whether brain disease changes the genetic effects on gene expression that are used to link genes to central nervous system traits. Using about 2.35 million single-nucleus profiles from 391 disease and control brains, it identified 13,939 genes with expression QTLs, and 16.7-40.8% of them, depending on cell type, had allelic effects that depended on disease. Of 501 colocalizations across 30 traits, 23.6% depended on disease. An analysis limited to 183 control brains found 91 more colocalizations, and single-cell Mendelian randomization in this group nominated 140 putatively causal gene-trait links, 11 of which replicated in UK Biobank. The results show why disease context matters when choosing eQTL references for causal inference.

title: Predicting RNA-seq coverage from DNA sequence as a unifying model of gene regulation
synopsis: This work presents Borzoi, a deep learning model that predicts cell-type- and tissue-specific RNA-seq coverage directly from DNA sequence. It aims to capture several layers of gene regulation in one model. Statistics derived from the predicted coverage are used to score how variants affect transcription, splicing and polyadenylation. On quantitative trait loci, Borzoi is competitive with, and often outperforms, state-of-the-art models trained on single regulatory functions. Attribution analyses recover cis-regulatory motifs that drive expression and post-transcriptional regulation. Because RNA-seq data are abundant, this offers a scalable, unified route for interpreting noncoding variants.

title: Genome-wide characterization of 54 urinary metabolites reveals molecular impact of kidney function
synopsis: This study maps the genetic determinants of urinary metabolite levels to gain molecular insight into kidney function. The authors meta-analysed genome-wide association studies of 54 metabolites measured by proton NMR in 8,011 people from three European cohorts, including both people with type 1 diabetes and general-population samples. They found 54 associations for 19 metabolites, 33 of them not previously reported for related urinary or blood traits. Two-sample Mendelian randomization suggested that eGFR causally affects 13 urinary metabolite levels. Urinary ethanolamine was associated with higher eGFR, which points to a possible protective role. The resulting catalogue of genetic associations supports further work on how urinary metabolites relate to health and disease.

title: ChromBPNet: bias factorized, base-resolution deep learning models of chromatin accessibility reveal cis-regulatory sequence syntax, transcription factor footprints and regulatory variants
synopsis: This preprint introduces ChromBPNet, a lightweight deep learning model that predicts base-resolution chromatin accessibility profiles from DNA sequence. It explicitly separates enzyme-specific assay biases from the sequence determinants of accessibility. This allows robust discovery of transcription factor motif lexicons, cooperative motif syntax and precise footprints across assays and sequencing depths. In extensive benchmarks it is competitive with much larger models at predicting variant effects on accessibility, pioneer factor binding and reporter activity across cell contexts and ancestries, and it explains which regulatory syntax a variant disrupts. The model helps prioritize and interpret regulatory variants underlying complex traits and rare diseases.

title: DNA methylation models of protein abundance across the lifecourse
synopsis: This study asks how well DNA methylation-based predictors of protein abundance (episcores) capture non-genetic variation in proteins across the lifecourse. Using blood samples from the ALSPAC cohort at ages 7-24 and from mothers antenatally and in midlife, it tested 14 published episcores, trained new age-specific ones and compared them across ages, with and without adjusting for genotype. Published episcores tracked protein levels in midlife (10 of 14) and at age 24 (9) but at no point in childhood, and several explained variation beyond genetics. Newly trained models transferred only partly between ages. Overall, episcores work better in adults than in children.

title: DNA methylation-based predictors of metabolic traits in Scottish and Singaporean cohorts
synopsis: This study used blood DNA methylation from more than 17,000 Generation Scotland participants to run epigenome-wide association studies and train epigenetic scores for six metabolic traits, including BMI, body fat, waist-hip ratio, glucose and cholesterol. A marginal EWAS gave up to 12,033 significant CpGs for BMI, whereas a joint Bayesian penalized model gave only 27 high-confidence associations. The scores transferred to Scottish and Singaporean test cohorts, with the BMI score explaining 20.8% of variance in HELIOS and 14.4% in LBC1936. Performance for body fat varied by ancestry subgroup, and the scores were associated with cognitive function. The results show that modeling correlation across the methylome changes EWAS conclusions and that methylation proxies of metabolic traits work across populations.

title: Nucleotide Transformer: building and evaluating robust foundation models for human genomics
synopsis: This work builds and evaluates the Nucleotide Transformer, a family of DNA foundation models from 50 million to 2.5 billion parameters. They were pretrained on 3,202 human genomes and 850 genomes from other species. The models produce context-aware sequence representations that support accurate molecular phenotype prediction even with little labeled data, and they can be fine-tuned cheaply for many genomics tasks. Without supervision, their attention concentrates on key genomic elements, and their outputs improve genetic variant prioritization. The study supports large-scale pretraining as a general approach for predicting molecular phenotypes from sequence.

title: Exome sequencing in Asian populations identifies low-frequency and rare coding variation influencing Parkinson's disease risk
synopsis: This study asks whether rare protein-altering variants explain part of Parkinson's disease risk in Asian populations. Whole-exome sequencing and gene-based tests were run on 4,298 cases and 5,512 controls of Asian ancestry, with replication in a further 5,585 cases and 5,642 controls. GBA1 and SMPD1 were significantly associated with risk. In vitro enzyme assays showed that SMPD1 variants with reduced activity carried the strongest association. Most SMPD1 carriers had the Asian-specific p.Pro332Arg variant (OR 2.16, P = 4.47 × 10^-8), which highlights the value of sequencing diverse ancestries.

title: Sequence modeling and design from molecular to genome scale with Evo
synopsis: This work introduces Evo, a long-context genomic foundation model trained on millions of prokaryotic and phage genomes. It also reports scaling laws for models trained on DNA. Evo works across DNA, RNA and protein, giving zero-shot function predictions competitive with specialized language models. It also generated functional CRISPR-Cas and transposon systems, which the authors describe as the first protein-RNA and protein-DNA codesign with a language model. The model captures how small mutations affect whole-organism fitness and can generate megabase-scale sequences with plausible genome organization, which broadens sequence modeling from single molecules to whole genomes.

title: APOL1 Bi- and Monoallelic Variants and Chronic Kidney Disease in West Africans
source: The New England journal of medicine
synopsis: This case-control study asks whether APOL1 risk variants, known to drive chronic kidney disease in Black Americans, are linked to kidney disease in West Africans. It analyzed 8355 participants from Ghana and Nigeria with CKD, biopsy-proven glomerular disease, or no kidney disease, using logistic regression adjusted for site, age, and sex. Two risk alleles were carried by 29.7% of participants and one by 43.0%. Two alleles raised the odds of CKD by 25% and of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis by 84%, and a single allele raised them by 18% and 61%. This suggests that carrying one risk allele also matters, even though APOL1 risk is usually described as recessive.

title: Whole-genome sequencing in 333,100 individuals reveals rare non-coding single variant and aggregate associations with height
lab: the NHLBI Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine (TOPMed) Consortium
synopsis: This study asks how rare non-coding variants in regulatory elements affect height. It ran a whole-genome sequencing association analysis in 333,100 individuals from UK Biobank, TOPMed, and All of Us. The analysis tested single variants and aggregates of variants below 0.1% frequency, grouped by proximal-regulatory, intergenic-regulatory, and deep-intronic annotation. It found 29 independent variants beyond previously reported signals, with effects from -7 cm to +4.7 cm. Replicated aggregate signals included variants near HMGA1 linked to about 5 cm greater height and conserved variants in MIR497HG. The work offers a framework for finding large-effect rare regulatory variants for complex traits.

title: Integration of variant annotations using deep set networks boosts rare variant association testing
synopsis: Rare variant association tests have limited power because few people carry each allele and many tests are run, and existing methods do not combine variant annotations in a data-driven way. This paper introduces DeepRVAT, a set neural network that learns a gene impairment score from rare variant annotations and phenotypes, and that score is not tied to any one trait. Applied to UK Biobank exome data for 34 quantitative and 63 binary traits, it found substantially more associated genes and better identified individuals at high genetic risk. The method gives calibrated, computationally efficient rare variant tests at biobank scale, supporting both gene discovery and trait prediction.

title: Polygenic scores and their applications in kidney disease
synopsis: This review looks at how polygenic scores, which add up the small effects of many GWAS variants, can improve risk prediction for chronic kidney disease and other complex disorders. It covers evolving methods for building scores, best practices for validating and reporting their performance, and study designs needed for clinical implementation. Some scores now have effects large enough to be clinically actionable. Their use is still limited by partial transfer across ancestries, a lack of validated models that combine polygenic, monogenic, family-history, and clinical factors, and missing prospective evidence of clinical utility and cost-effectiveness. The review focuses on nephrology applications and the refinements still required.

title: Fine-mapping across diverse ancestries drives the discovery of putative causal variants underlying human complex traits and diseases
lab: the Schizophrenia Workgroup of Psychiatric Genomics Consortium
synopsis: GWAS loci often contain many variants with similar evidence, which makes it hard to identify the causal ones, and most fine-mapping has used only European-ancestry data. This paper presents SuSiEx, a cross-population fine-mapping method that works on summary statistics. It combines any number of ancestries, models population-specific allele frequencies and linkage disequilibrium, and allows multiple causal variants per region. Simulations showed it is accurate and computationally efficient. It improved fine-mapping of quantitative traits in UK Biobank and Taiwan Biobank, and of schizophrenia loci when East Asian and European GWAS were combined. The work shows how ancestral diversity can sharpen causal variant resolution.

title: Systematic rare variant analyses identify RAB32 as a susceptibility gene for familial Parkinson's disease
lab: the Project MinE ALS Sequencing Consortium
synopsis: Most familial Parkinson's disease cases lack an identified causal variant. To find high-risk variants, this study uniformly processed exome sequencing data from 2,184 index familial cases and 69,775 controls. Exome-wide analyses pointed to RAB32, where the p.S71R variant was found in about 0.7% of familial cases versus 0.004% of controls, an odds ratio of 65.5. The variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and segregated with disease in three families. Functional experiments showed it increases the kinase activity of LRRK2, a known Parkinson's gene that interacts with RAB32. This links RAB biology to a central pathological mechanism in Parkinson's disease.

title: A cell type–specific approach to elucidate the role of miR-96 in inner ear hair cells
synopsis: Mutations in microRNA-96 cause progressive hearing loss in mice and humans, but its targets in inner ear hair cells are not well defined. This study produced the first hair cell-specific bulk RNA-seq dataset from newborn wildtype, heterozygous, and homozygous Mir96 Dmdo mutant mice, followed by differential expression, gene ontology, and protein interaction analyses. Homozygous mutants showed 215 upregulated and 428 downregulated genes. Downregulated genes included known deafness and hair cell development genes such as Myo15a, Myo7a, Ush1c, Gfi1, and Ptprq. Upregulated genes tended to be expressed in supporting cells, which suggests miR-96 represses supporting-cell programs in hair cells. The data are publicly available in gEAR.

title: Leveraging functional genomic annotations and genome coverage to improve polygenic prediction of complex traits within and between ancestries
synopsis: This paper introduces SBayesRC, a method that combines GWAS summary statistics with functional genomic annotations to improve polygenic prediction. Annotations can shape both the probability that a variant is causal and the distribution of its effect size. Across 50 traits and diseases, using about 7 million common SNPs and 96 annotations, it improved accuracy by 14% in European ancestry and up to 34% across ancestries compared with SBayesR, which uses no annotations. It also outperformed LDpred2, PRS-CSx, and other methods. Evolutionarily constrained regions contributed most to accuracy, and an interaction between SNP density and annotations suggests that annotated whole-genome sequence data could improve prediction further.

title: Drugst.One — a plug-and-play solution for online systems medicine and network-based drug repurposing
synopsis: Many computational tools can propose candidates for drug repurposing, but they are often hard to install and do not let users explore networks visually. This work introduces Drugst.One, a platform that turns systems biology software into an interactive web tool for building and analyzing protein-drug-disease networks, using only three lines of code. To show that it adapts to different tools, the platform has been integrated with 21 computational systems medicine tools. It is available at drugst.one and aims to make network-based drug repurposing methods easier for researchers to reach and use.

title: Large-scale whole-exome sequencing of neuropsychiatric diseases and traits in 350,770 adults
synopsis: This study asks how protein-coding variants contribute to neuropsychiatric conditions, which until now have been mapped mostly through common noncoding loci. Using whole-exome sequencing of 350,770 UK Biobank adults, the authors tested coding variants against 46 diseases and 23 traits. They found 20 new disease genes, 16 of which affected longitudinal disease risk, and 30 new trait genes, with SYNGAP1 showing pleiotropic effects across cognitive domains. Genetic correlations at the coding-variant level showed shared signals between neurodegenerative diseases and mental disorders. Multi-omics analysis pointed to brain structure, blood proteins and inflammation as possible mediators of these gene-phenotype links.

title: Tissue-specific enhancer–gene maps from multimodal single-cell data identify causal disease alleles
lab: the Accelerating Medicines Partnership® RA/SLE Program and Network
synopsis: Finding the causal variants and genes behind GWAS loci requires cell-type-specific enhancer-gene maps, which are hard to build experimentally in primary human tissue. This work presents SCENT, a nonparametric method that links enhancer chromatin accessibility to gene expression in single-cell multimodal RNA and ATAC sequencing data. Applied to 9 datasets with more than 120,000 cells or nuclei, it produced 23 cell-type-specific maps. These maps were strongly enriched for causal eQTL variants and for GWAS variants across 1,143 diseases and traits. They also nominated causal genes for common and rare diseases and linked somatic mutation hotspots to target genes, offering a scalable way to interpret noncoding variants.

title: Genomic data in the All of Us Research Program
synopsis: This paper describes the genomic data release of the All of Us Research Program, a US cohort that aims to enroll a diverse group of one million people. The release contains 245,388 clinical-grade genome sequences, with 77% of participants from communities historically under-represented in biomedical research and 46% from under-represented racial and ethnic minorities. It identified more than 1 billion variants, over 275 million of them previously unreported. Using linked electronic health records, the authors tested 3,724 known variant-disease associations across 117 diseases and found high replication rates in participants of both European and African ancestry. Summary data are public, and individual-level data are available through a controlled workbench.

title: PRS-Net: Interpretable polygenic risk scores via geometric learning
synopsis: Standard polygenic risk scores are linear models and may miss nonlinear relationships between genotype and phenotype. This work introduces PRS-Net, a deep learning framework that first breaks the genome-wide score down into gene-level contributions. It then models gene-gene interactions with a graph neural network, and an attention-based readout module makes the model interpretable. Across several complex diseases, PRS-Net consistently outperformed baseline PRS methods at predicting disease. Its interpretability was demonstrated by identifying genes and gene-gene interactions that influence risk of Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis, so the framework serves both risk prediction and biological discovery.

title: The cells of the sensory epithelium, and not the stria vascularis, are the main cochlear cells related to the genetic pathogenesis of age-related hearing loss
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: Earlier studies that combined GWAS results with transcriptomic data disagreed on which inner-ear cells drive the genetic risk of age-related hearing loss: cochlear sensory epithelial cells or stria vascularis cells. To resolve this, the authors combined four age-related hearing loss GWAS datasets with four independent inner-ear single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets. Their analysis clearly pointed to cochlear sensory epithelial cells as the main cell type behind the genetic predisposition. They also explain the analytical limitation that caused earlier studies to miss the enrichment in these cells. This finding helps direct mechanistic and therapeutic research on hearing loss toward the relevant cell populations.

title: The predictive capacity of polygenic risk scores for disease risk is only moderately influenced by imputation panels tailored to the target population
synopsis: Polygenic risk scores lose accuracy when GWAS done mainly in Europeans are applied to other ancestries, and genotype imputation is a key step in building these scores. This study asks whether imputing the target cohort with a reference panel matched to its ancestry improves prediction when the discovery and target populations differ. Using ancestrally distinct groups from the UK Biobank and other resources, the authors built ancestry-homogeneous imputation panels, imputed target sets, computed scores for binary phenotypes, and compared prediction accuracy. An ancestry-matched panel gave only a marginal improvement, and only under specific conditions. This suggests that the choice of imputation panel is not a major lever for improving cross-ancestry prediction.

title: Analysis of rare Parkinson's disease variants in millions of people
synopsis: Many rare variants reported for Parkinson's disease have never been replicated, or have failed to replicate. This study carried out a large-scale replication using 27,590 cases, 6,701 proxy cases and more than 3.1 million controls from 23andMe, UK Biobank and AMP-PD. The authors selected 834 ClinVar-annotated variants in known Parkinson's disease genes and meta-analyzed summary statistics across the three datasets. Five variants, including ones in GBA1 and LRRK2, remained significant after Bonferroni correction, and eight more emerged as strong candidates. As the largest rare-variant meta-analysis for the disease to date, it clarifies which reported variants hold up and shows how hard it is to study rare variants in large cohorts.

title: MESuSiE enables scalable and powerful multi-ancestry fine-mapping of causal variants in genome-wide association studies
synopsis: Fine-mapping of genome-wide association signals is usually done in one ancestry at a time, which limits how precisely causal variants can be pinpointed. This paper introduces MESuSiE, a probabilistic method that works on summary statistics from several ancestries. It accounts for each ancestry's linkage disequilibrium pattern, models shared and ancestry-specific causal SNPs, and uses variational inference so it scales. In simulations and in fine-mapping of four lipid traits in European and African samples, it improved resolution by 19.0% to 72.0% over existing approaches and ran about ten times faster. The causal signals it sorted into shared and ancestry-specific groups showed stronger functional enrichment.

title: Benchmarking of deep neural networks for predicting personal gene expression from DNA sequence highlights shortcomings
synopsis: Deep learning models that predict gene expression from DNA sequence are usually judged on how well they predict across genes. They are rarely tested on whether they explain expression differences between individuals. Using paired whole-genome sequencing and expression data from 839 individuals in the ROSMAP study, this benchmark tested current models across individuals at a range of loci. The models often predicted the wrong direction for variant effects on expression. The authors trace this to sequence motif grammar the models have not learned well enough, and they suggest new training strategies. These results matter for anyone hoping to use these models to interpret personal genomes.

title: Personal transcriptome variation is poorly explained by current genomic deep learning models
synopsis: Genomic deep learning models predict expression levels across genes and cell types well from the reference genome. It is less clear whether they can explain expression differences between people caused by cis-regulatory variants. This study tested four state-of-the-art models on paired personal genome and transcriptome data. All four did poorly at explaining expression variation across individuals. They also often predicted the wrong direction of effect for cis-regulatory variants. The findings show a major gap that must be closed before these models can reliably interpret noncoding variation in individual genomes.

title: DNA language models are powerful predictors of genome-wide variant effects
synopsis: Finding the causal variants behind GWAS associations is hard, and testing them experimentally is costly. This work introduces GPN, a DNA language model pretrained without supervision on genomic sequence, which extends an approach that already works for proteins to the whole genome. Trained on unaligned reference genomes of Arabidopsis thaliana and seven related Brassicales species, it learned gene structure and DNA motifs with no labels. Its variant effect predictions, evaluated against 1001 Genomes allele frequencies and a large GWAS database, beat conservation scores such as phyloP and phastCons. Because it needs only DNA sequence, the method can be trained for any species, including those with few annotations.

title: Systematic differences in discovery of genetic effects on gene expression and complex traits
synopsis: Most GWAS signals point to noncoding regulatory variants, yet known eQTLs explain only a small share of them. This study compares GWAS and cis-eQTL hits and finds that they differ systematically. eQTLs cluster tightly near transcription start sites, while GWAS hits do not. Genes near GWAS hits are enriched for functional annotations, are under strong selective constraint and have complex regulatory landscapes. Genes near eQTLs show the opposite pattern. The authors propose a model in which natural selection on complex traits makes functionally relevant eQTLs harder to discover. This argues for complementary functional approaches alongside the next generation of eQTL studies.

title: A new method for multiancestry polygenic prediction improves performance across diverse populations
synopsis: Polygenic risk scores perform worse in non-European populations, which raises concerns about clinical use and health equity. This paper presents CT-SLEB, a scalable method that builds scores from ancestry-specific GWAS summary statistics. It combines clumping and thresholding, empirical Bayes and superlearning. The method was compared with nine alternatives using large simulations and data from 23andMe, the Global Lipids Genetics Consortium, All of Us and UK Biobank. These covered 5.1 million people, 1.18 million of them from four non-European populations, across 13 traits. CT-SLEB clearly beat simple alternatives in non-European groups and matched or exceeded a more computationally intensive method.

title: Shared and organ-specific gene-expression programs during the development of the cochlea and the superior olivary complex
synopsis: The cochlea and the central auditory system must develop in coordination, but the gene expression programs they share have not been studied systematically. This study used mRNA and small-RNA sequencing of the cochlea and superior olivary complex at three developmental timepoints (E16, P0 and P16). Differentially regulated mRNAs and microRNAs formed shared and organ-specific clusters, linked to functions such as inner ear development, Wnt signalling, potassium transport and axon guidance. Target enrichment, combined with opposite expression trends between miRNAs and their targets, pointed to six miRNAs as candidate regulators of both subsystems. One of them is miR-96, already known to be essential for auditory development, which supports the approach.

title: Evaluation of European-based polygenic risk score for breast cancer in Ashkenazi Jewish women in Israel
synopsis: Most breast cancer GWAS have been done in women of European ancestry, so it is unclear how well the resulting polygenic risk scores work in other groups. This study tested European-based scores, built from Breast Cancer Association Consortium data, in Ashkenazi Jewish women in Israel. It used 2,161 women from the consortium's Israeli cohort and an independent group of 181 women from Hadassah Medical Center. In the first cohort the best score gave an odds ratio of 1.56 per standard deviation, and 2.10 for the top 10% versus the middle quintile. In the Hadassah cohort the odds ratios were 1.58 for the best score and 1.64 for the established 313-SNP score. Existing European scores can therefore identify Ashkenazi Jewish women at clearly elevated risk.

title: Large-scale rare variant burden testing in Parkinson's disease
synopsis: This study asks how rare genetic variants contribute to Parkinson's disease risk, an area previously lacking large-scale analysis. Using whole genome and exome sequencing from 7,184 cases, 6,701 proxy cases and 51,650 controls across AMP-PD, NIH, UK Biobank and Genentech, it ran burden test meta-analyses on rare protein-altering variants prioritized by predicted functional impact. Known risk genes GBA1 and LRRK2 reached exome-wide significance. Potential new associations were found in B3GNT3, AUNIP, ADH5, TUBA1B, OR1G1, CAPN10 and TREML1, but none replicated across independent datasets. B3GNT3 and TREML1 may point to a role for neuroinflammation. It is the largest rare-variant analysis of Parkinson's disease to date.

title: CARMA is a new Bayesian model for fine-mapping in genome-wide association meta-analyses
Current sequence-based models capture gene expression determinants in promoters but mostly ignore distal enhancers
synopsis: This study tests whether deep sequence-to-expression models such as Enformer learn causal regulatory signals, given that they are trained only on natural variation between human genes. Model predictions were compared with two large observational studies and five deep perturbation assays. Enformer largely captures the causal determinants of promoter activity, but the models fail to capture enhancer effects, especially at medium to long distances and for highly expressed promoters. Distal elements have little influence on predictions, and the models use long-range information far less than their receptive fields suggest, probably because of growing class imbalance with distance. The results support in silico analysis of promoters and promoter variants, and suggest that modeling distal regulation will need new kinds of training data.

title: Polygenic architecture of rare coding variation across 394,783 exomes
synopsis: This study measures how much heritability comes from rare coding variation and how it relates to common-variant architecture. Using 394,783 UK Biobank exomes and 22 traits and diseases, it estimates heritability explained by the gene-wise burden of rare coding variants. Rare coding variants explain 1.3% of phenotypic variance on average, mostly through ultrarare loss-of-function variants, and about 2% for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Common and rare variants implicate the same cell types and have similar genetic correlations, but burden heritability is concentrated in fewer significant and constrained genes. Rare coding variants should point to a tractable set of large-effect genes but add only modestly to missing heritability and risk prediction.

title: FinnGen provides genetic insights from a well-phenotyped isolated population
synopsis: This study tests whether a bottlenecked population with rich health-register data can speed discovery in common disease genetics. It analyzes 224,737 Finnish participants, many recruited through hospitals, meta-analyzed with Estonian and UK biobank data. In 15 well-studied diseases it found 30 new associations, mostly low-frequency variants enriched in Finland. A GWAS of 1,932 disease end points produced 2,733 genome-wide significant associations at 2,496 loci. Fine-mapping implicated 148 coding variants, 62 of which were enriched more than twofold in Finland compared with other Europeans. The work shows how founder populations can reveal low-frequency, high-impact variants that point to disease biology.

title: The LHX2-OTX2 transcriptional regulatory module controls retinal pigmented epithelium differentiation and underlies genetic risk for age-related macular degeneration
synopsis: This study asks which transcription factors control the identity of the retinal pigmented epithelium and how their binding sites relate to genetic risk for age-related macular degeneration. Stem-cell-derived human RPE, mouse functional studies, and transcriptomic and proteomic profiling show that LHX2 and OTX2 work together with LDB1 and SWI/SNF in a module that regulates the RPE transcriptome. The LHX2-OTX2 binding sites were intersected with eQTLs, RPE ATAC-seq and AMD GWAS data, and reporter assays validated a candidate variant. This identified a causal variant that alters TRPM1 expression by changing LHX2 activity at its promoter. The work links a developmental regulatory module to a mechanism of risk for a common blinding disease.

title: Discovery and systematic characterization of risk variants and genes for coronary artery disease in over a million participants
synopsis: This study aims to find more coronary artery disease risk loci and to work out their likely causal variants and genes. It ran a GWAS of 181,522 cases among 1,165,690 mostly European-ancestry participants, which found 241 associations, including 30 new loci. Meta-analysis with a Japanese GWAS added 38 more new loci. Functionally informed fine-mapping narrowed 42 signals to fewer than five candidate variants, and combining eight methods prioritized 220 candidate genes. Clustering implicated developmental, cell cycle and vascular cell migration processes. CRISPR experiments validated an enhancer in MYO9B that appears to affect vascular cell motility. The work characterizes more than 250 risk loci to guide experimental follow-up.

title: Meta-analysis fine-mapping is often miscalibrated at single-variant resolution
lab: the China Kadoorie Biobank Collaborative Group
synopsis: This study examines whether fine-mapping GWAS meta-analyses with methods designed for a single cohort gives well-calibrated results. It shows that differences between cohorts, such as sample size, phenotyping and imputation, degrade calibration. It introduces SLALOM, a summary-statistics quality-control method that flags suspicious loci by detecting outlying association statistics, and validates it in simulations and the GWAS Catalog. In 14 Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative meta-analyses, 67% of loci looked suspicious, and these loci were depleted for nonsynonymous lead variants. There was little evidence that meta-analysis improved fine-mapping over individual biobanks. Fine-mapping results from heterogeneous meta-analyses should be interpreted with great caution.

title: A framework for detecting noncoding rare-variant associations of large-scale whole-genome sequencing studies
lab: the NHLBI Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine (TOPMed) Consortium
synopsis: This study addresses how to test rare noncoding variants for association with complex traits in large whole-genome sequencing studies, where existing variant-set methods are limited. It presents STAARpipeline, an efficient framework that annotates WGS data and runs both gene-centric and window-based analyses. Gene-centric tests group noncoding variants by functional category using STAAR, while non-gene-centric tests use SCANG-STAAR with fixed or dynamic windows. Both incorporate multiple functional annotations. Applied to four lipid traits in 21,015 TOPMed samples, it identified noncoding rare-variant sets, several of which replicated in 9,123 additional samples, and it was also applied to five other traits. It gives a scalable tool for studying the noncoding rare-variant genome.

title: The construction of cross-population polygenic risk scores using transfer learning
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: Polygenic risk scores built from European-ancestry GWAS predict poorly in other ancestry groups, and large non-European GWAS remain scarce. This study proposes TL-PRS, a transfer learning method that uses gradient descent to fine-tune a baseline PRS model trained on a large-ancestry GWAS so that it fits data from the target ancestry. The method was applied to seven quantitative and two binary traits in 10,285 South Asian and 8,168 African-ancestry UK Biobank participants. With PRS-CS as the baseline, TL-PRS raised predicted R2 by 25% on average in South Asian samples and 29% in African samples. The approach makes better use of limited non-European data and helps narrow ancestry gaps in genetic prediction.

title: A saturated map of common genetic variants associated with human height
synopsis: This study asks whether GWAS can capture nearly all common-variant heritability for human height. A GWAS of 5.4 million individuals of diverse ancestries found 12,111 independent significant SNPs that account for nearly all common SNP-based heritability. The SNPs fall within 7,209 genomic segments covering about 21% of the genome, and regions with dense associations are enriched for biologically relevant genes. Out of sample, these SNPs explain 40% of height variance in Europeans but only about 10-20% in other ancestries. Effect sizes are similar across ancestries, which points to linkage disequilibrium and allele-frequency differences as the cause of weaker prediction. The map is saturated for European ancestry, while other ancestries need further work.

title: Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative: Powering genetic discovery across human disease
synopsis: Most biobanks are dominated by individuals of European ancestry, which limits genetic discovery and prediction for other groups. This paper introduces the Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative, a network of 23 biobanks on four continents covering more than 2.2 million individuals with genetic data linked to electronic health records. Using harmonized genotypes and phenotypes, the network meta-analyzes GWAS summary statistics for 14 example diseases and endpoints. It shows that GWAS from diverse biobanks can be combined despite differences in case definitions, recruitment and cohort characteristics. The combined analyses increase power, help with understudied diseases, improve risk prediction, and support nominating disease genes and drug candidates.

title: Alternative cleavage and polyadenylation generates downstream uncapped RNA isoforms with translation potential
synopsis: This study examines whether alternative cleavage and polyadenylation (APA) does more than end transcripts. The authors identify thousands of previously undescribed 5' uncapped, polyadenylated transcripts that resist exonucleases because of structured RNA and N6-methyladenosine at their 5' ends. These transcripts appear downstream of APA sites within their host genes, are induced when APA is activated, and are enriched in polysomes. APA was shown to promote downstream translation initiation, non-canonical protein output and changes in peptides presented at the cell surface. In Bcl2, an anti-apoptotic gene, the entire coding sequence is produced as such a transcript from APA sites in the 5' UTR. APA thus emerges as a source of new translatable RNAs.

title: Identifying disease-critical cell types and cellular processes by integrating single-cell RNA-sequencing and human genetics
synopsis: GWAS have identified many disease loci, but the cell types and states through which these loci act often remain unknown. This study introduces sc-linker, a framework that combines single-cell RNA-seq, epigenomic SNP-to-gene maps and GWAS summary statistics to infer disease-relevant cell types and cellular programs. The inferred enrichments recovered known biology and pointed to GABAergic neurons in major depressive disorder, a disease-dependent M-cell program in ulcerative colitis, and a complement cascade process in multiple sclerosis. In autoimmune disease, both healthy and disease-dependent immune programs were implicated, whereas only disease-dependent epithelial programs were, suggesting the epithelial programs reflect disease response rather than initiation. The framework helps link genetic risk to specific pathogenic processes.

title: SAIGE-GENE+ improves the efficiency and accuracy of set-based rare variant association tests
synopsis: Large biobank sequencing makes it possible to test rare variants gene by gene, but the existing SAIGE-GENE method shows inflated type I error in variance-component tests restricted to very rare variants (MAF at or below 0.1% or 0.01%). This study presents SAIGE-GENE+, which greatly improves type I error control and computational efficiency. The authors also show that combining multiple MAF cutoffs and functional annotations increases power. Applied to UK Biobank whole-exome sequencing data for 30 quantitative and 141 binary traits, SAIGE-GENE+ identified 551 gene-phenotype associations. The method makes well-calibrated rare variant association testing practical at biobank scale.

title: Efficient and accurate frailty model approach for genome-wide survival association analysis in large-scale biobanks
synopsis: Biobanks that link genetic data to electronic health records make it possible to study the genetics of age at onset, disease progression and lifespan. This study proposes an efficient frailty-model approach for genome-wide survival analysis of censored time-to-event phenotypes that accounts for population structure and relatedness. It uses optimization strategies to reduce computational cost and a saddlepoint approximation to handle heavy censoring (above 90%) and low-frequency variants down to a minor allele count of 20. The method was evaluated in simulations and on five heavily censored phenotypes in about 400,000 UK Biobank and 180,000 FinnGen participants. Results for 871 UK Biobank time-to-event phenotypes are available in a PheWeb browser.

title: Two-layer design protects genes from mutations in their enhancers
Polygenic enrichment distinguishes disease associations of individual cells in single-cell RNA-seq data
synopsis: This study asks how to link single-cell expression data to polygenic disease risk without relying on predefined cell-type labels. The authors introduce scDRS, which scores each cell for excess expression of GWAS-implicated disease genes, and apply it to 74 diseases and traits across 1.3 million cells from 31 tissues. At the cell-type level, results broadly matched known associations. At the single-cell level, scDRS found disease-associated subpopulations missed by existing labels, including T cells in inflammatory bowel disease, neurons in schizophrenia and hepatocytes linked to triglyceride levels. Genes whose expression correlated with the score were strongly enriched for known drug targets and Mendelian disease genes, which supports use of the method for target discovery.

title: Systematic single-variant and gene-based association testing of thousands of phenotypes in 394,841 UK Biobank exomes
synopsis: This study asks how rare coding variation contributes to human disease and traits across a broad range of phenotypes. It runs single-variant and gene-based association tests for 4,529 phenotypes in 394,841 UK Biobank participants with exome sequences. Whether an association is discovered depends strongly on variant frequency, and discovery also correlates with measures of deleteriousness and natural selection. The results are released as a public resource with the Genebass browser, which makes it fast to look up rare-variant associations and allelic series.

title: CellRegMap: a statistical framework for mapping context‐specific regulatory variants using scRNA‐seq
synopsis: Population-scale single-cell RNA-seq makes it possible to study genetic effects on expression at cellular resolution. However, current methods depend on predefined discrete cell types. CellRegMap is a statistical framework that tests for and quantifies genotype-by-context interactions at known eQTL, covering cell subtypes and continuous cell-state transitions. The framework was validated on simulated data. Applied to two studies of differentiating iPSCs, it found hundreds of eQTL whose effects vary across cellular contexts. It also found fine-grained regulation in neuronal subtypes at eQTL that colocalize with disease variants, which helps explain context-dependent disease mechanisms.

title: The sequences of 150,119 genomes in the UK Biobank
synopsis: This paper reports whole-genome sequencing of 150,119 UK Biobank participants. It identifies 585 million SNPs, about 7% of all possible human SNPs, along with 58.7 million indels, 895,055 structural variants and 2.5 million microsatellites. A depletion rank score of genomic windows measures sequence constraint and shows that coding exons make up only a small fraction of strongly conserved regions. The study defines British Irish, African and South Asian cohorts and releases a haplotype reference panel that can impute most variants carried by three or more people. The authors also report large-effect rare-variant trait associations that exome sequencing and imputation had missed.

title: Fine-mapping from summary data with the “Sum of Single Effects” model
synopsis: This paper extends the SuSiE fine-mapping model from individual-level data to summary statistics, meaning GWAS z-scores plus LD estimated from a reference panel. It gives a general strategy that swaps the regression likelihood for a summary-data likelihood. The same framing also shows how existing methods such as FINEMAP and CAVIAR implicitly handle summary data. The authors build diagnostics that detect inconsistencies between z-scores and LD, and a refinement procedure that improves model fits. In simulations, SuSiE on summary data matches the best available summary-data methods in both speed and accuracy, which makes it a practical tool for routine fine-mapping.

title: A sequence-based global map of regulatory activity for deciphering human genetics
synopsis: This work aims to map any DNA sequence or variant to its regulatory activities. Sei is a deep learning model that predicts 21,907 chromatin profiles across more than 1,300 cell lines and tissues. From these predictions it learns sequence classes, a vocabulary of regulatory activities such as cell type-specific enhancer functions. Tissue-specific expression, eQTL and evolutionary constraint data support the predictions. Sequence classes can describe the tissue-specific regulatory architecture of complex traits and suggest mechanisms for individual pathogenic regulatory mutations, making Sei a general resource for interpreting noncoding variation.

title: Variant to function mapping at single-cell resolution through network propagation
synopsis: Linking GWAS variants to the cell types and states where they act is hard because single-cell data, especially epigenomic data, is sparse and noisy. SCAVENGE addresses this by using network propagation across a cell-similarity graph to map causal variants to their cellular context at single-cell resolution. The method was applied to blood traits across stages of hematopoiesis, to monocyte subsets linked to severe COVID-19 risk, and to intermediate lymphocyte developmental states that predispose to acute leukemia. It offers a general strategy for extracting more variant-to-function insight from single-cell genomic data.

title: Genome-wide association meta-analysis identifies 48 risk variants and highlights the role of the stria vascularis in hearing loss
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: This study looks for the genetic basis and cellular origins of hearing loss, a major cause of disability and a risk factor for dementia. A genome-wide association meta-analysis of clinically diagnosed and self-reported hearing impairment in 723,266 individuals found 48 significant loci, 10 of them novel. Many associations involved missense variants, and half of these lie in known familial hearing loss loci. Integrating the results with mouse cochlea and brain single-cell RNA-seq implicated spindle, root and basal cells of the stria vascularis. This points to that structure as a key mechanism and a possible therapeutic target.

title: The Tabula Sapiens: A multiple-organ, single-cell transcriptomic atlas of humans
synopsis: This paper builds a human reference single-cell transcriptomic atlas of nearly 500,000 cells from 24 tissues and organs, many taken from the same donor. The atlas characterizes more than 400 cell types, their distribution across tissues, and tissue-specific variation in gene expression. Sampling several tissues from one donor made it possible to track clonal T cells across tissues, estimate tissue-specific mutation rates in B cells, and compare cell-cycle state and proliferative potential of shared cell types. The atlas also revealed cell type-specific RNA splicing, and it gives a broad reference for interpreting cell type-specific genetic effects.

title: Improving polygenic prediction in ancestrally diverse populations
synopsis: Polygenic risk scores predict less accurately outside European-ancestry populations, which limits their clinical value elsewhere and could widen health disparities. This paper presents PRS-CSx, which combines GWAS summary statistics from several populations. A shared continuous shrinkage prior links genetic effects across ancestries, so the method can pool information and use differences in linkage disequilibrium between discovery samples. In simulations covering varied genetic architectures, cross-population overlap and sample sizes, PRS-CSx outperformed alternative methods. It also improved prediction of quantitative traits and schizophrenia risk in non-European populations. This gives a practical way to get more out of the growing but still underpowered non-European GWAS.

title: Predicting RNA splicing from DNA sequence using Pangolin
synopsis: This paper asks how accurately splice site strength can be predicted from DNA sequence across tissues. It introduces Pangolin, a deep learning model trained to predict tissue-specific splicing. Pangolin outperformed state-of-the-art methods on a range of splicing prediction tasks. It was also better at predicting how common, rare and lineage-specific variants affect splicing. The model identified loss-of-function mutations with high accuracy and recall, especially mutations that are neither missense nor nonsense. This makes Pangolin useful for flagging pathogenic noncoding and synonymous variants that standard annotation often misses.

title: Mapping genomic loci implicates genes and synaptic biology in schizophrenia
synopsis: This study maps common-variant risk for schizophrenia, a disorder with 60-80% heritability. A two-stage GWAS of up to 76,755 cases and 243,649 controls found associations at 287 distinct loci. The associations were concentrated in genes expressed in excitatory and inhibitory neurons, not in other tissues. Fine-mapping and functional genomic data prioritized 120 genes, 16 of which carry credible causal coding or UTR variants, and pointed to synaptic organization, differentiation and transmission. The prioritized genes overlapped genes hit by rare disruptive variants in schizophrenia and in neurodevelopmental disorders, including GRIN2A and SP4. This shows common and rare risk converging and gives a resource for mechanistic follow-up.

title: Single-cell eQTL mapping identifies cell type–specific genetic control of autoimmune disease
synopsis: This study asks how genetic variation shapes immune gene expression at the level of individual cell types and how that relates to autoimmune disease. Single-cell RNA sequencing of 1,267,758 peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 982 healthy donors identified 26,597 independent cis-eQTLs and 990 trans-eQTLs across 14 cell types, most with cell type-specific effects. Some eQTLs changed their allelic effects as B cells moved from naive to memory states. Mendelian randomization traced how 305 autoimmune risk loci act at the cellular level. The work shows that population-scale single-cell data can resolve the cell context of disease-associated variants.

title: New insights into the genetic etiology of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias
synopsis: This study set out to extend the genetic map of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. A two-stage GWAS of 111,326 clinically diagnosed or proxy cases and 677,663 controls found 75 risk loci, 42 of them new at the time of analysis. Pathway analyses confirmed amyloid and tau involvement and highlighted microglia. Gene prioritization at the new loci pointed to 31 genes, suggesting further processes such as TNF-alpha signaling through the linear ubiquitin chain assembly complex. A new genetic risk score predicted future dementia and progression from mild cognitive impairment, with a 1.6- to 1.9-fold risk difference between the lowest and highest deciles beyond the effects of age and APOE e4.

title: Leveraging fine-mapping and multipopulation training data to improve cross-population polygenic risk scores
synopsis: Polygenic risk scores lose accuracy in non-European populations. This paper presents PolyPred, which combines a predictor of causal effects from functionally informed fine-mapping, meant to handle differences in linkage disequilibrium, with the existing BOLT-LMM predictor. PolyPred+ also uses training data from the target population. Across 49 traits in four UK Biobank populations, PolyPred improved accuracy over BOLT-LMM by 7% in South Asians and up to 32% in Africans, consistent with simulations. In East Asians, PolyPred+ trained on UK Biobank British and Biobank Japan data improved accuracy by 24% over BOLT-LMM and 12% over PolyPred. Versions that use only summary statistics gave similar gains.

title: Incorporating regulatory interactions into gene-set analyses for GWAS data: A controlled analysis with the MAGMA tool
synopsis: Gene-set analyses of GWAS data usually assign variants to nearby genes, but many causal variants act through distant regulatory elements. This study tested whether adding public regulatory-interaction datasets to proximity-based mapping in MAGMA improves gene-set results, using GWAS data for ten phenotypes. The authors found several pitfalls and confounders in such augmented analyses and introduced controls for them. With these controls, augmentation only occasionally strengthened enrichment in biologically relevant gene sets. Where it did, the genes responsible could be identified: brain regulatory interactions implicated the acetylcholine receptor subunits CHRNB2 and CHRNE in schizophrenia. The study gives a careful framework for separating real gains from spurious ones.

title: DNA methylation-based predictors of health: applications and statistical considerations
synopsis: DNA methylation changes with environment and disease, unlike fixed genetic risk, which makes it attractive for building health biomarkers. This review surveys methylation-based predictors for exposures such as age and smoking and for early detection or progression of cancer, cardiovascular disease and neurological disease. It assesses what machine learning has added and how widely key statistical practices have been adopted. These practices include data-driven feature selection, avoiding data leakage when estimating performance, and using training samples that are generalizable and adequately powered. The review is a guide to building and judging methylation predictors that will hold up in new data.

title: The DOMINO web-server for active module identification analysis
synopsis: Active module identification looks for subnetworks of a gene network that are enriched for activity signal from omics data, and these subnetworks can point to key molecular processes. This paper presents a web server that runs DOMINO, an active module identification algorithm previously shown to produce modules with a better rate of empirical validation. The server accepts gene identifiers from several organisms and supports interpretation with GO enrichment analysis, module visualizations and output formats suited to custom downstream analysis. It makes the method easier to use for researchers who do not want to install and run it locally.

title: CT-FOCS: a novel method for inferring cell type-specific enhancer–promoter maps
synopsis: This work asks how to identify enhancer-promoter links that are active only in one cell type or a small subset of cell types, which is a key step toward understanding cell type-specific gene regulation. The authors introduce CT-FOCS, a statistical method that uses linear mixed effect models to detect such links. They applied it to 808 FANTOM5 samples covering 472 cell lines, primary cells and tissues, where it inferred cell type-specific links more accurately than recent competing methods. The analysis also shows that strictly cell type-specific enhancer-promoter links are very uncommon in the human genome.

title: DunedinPACE, a DNA methylation biomarker of the pace of aging
synopsis: Evaluating interventions meant to slow human aging requires measures of how fast biological aging is happening. The authors modeled Pace of Aging from within-person decline in 19 indicators of organ-system integrity, measured at four time points over two decades in the Dunedin birth cohort. They then used elastic-net regression on reliable DNA methylation probes to condense this into a blood test taken at a single time point, called DunedinPACE. In five additional datasets, DunedinPACE had high test-retest reliability and was associated with morbidity, disability, mortality and childhood adversity. Its effect sizes were similar to those of GrimAge, and it improved prediction beyond GrimAge.

title: Epigenetic scores for the circulating proteome as tools for disease prediction
synopsis: This study asks whether DNA methylation signatures of circulating plasma proteins can help predict disease. Using four cohorts, the authors trained epigenetic scores (EpiScores) for 953 proteins, and 109 of these explained between 1% and 58% of the variance in protein levels after adjusting for known pQTL effects. When the scores were applied to 9,537 Generation Scotland participants followed for 14 years, they showed 130 associations with incident diseases. These associations were largely independent of immune cell composition, lifestyle factors and biological aging, and the diabetes-related scores matched known proteomic biomarkers. The scores may be useful for disease risk stratification.

title: Improved analyses of GWAS summary statistics by reducing data heterogeneity and errors
synopsis: Methods that use GWAS summary statistics usually need an LD reference sample, and errors in either data source or differences between them can bias results. The authors propose DENTIST, a quality control method that uses LD among variants to detect and remove these errors and inconsistencies. In simulations, DENTIST substantially reduced false positives when detecting secondary signals with conditional and joint analysis, especially for imputed rare variants, where the false-positive rate fell from over 28% to under 2% when the GWAS and reference were heterogeneous. It also improved fine-mapping, so it is a useful preprocessing step for many summary-data analyses.

title: Lineage-tracing and translatomic analysis of damage-inducible mitotic cochlear progenitors identifies candidate genes regulating regeneration
synopsis: This study asks whether cells of the greater epithelial ridge in the neonatal mouse cochlea can regenerate supporting cells by cell division. After Lgr5-positive supporting cells were ablated with Lgr5-DTR mice, lineage tracing showed that progenitor cells in the ridge divided and migrated into the organ of Corti to replace the lost cells. The regenerated cells had coordinated calcium activity, expressed markers of inner phalangeal cells, and survived into maturity. Translatome profiling with RiboTag and RNA sequencing identified 11 gene clusters, including damage-responsive genes linked to migration and proliferation. These genes are candidate regulators of cochlear regeneration.

title: An open approach to systematically prioritize causal variants and genes at all published human GWAS trait-associated loci
synopsis: Linking GWAS associations to their causal genes remains a major challenge. This resource performs systematic fine mapping and gene prioritization across 133,441 published GWAS loci, combining the GWAS Catalog and UK Biobank with transcriptomic, proteomic and epigenomic data and colocalization results across 92 cell types and tissues. A machine learning model trained on 445 curated gold-standard loci distinguished causal genes from nearby genes better than a model based on distance alone. The prioritized genes were enriched for approved drug targets (odds ratio 8.1). The results are available through the Open Targets Genetics web portal for gene and drug-target prioritization.

title: Exome sequencing and analysis of 454,787 UK Biobank participants
synopsis: This study used exome sequencing of 454,787 UK Biobank participants to examine how protein-altering variation affects human traits. It found 12 million coding variants, including about 1 million loss-of-function and 1.8 million deleterious missense variants, and tested them against 3,994 traits. This identified 564 genes with significant trait associations, and 91% of the rare-variant signals were independent of nearby common-variant GWAS signals. Findings include protective associations for hypertension, diabetes and asthma, and genes linked to brain imaging traits. Of the signals that could be tested in an independent cohort, 81% replicated, and associations were broadly consistent across ancestries.

title: Incorporating functional priors improves polygenic prediction accuracy in UK Biobank and 23andMe data sets
synopsis: This paper asks whether knowledge of genome function can make polygenic risk scores more accurate. It introduces LDpred-funct, which sets trait-specific priors on SNP effects from the baseline-LD model's coding, conserved, regulatory and LD-related annotations, then uses cross-validation to regularize the estimated effects. Across 21 heritable traits in the UK Biobank (average training N = 373K), it improved average prediction accuracy by 4.6% relative to SBayesR, the best method without functional information (average R2 = 0.144). For height, R2 reached 0.413, and adding 23andMe training data raised it to 0.431. The results show that functional annotation adds real predictive information to polygenic scores.

title: Effective gene expression prediction from sequence by integrating long-range interactions
synopsis: This work tackles a central open problem: predicting how noncoding DNA sequence controls gene expression in different cell types. It presents Enformer, a deep learning model that predicts expression from sequence and can draw on regulatory elements up to 100 kb away. Enformer predicts expression substantially more accurately than earlier sequence models. It also predicts variant effects better, both for natural genetic variants and for saturation mutagenesis measured by massively parallel reporter assays. From sequence alone, it learned to predict enhancer–promoter interactions about as well as methods that take experimental data as input. These gains should help fine-map disease associations and interpret how cis-regulatory sequence evolves.

title: Identifying causal variants by fine mapping across multiple studies
synopsis: As GWAS of the same trait become available for several populations, their different linkage disequilibrium patterns offer a way to pinpoint causal variants more precisely. This paper introduces MsCAVIAR, which extends the CAVIAR fine-mapping framework to multiple studies using a random effects model. It needs only summary statistics and LD matrices, and it models uncertainty in association statistics with a multivariate normal model. It allows several causal variants per locus and lets SNP effect sizes differ between populations. The method is evaluated in simulations and in a trans-ethnic, trans-biobank fine-mapping analysis of HDL cholesterol, showing how combining diverse cohorts can sharpen fine mapping.

title: A cell-type-specific atlas of the inner ear transcriptional response to acoustic trauma
synopsis: This study asks how each cell type in the inner ear responds at the transcriptional level to noise trauma, the cause of noise-induced hearing loss. Using RiboTag and single-cell RNA sequencing in mouse, it profiles the inner ear before and after noise exposure. The transcription factors STAT3 and IRF7 and immune-related genes were induced in all cell types, but cell-type-specific changes dominated. The ATF3/ATF4 stress pathway was induced in noise-resilient type 1A neurons, potassium transport genes fell in the lateral wall, and mRNA metabolism genes fell in outer hair cells. Deafness genes were downregulated in most cell types. The data are publicly available in gEAR and can guide drug development for noise-induced hearing loss.

title: Large-scale cis- and trans-eQTL analyses identify thousands of genetic loci and polygenic scores that regulate blood gene expression
synopsis: This study maps how genetic variation regulates gene expression in blood, using data from 31,684 individuals in the eQTLGen Consortium. Cis-eQTLs were found for 88% of genes and replicated across many tissues. Trans-eQTLs were found for 37% of 10,317 trait-associated variants tested but replicated less often, partly because of limited power and confounding by cell type composition. Single-cell RNA-seq data helped identify trans effects acting within cells, and transcription factors were the main mechanism behind trans effects. Expression of 13% of genes correlated with polygenic scores for 1,263 phenotypes, pointing to candidate drivers of those traits. The result is a large eQTL resource for interpreting complex traits.

title: Genome-wide association studies
gEAR: Gene Expression Analysis Resource portal for community-driven, multi-omic data exploration
Computationally efficient whole-genome regression for quantitative and binary traits
synopsis: Running genome-wide association tests on biobanks with thousands of phenotypes is computationally costly, especially when the model must account for relatedness or population structure. This paper introduces REGENIE, a machine-learning method that fits whole-genome regression for quantitative and binary traits. It analyzes many phenotypes in parallel and loads only local segments of the genotype matrix into memory, which saves substantial compute time and memory. It also includes a fast approximate Firth logistic regression test for unbalanced case-control traits. In the UK Biobank, with up to 407,746 individuals, the method was both accurate and much faster, making large multi-trait GWAS practical.

title: An atlas of alternative polyadenylation quantitative trait loci contributing to complex trait and disease heritability
synopsis: This study asks whether genetic effects on alternative polyadenylation (APA) of 3'UTRs help explain noncoding GWAS signals. Using GTEx data from 46 tissues in 467 individuals, it maps about 0.4 million common variants associated with APA (3'aQTLs). These variants can alter poly(A) motifs, RNA secondary structure and RNA-binding protein sites, and CRISPR experiments confirmed that they can change APA. The mapping also identified APA regulators such as LARP4. 3'aQTLs colocalize with about 16.1% of trait-associated variants and largely differ from expression QTLs. This makes APA a distinct and substantial mechanism linking genetic variation to complex traits and disease.

title: ArchR is a scalable software package for integrative single-cell chromatin accessibility analysis
synopsis: Software for analyzing single-cell chromatin accessibility data has not kept pace with the data's growing scale. This paper presents ArchR, an R package for end-to-end analysis of these data. It covers doublet removal, clustering and cell type identification, peak calling, trajectory inference, linking regulatory elements to genes, and transcription factor footprinting. It can also predict gene expression from accessibility and integrate with scRNA-seq. ArchR analyzed over 1.2 million cells in 8 hours on a standard laptop. This makes large single-cell regulatory studies practical with modest computing resources.

title: Sequencing of 53,831 diverse genomes from the NHLBI TOPMed Program
lab: the NHLBI Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine (TOPMed) Consortium
synopsis: This paper describes the design, resources and early findings of the TOPMed program, which sequenced whole genomes to study the genetics of heart, lung, blood and sleep disorders. In the first 53,831 participants, who come from diverse backgrounds and have rich phenotype data, the program found more than 400 million single-nucleotide and indel variants. Of these, 97% have frequencies below 1% and 46% are singletons. Assembly of unmapped reads and focused analysis of highly variable loci uncovered further variants. The resource includes a variant browser and an imputation server. Combining TOPMed haplotypes with modern imputation lets association studies reach variants as rare as about 0.01%.

title: Regulatory genomic circuitry of human disease loci by integrative epigenomics
synopsis: Most disease-associated loci (93%) are non-coding, and regulatory annotations remain incomplete. The authors built EpiMap, a compendium of 10,000 epigenomic maps across 800 samples. From it they defined chromatin states, high-resolution enhancers, enhancer modules, upstream regulators and target genes. They used EpiMap to annotate 20,000 loci associated with 232 traits, predicting relevant tissues, candidate causal variants and tissue-specific target genes. Multifactorial traits were split into tissue-specific factors, and top loci often had several driver variants acting through multiple enhancers, genes or tissues, which points to extensive pleiotropy. The resource shows how dense epigenomic annotation helps interpret non-coding disease loci.

title: A comprehensive enhancer screen identifies TRAM2 as a key and novel mediator of YAP oncogenesis
synopsis: The co-transcriptional factor YAP is activated in many solid tumors and binds thousands of enhancers through TEAD4, but most of these sites have unknown function. The authors mapped YAP/TEAD4-bound enhancers with genome-wide ChIP profiling. They then used a genetic screen to find which enhancers are needed for YAP-driven proliferation. They focused on an enhancer of TRAM2, a gene whose expression tracks YAP activity in nearly all tumor types. TRAM2 reproduced YAP-induced proliferation, migration and invasion, was associated with poor patient survival, and acted largely through its direct client FSTL-1. These results point to TRAM2 as a mediator of YAP-driven cancer aggressiveness.

title: DOMINO: a network‐based active module identification algorithm with reduced rate of false calls
synopsis: Active module identification algorithms search gene networks for subnetworks enriched in omics activity signals, but it has been unclear whether their results are specific to the data analyzed. The authors evaluated six popular methods on gene expression and GWAS data. GO terms enriched in modules from real data often also appeared in modules found on randomly permuted data. To correct for this bias, they developed a permutation-based procedure that empirically evaluates reported GO terms, and they used it to define five new performance criteria. They also introduced DOMINO, a new algorithm that outperformed the six existing methods in extensive tests on both data types.

title: Genetic mapping of developmental trajectories for complex traits and diseases
synopsis: Turning GWAS signals into biological insight remains difficult. This study presents a method that combines GWAS results with single-cell RNA-seq data on developmental processes. The method links cell differentiation trajectories to traits, identifies the pathways behind those links, and prioritizes target genes that tie trajectories, pathways and genetic risk together. Applied to 11 traits and 12 scRNA-seq datasets, it recovered known connections such as cortical inhibitory interneuron maturation with schizophrenia, hepatocytes with cholesterol levels, and pancreatic beta cells with type 2 diabetes. For each link it nominated top candidate genes. The approach may help explain how genetic risk acts through developmental processes and could guide drug target selection.

title: Trans-ancestry genome-wide association meta-analysis of prostate cancer identifies new susceptibility loci and informs genetic risk prediction
synopsis: Prostate cancer is highly heritable, and its incidence differs widely across ancestry groups. This multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis of 107,247 cases and 127,006 controls found 86 new independent risk variants, bringing the known total to 269. Men in the top decile of the genetic risk score had odds ratios ranging from 5.06 in European-ancestry men to 3.74 in African-ancestry men. The mean risk score was 2.18 times higher in African-ancestry men and 0.73 times lower in East Asian-ancestry men than in European-ancestry men. These results suggest germline variation contributes to population differences in prostate cancer risk and support risk-score-based personalized prediction.

title: LDpred2: better, faster, stronger
synopsis: LDpred is a widely used method for building polygenic scores from GWAS summary statistics and a linkage disequilibrium matrix, but it has limitations that can reduce prediction accuracy. LDpred2 addresses these issues and adds two options: a sparse option that can set effects exactly to zero, and an auto option that learns the model parameters from the data. On simulated and real data, LDpred2 was more robust and accurate than the original version. Across 8 real traits it reached a mean AUC of 65.1%, compared with 63.8% for lassosum, 62.9% for PRS-CS and 61.5% for SBayesR. Accuracy improved further when it was run genome-wide rather than per chromosome.

title: Functionally informed fine-mapping and polygenic localization of complex trait heritability
synopsis: Fine-mapping aims to identify causal variants behind complex traits.
