PolyFun improves it by using functional annotations across the whole genome to set prior causal probabilities for methods such as SuSiE and FINEMAP. In simulations it remained well calibrated and found over 20% more variants with posterior causal probability above 0.95. Across 49 UK Biobank traits (average n about 318,000), PolyFun with SuSiE identified 3,025 such variant-trait pairs, more than 32% more than SuSiE alone. Using per-SNP heritability estimates, the authors found the minimal SNP sets explaining half of common-SNP heritability, ranging from 28 SNPs for hair color to 2 million for number of children.

title: Expression pattern of cochlear microRNAs in the mammalian auditory hindbrain
synopsis: This study asks whether microRNAs abundant in the cochlea are also part of the gene set shared between the peripheral and central auditory systems. The authors measured 12 cochlea-abundant miRNAs by qRT-PCR in mouse cochlea, auditory hindbrain and prefrontal cortex at embryonic day 16 and postnatal days 0 and 30, and used in situ hybridization to map where they are expressed. All 12 were expressed in every tissue. Eleven differed between tissues and nine between developmental stages. The hindbrain's expression pattern over time resembled the prefrontal cortex more than the cochlea, and the miRNAs were widely expressed in the cochlear nucleus and superior olivary complex. These miRNAs are candidate entry points for studying gene regulatory networks across the auditory system.

title: Identification and characterization of key long non-coding RNAs in the mouse cochlea
synopsis: Long non-coding RNAs regulate many biological systems, but their roles in the auditory system are largely unexplored. The authors used specific criteria to select four lncRNAs that are expressed in the mouse cochlea, conserved in the human transcriptome and relevant to inner ear function. Bioinformatic analysis showed they lack coding potential and have little evolutionary conservation, which is typical of lncRNAs. RNAscope imaging showed each one localized to particular inner ear cell types, with distinct subcellular patterns and variable expression across mouse tissues. The study also proposes a possible pathway for Gas5 in the inner ear. The approach can serve as a template for studying other sensory lncRNAs and may help explain unresolved genetic causes of hearing loss.

title: Genetic mapping of etiologic brain cell types for obesity
synopsis: This study asks which cell types mediate genetic predisposition to obesity. The authors developed a new method to combine single-cell RNA-seq data from 727 mouse cell types across 17 organs with body mass index GWAS data from more than 457,000 people. They found 26 cell types significantly enriched for BMI heritability, all of them neuronal, spread across regions including the hypothalamus, midbrain, hippocampus, thalamus, cortex and brainstem. Analysis of genes carrying obesity-associated coding mutations replicated the midbrain cell types in the anterior pretectal nucleus and periaqueductal gray. The results point to brain circuits for sensory integration, learning and memory in obesity and give testable hypotheses for mechanistic follow-up.

title: Open Targets Genetics: systematic identification of trait-associated genes using large-scale genetics and functional genomics
synopsis: This paper describes Open Targets Genetics, an open-access resource that links GWAS-associated loci to their likely causal variants and genes. It combines human GWAS results with functional genomics data, including gene expression, protein abundance and chromatin interaction and conformation data, from many cell types and tissues. Users can search by variant, gene or study, prioritize causal variants and genes, and view colocalization analyses between diseases and molecular traits across 92 cell types and tissues, including the eQTL Catalogue. The data are available through a web portal, as bulk downloads and through a GraphQL API, and the software is open source. The resource supports systematic gene prioritization for drug target discovery and drug repurposing.

title: The GTEx Consortium atlas of genetic regulatory effects across human tissues
synopsis: The Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project dissects how genetic variation affects gene expression and splicing.

title: GFI1 functions to repress neuronal gene expression in the developing inner ear hair cells
synopsis: This study asks which genes the transcription factor GFI1 controls downstream in developing inner ear hair cells. Using Gfi1cre;RiboTag mice, the authors profiled the hair cell translatome with and without GFI1. Hair cells lacking GFI1 showed systematic downregulation of hair cell differentiation genes and strong upregulation of neuronal genes, including Pou4f1, Neurod1, Atoh1 and Insm1. The upregulated genes matched the NEUROD1 regulon and are normally expressed before GFI1 turns on. Auditory and vestibular hair cells shared few differentially expressed genes, which suggests GFI1 plays different roles in the two systems. The authors propose that GFI1 both represses neuronal genes and activates genes needed for hair cell maturation, which bears on hair cell regeneration.

title: Dynamic incorporation of multiple in silico functional annotations empowers rare variant association analysis of large whole-genome sequencing studies at scale
lab: the NHLBI Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine (TOPMed) Consortium
synopsis: Common rare-variant association tests make limited use of information about variant function. This paper introduces STAAR, a scalable rare-variant set test that uses variant categories and multiple in silico annotations through dynamic weighting. The annotations are summarized as annotation principal components. STAAR accounts for population structure and relatedness and handles both continuous and binary traits in biobank-scale whole-genome sequencing studies. Applied to four lipid traits in 12,316 discovery and 17,822 replication samples from the TOPMed program, it found and replicated new rare-variant associations with LDL cholesterol. These included disruptive missense variants in NPC1L1 and an intergenic region near APOC1P1. The method makes rare-variant analysis of large sequencing cohorts more powerful.

title: Polygenic background modifies penetrance of monogenic variants for tier 1 genomic conditions
synopsis: This study asks whether polygenic background changes disease risk in people who carry high-impact monogenic variants. Among 80,928 individuals, the authors studied three tier 1 genomic conditions: familial hypercholesterolemia, hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, and Lynch syndrome. Among carriers of monogenic risk variants, risk of disease by age 75 varied widely with polygenic background. It ranged from 17% to 78% for coronary artery disease, 13% to 76% for breast cancer and 11% to 80% for colon cancer. The results suggest that adding polygenic scores to monogenic findings could make risk estimates for carriers more accurate and improve clinical genetic counseling.

title: Systematic identification of functional SNPs interrupting 3’UTR polyadenylation signals
synopsis: This study looks for common genetic variants that affect gene expression and human traits by changing 3'UTR alternative polyadenylation. The authors found 2,305 SNPs that disrupt the canonical polyadenylation signal or its main variant. Using pA-QTL tests on GTEx RNA-seq data, they showed that 330 of these SNPs were significantly associated with how often their poly(A) site was used. Most disrupting alleles reduced cleavage at the site and lengthened the 3'UTR, but about 10% increased use of an upstream site and shortened it. A few dozen of these SNPs colocalized with eQTL or GWAS signals. Alleles that lengthened the 3'UTR were linked to lower gene expression, suggesting shorter isoforms are more stable. A genome-wide scan of other 3'UTR variants found thousands more pA-QTLs with weaker effects.

title: Expanded encyclopaedias of DNA elements in the human and mouse genomes
synopsis: This paper summarizes phase III of the ENCODE Project, which set out to map the functional elements of the human and mouse genomes more completely. The project profiled RNA transcription, chromatin structure and modification, DNA methylation, chromatin looping, and transcription factor and RNA-binding protein occupancy across many cell types and tissues, and produced 5,992 new datasets, including a systematic series across mouse fetal development. By combining selected regulatory datatypes, the authors built a registry of 926,535 human and 339,815 mouse candidate cis-regulatory elements, covering 7.9% and 3.4% of the two genomes. The registry can be searched through the SCREEN web server, and it is a widely used reference for annotating noncoding variation.

title: Tutorial: a guide to performing polygenic risk score analyses
synopsis: Polygenic risk scores estimate an individual's genetic liability to a trait from their genotypes and GWAS summary data. They are now used routinely in biomedical research, but there are few guidelines for computing them, which leads to inconsistent studies and misread results. This tutorial gives detailed guidance on standard quality control, compares methods for calculating scores, and comes with an introductory online tutorial. It also corrects common misconceptions about PRS results, recommends best practice, and outlines open challenges. It is a practical reference for anyone building or interpreting polygenic scores, which are becoming more powerful as GWAS sample sizes grow.

title: PWAS: proteome-wide association study—linking genes and phenotypes by functional variation in proteins
synopsis: This paper introduces the proteome-wide association study (PWAS), a method for finding gene-phenotype associations that act through changes in protein function. For each protein-coding gene, PWAS combines all the variants affecting it and uses machine learning and probabilistic models to estimate their joint effect on the protein's function. It then tests whether differences in that predicted function between individuals correlate with the phenotype. Because it scores genes rather than single variants, the approach can capture complex inheritance, including recessive effects. In comparisons with GWAS and other methods, PWAS recovered known causal coding genes and found new associations, and it is available as a command-line tool.

title: A Simple New Approach to Variable Selection in Regression, with Application to Genetic Fine Mapping
source: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology
synopsis: This paper proposes a new approach to variable selection in linear regression that focuses on quantifying uncertainty about which variables to select. The sum of single effects (SuSiE) model writes the sparse coefficient vector as a sum of single-effect vectors, each with one nonzero element. It is fitted by iterative Bayesian stepwise selection, which is as fast as classical stepwise methods but computes a distribution over candidate variables at each step instead of picking one. The procedure optimizes a variational approximation to the posterior and yields a credible set of variables for each effect. The method suits fine mapping, where predictors are highly correlated and effects are sparse: it outperformed existing methods in simulations and was applied to fine mapping splicing QTLs.

title: The mutational constraint spectrum quantified from variation in 141,456 humans
synopsis: This study uses predicted loss-of-function variants to measure how tolerant each human gene is to inactivation. The Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) combines 125,748 exomes and 15,708 genomes. After filtering sequencing and annotation artefacts, the authors identified 443,769 high-confidence predicted loss-of-function variants. Using an improved model of human mutation rates, they ranked protein-coding genes along a spectrum of mutational constraint and validated it against model organism data and engineered human cell lines. The constraint metrics improve power for gene discovery in both rare and common disease and are now a standard tool for variant and gene interpretation.

title: Polygenic risk scores: from research tools to clinical instruments
synopsis: This review asks whether polygenic risk scores, which have been widely validated in research studies, are ready for clinical use. Built from GWAS-identified variants, the scores capture part of an individual's genetic susceptibility, but their ability to discriminate cases from controls in the general population is still low. The authors argue that scores may be more useful where the prior probability of disease is higher, for example to support diagnosis in early disease or to guide treatment choices. They also discuss the weaker evidence base for non-European ancestries and the difficulty of turning a percentile score into a lifetime risk. The review sets out what must be resolved before clinical adoption.

title: Transcription Dynamics Regulate Poly(A) Tails and Expression of the RNA Degradation Machinery to Balance mRNA Levels
synopsis: This study asks how mRNA synthesis and degradation are coordinated in mammalian cells. When specific genes are transcribed more slowly, their mRNAs gain more m6A, are preferentially targeted by the CCR4-Not complex, and end up with shorter poly(A) tails and lower stability. Internal ribosome entry sites act as transcriptional pause sites and have the same effects. When transcription changes globally, cells buffer mRNA levels by adjusting expression of the degradation machinery. Stress that impedes elongation strongly inhibits the machinery and stabilizes mRNAs, while enhanced transcription after B cell activation or glucose stimulation has the opposite effect. The findings describe two pathways linking transcription to mRNA stability.

title: A reference map of the human binary protein interactome
synopsis: This paper presents HuRI, a systematic all-by-all reference map of binary interactions between human proteins, intended to link genome function to cellular organization. It contains about 53,000 protein-protein interactions, roughly four times the number of high-quality curated interactions from small-scale studies. Combined with genome, transcriptome and proteome data, HuRI lets protein interactions be studied in most physiological or disease contexts. The authors use it to assign subcellular roles to interactions and to infer tissue-specific networks, which point to possible mechanisms behind tissue-specific phenotypes of Mendelian diseases. HuRI is a proteome-wide resource for connecting genetic variation to phenotype.

title: The nf-core framework for community-curated bioinformatics pipelines
Activity-by-contact model of enhancer–promoter regulation from thousands of CRISPR perturbations
synopsis: This study asks how enhancers choose which genes they regulate and whether general rules can predict these connections across cell types. The authors developed CRISPRi-FlowFISH, which perturbs enhancers in their native genomic context, and used it to test more than 3,500 potential enhancer-gene connections for 30 genes. A simple activity-by-contact model, which combines enhancer activity with 3D contact frequency, predicted the connections in this dataset substantially better than earlier methods. Because the model needs only chromatin state measurements, it can produce genome-wide enhancer-gene maps for a given cell type. That makes it useful for linking noncoding disease risk variants to the genes they likely affect.

title: MaveDB: an open-source platform to distribute and interpret data from multiplexed assays of variant effect
synopsis: Multiplexed assays of variant effect, such as deep mutational scans and massively parallel reporter assays, measure the impact of thousands of sequence variants in one experiment, but there was no standard resource for finding and sharing these data. This paper presents MaveDB, a public repository for large-scale variant effect measurements designed to work with downstream interpretation tools. It also describes the first such tool, MaveVis, which retrieves, visualizes and contextualizes variant effect maps. By centralizing these datasets, the platform aims to make them easier to reuse in basic research and clinical variant interpretation.

title: Scaling computational genomics to millions of individuals with GPUs
synopsis: Most genomics methods were built for tens to thousands of samples, but biobank-scale studies now require analyses of millions. This paper asks whether general-purpose GPU computing libraries such as PyTorch and TensorFlow can deliver efficient, low-cost genomic computation at that scale. Compared with CPU implementations, the GPU approach cut runtime by more than 200-fold and cost by about 5 to 10-fold. Because these libraries are widely available and easy to use, the authors argue that GPUs could become a standard tool for large-scale computational genomics.

title: GWAS Identifies 44 Independent Associated Genomic Loci for Self-Reported Adult Hearing Difficulty in UK Biobank
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: Age-related hearing impairment is common and heritable, but its genetic causes are largely unknown. This study ran genome-wide association studies on two self-reported hearing phenotypes in more than 250,000 UK Biobank participants aged 40 to 69. It found 44 independent genome-wide significant loci, 34 of them new for any form of hearing loss. The implicated genes were enriched for synaptic, nervous system, inner ear and cognitive processes, and the trait was genetically correlated with personality and psychological traits. Protein localization in mouse cochlea pointed to roles for NID2, CLRN2 and ARHGEF28. The study suggests new therapeutic targets and shows that simple self-reported phenotypes can support genetic discovery in very large samples.

title: A global overview of pleiotropy and genetic architecture in complex traits
synopsis: This study asks how widespread pleiotropy is across the genome and how genetic architecture differs among complex traits. The authors analyzed 4,155 public GWASs and examined a well-powered subset covering 558 traits in detail. Trait-associated loci covered more than half of the genome, and 90% of them overlapped loci for multiple traits. Likely causal variants were enriched in coding and flanking regions and in regulatory elements, and traits differed in polygenicity and discoverability. All results are available to query in the GWAS ATLAS resource, which provides a broad reference for comparing genetic architecture across traits.

title: The “All of Us” Research Program
synopsis: This paper describes the All of Us Research Program, which plans to enroll at least one million diverse US participants to address the small size, limited diversity and thin phenotyping of many existing cohorts. Participants contribute health questionnaires, electronic health records, physical measurements, digital health data and biospecimens through more than 340 recruitment sites. As of July 2019, more than 175,000 participants had provided biospecimens, over 80% of them from groups historically underrepresented in biomedical research, and EHR data had been collected for more than 112,000 participants. The resource is intended to support precision medicine research that accounts for individual variation in biology, lifestyle and environment.

title: A CRISPR-Cas9 screen identifies essential CTCF anchor sites for estrogen receptor-driven breast cancer cell proliferation
synopsis: Estrogen receptor alpha drives many breast cancers by activating enhancers, which depends on chromatin loops stabilized by CTCF and cohesin. This study asks whether specific CTCF-binding elements are required for ERα-driven cell proliferation. The authors ran a CRISPR screen targeting CTCF sites near ERα-bound enhancers and identified four functional elements. One of them alters chromatin conformation to support activation of PREX1, a key ERα target gene. High PREX1 expression marked ERα dependency in cell lines and was associated with good outcome after anti-hormonal therapy. The results show that particular CTCF-mediated chromatin structures are needed for hormone-driven breast cancer growth.

title: PRSice-2: Polygenic Risk Score software for biobank-scale data
synopsis: Polygenic risk scores are widely used in biomedical research, and biobank-scale data require software that is efficient and scalable. This paper introduces PRSice-2, a program that automates PRS analysis on genotyped or imputed data. It computes empirical P-values that are not inflated by overfitting, supports different inheritance models, and can test multiple continuous and binary traits together. PRSice-2 was much faster and more memory-efficient than PRSice-1, LDpred and lassosum, with comparable predictive power. That efficiency becomes more important as datasets grow and PRS are used in high-dimensional and gene set-based analyses.

title: A Fast and Flexible Framework for Network-Assisted Genomic Association
synopsis: This paper asks whether network propagation over protein interaction networks can strengthen and interpret genome-wide association signals. The authors built NAGA, a tool that draws on the NDEx network resource to choose, from thousands of protein networks, the ones that work best for a given study. A genome-wide analysis finishes in under five minutes on a laptop. On schizophrenia data, NAGA recovered many known disease genes and strengthened associations with less expected genes such as amyloid beta precursor. Across eight gene-disease tasks, it beat conventional approaches at recovering known genes and at producing replicable results. It also links to Cytoscape for visualization and further analysis.

title: The EXPANDER Integrated Platform for Transcriptome Analysis
synopsis: This paper describes EXPANDER, a software package for analyzing transcriptome data from RNA-seq or expression arrays, with built-in support for 18 organisms. Starting from a gene expression matrix, it covers preprocessing, normalization, differential expression, clustering, biclustering, supervised grouping, functional and pathway enrichment, and network and motif analysis. Each step uses established algorithms, and many of them come from the developers' own lab. The tool has been developed since 2003 and has over 18,000 downloads and 540 citations. The recent version adds combined analysis of expression and ChIP-seq data to better infer transcriptional networks. Its interface gives non-specialists access to these methods in one place.

title: CUT&Tag for efficient epigenomic profiling of small samples and single cells
synopsis: This paper presents CUT&Tag, a method for mapping chromatin features at high resolution in small numbers of cells. An antibody binds a chromatin protein inside the cell and then tethers a protein A-Tn5 transposase fusion. When activated, the transposase produces sequencing libraries with high resolution and very low background. The whole procedure, from live cells to sequencing-ready libraries, runs in a single tube or microwell within one day, and it can be scaled up for high throughput. The authors used it to profile histone modifications, RNA Polymerase II and transcription factors in low cell numbers and in single cells. This makes epigenomic profiling practical for scarce samples.

title: Polygenic prediction via Bayesian regression and continuous shrinkage priors
synopsis: This paper introduces PRS-CS, a method for building polygenic risk scores from GWAS summary statistics and an external linkage disequilibrium reference panel. It uses high-dimensional Bayesian regression with a continuous shrinkage prior on SNP effect sizes. The prior holds up across different genetic architectures, is computationally efficient, and allows local LD patterns to be modeled jointly. In simulations based on UK Biobank data, PRS-CS outperformed existing methods across many architectures, especially with large training samples. In the Partners HealthCare Biobank, it predicted six common diseases and six quantitative traits more accurately than the alternatives. This makes it a strong option for summary-statistics-based genetic prediction.

title: Clinical use of current polygenic risk scores may exacerbate health disparities
synopsis: This perspective asks whether clinical use of polygenic risk scores could widen health disparities. It argues that current scores are several times more accurate in people of European ancestry than in other groups. This is an unavoidable result of the Eurocentric makeup of genome-wide association studies. Unlike most biomarkers or drugs, using these scores in the clinic today would systematically benefit European-descent populations more. Early efforts to diversify studies look promising, even with non-European samples much smaller than the largest studies. The authors call for prioritizing diversity in genetic studies and publicly releasing summary statistics so the scores do not deepen inequities.

title: Opportunities and challenges for transcriptome-wide association studies
synopsis: This perspective asks how well transcriptome-wide association studies can identify causal genes at GWAS loci. TWAS combines GWAS results with gene expression data. The authors use simulations and literature-curated candidate causal genes for schizophrenia, LDL cholesterol and Crohn's disease. At some loci TWAS correctly prioritizes the likely causal gene. At others it flags several genes, some probably non-causal, because they share eQTLs. The problem is worst when expression data come from tissues or cell types unrelated to the trait. Even so, TWAS beats simple baselines. The authors propose best practices and directions for improving eQTL-based gene prioritization.

title: ACAT: A Fast and Powerful p Value Combination Method for Rare-Variant Analysis in Sequencing Studies
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: This paper tackles a weakness of set-based rare-variant tests: they lose power when only a few variants in a set are causal, and their power depends on the number, effect sizes and directions of causal variants and on the weights chosen. The authors propose ACAT, a fast p-value combination method based on the Cauchy distribution. ACAT-V combines variant-level p-values and is strong when few variants are causal. ACAT-O combines the burden test, SKAT and ACAT-V into one omnibus test. In simulations and in whole-genome sequencing data from the ARIC study, ACAT-O gave more robust and higher power than the alternatives, which makes it useful for sequencing association studies.

title: DNA methylation GrimAge strongly predicts lifespan and healthspan
synopsis: This study asks whether plasma protein levels can be estimated from DNA methylation and combined into a predictor of lifespan. The authors built seven methylation-based surrogates for plasma proteins, including PAI-1 and GDF15, and an estimator of smoking pack-years. They combined these into a composite clock called DNAm GrimAge, with an age-adjusted version, AgeAccelGrim. In validation data from thousands of people, GrimAge predicted time to death (P=2.0E-75), coronary heart disease (P=6.2E-24) and cancer (P=1.3E-12) better than existing epigenetic clocks. AgeAccelGrim tracked comorbidity count (P=3.45E-17). Methylation-based PAI-1 was associated with lifespan and type 2 diabetes. These biomarkers could support studies of aging interventions.

title: BOADICEA: a comprehensive breast cancer risk prediction model incorporating genetic and nongenetic risk factors
synopsis: This work extends the BOADICEA breast cancer risk model to combine genetic and nongenetic risk factors in one framework. The model includes truncating variants in BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, CHEK2 and ATM, a 313-SNP polygenic risk score explaining 20% of polygenic variance, a residual familial component, lifestyle, hormonal and reproductive factors, and mammographic density, and it can handle missing information. Of the individual factors, the polygenic score gives the widest spread of predicted risk, followed by mammographic density. With all factors combined, predicted lifetime risk for women in the UK ranges from 2.8% at the 1st percentile to 30.6% at the 99th. This supports risk-stratified screening and prevention decisions.

title: A Genome-wide Framework for Mapping Gene Regulation via Cellular Genetic Screens
synopsis: Over a million candidate regulatory elements are known in the human genome, but few have been validated or linked to their target genes. This study borrows the logic of eQTL mapping. It introduces random combinations of CRISPRi (dCas9-KRAB) perturbations into many cells and reads out the effects by single-cell RNA-seq. Two experiments perturbed 5,920 candidate enhancers across 254,974 single-cell transcriptomes and identified 664 cis enhancer-gene pairs, 470 of them high-confidence. These pairs were enriched for specific transcription factors and non-housekeeping genes, and the enhancers tended to sit near their targets both along the genome and in 3D. The framework allows large-scale experimental mapping of enhancer-gene links without relying on common variants or linkage disequilibrium.

title: Predicting Splicing from Primary Sequence with Deep Learning
synopsis: This study asks whether splice junctions can be predicted from pre-mRNA sequence alone. The authors train a deep neural network that predicts splice sites accurately from an arbitrary transcript sequence, which makes it possible to identify noncoding variants that create cryptic splicing. Synonymous and intronic variants predicted to alter splicing validated at a high rate in RNA-seq and are strongly deleterious in human populations. Predicted splice-altering de novo mutations were enriched in patients with autism and intellectual disability compared with controls, and 21 of 28 tested cases validated by RNA-seq. The authors estimate that 9-11% of pathogenic mutations in rare genetic disorders act through cryptic splicing, a class of disease variation that is often missed.

title: Polygenic Risk Scores for Prediction of Breast Cancer and Breast Cancer Subtypes
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: This study builds polygenic risk scores for breast cancer, optimized separately for estrogen receptor-positive and -negative disease. They were developed from 94,075 cases and 75,017 controls of European ancestry using stepwise or lasso regression. The best scores were tested in 10 prospective studies and in 190,040 UK Biobank women. The best 313-SNP score gave an odds ratio of 1.61 per standard deviation and an AUC of 0.630. Women in the top 1% had a lifetime risk of 32.6%. The score was well calibrated, including in the tails of the distribution. This supports using it for risk-based screening and prevention.

title: The NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog of published genome-wide association studies, targeted arrays and summary statistics 2019
synopsis: This update describes the 2019 state of the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog, a curated collection of published genome-wide association studies. Its scope now also covers targeted and exome arrays. As of September 2018, it held 5,687 GWAS with 71,673 variant-trait associations from 3,567 publications. It also contained 284 full summary-statistics datasets representing about 6 billion variant-trait statistics. New infrastructure includes a RESTful API for programmatic access, an improved web interface, a summary-statistics database, and a proposed community-standard format for summary statistics. The resource underpins downstream work such as fine-mapping, studies of disease mechanism, and target discovery.

title: Helios is a key transcriptional regulator of outer hair cell maturation
synopsis: This mouse study asks which factors drive outer hair cells in the cochlea to mature into their functional state, as distinct from inner hair cells. The transcription factor Helios, encoded by Ikzf2, is expressed in postnatal outer hair cells. In the cello mouse, a point mutation in Ikzf2 causes early-onset sensorineural hearing loss. Mutant outer hair cells show sharply reduced prestin-dependent electromotility and lower expression of key genes such as Slc26a5 and Ocm. Forcing Ikzf2 expression in inner hair cells turned on outer hair cell genes, turned down inner hair cell genes, and gave the cells electromotility. Helios is therefore an essential regulator of outer hair cell identity and hearing.

title: Expert specification of the ACMG/AMP variant interpretation guidelines for genetic hearing loss
synopsis: Clinical testing for hearing loss sequences many genes and often finds novel variants, so consistent variant interpretation is essential. A ClinGen expert panel adapted the ACMG/AMP variant interpretation guidelines specifically for hearing loss genes. Three rules were left unchanged, four were removed, and 21 were given disease-specific specifications. The panel tested and refined the rules on a pilot set of 51 variants. Applying the specified rules and pooling evidence across laboratories changed the classification of 37% of them (19/51). The hearing-loss-specific rules should make variant classification more consistent and improve diagnosis.

title: The UK Biobank resource with deep phenotyping and genomic data
synopsis: This paper describes the genetic data of UK Biobank, a prospective cohort of about 500,000 UK participants aged 40-69 at recruitment. Participants have rich phenotypes, including biomarkers and imaging, and are linked to their health records. The paper covers centralized genotype quality control and the characterization of population structure and relatedness. It also describes efficient phasing and imputation, which expand the testable variants to about 96 million. Classical alleles at 11 HLA genes were imputed as well, and these recovered known HLA-disease associations. The open resource supports large-scale discovery of genetic associations and the genetic basis of complex traits.

title: Fine-mapping type 2 diabetes loci to single-variant resolution using high-density imputation and islet-specific epigenome maps
synopsis: This study asks how far type 2 diabetes genetic discovery and fine-mapping can go with very large samples and dense imputation. It combines data from 898,130 European-descent individuals, 9% of them cases, and adds islet-specific epigenomic annotations. The analysis finds 243 risk loci, 135 of them new, containing 403 distinct association signals. It also finds 80 lower-frequency index variants. At 51 signals a single variant has over 80% posterior probability of association, and adding islet regulatory annotations raises that to 73. Eighteen genes have coding-variant associations that point to therapeutic targets. Chip heritability explains 18% of risk, and people at the two extremes of a polygenic score differ more than ninefold in prevalence.

title: Genomic Landscape and Mutational Signatures of Deafness-Associated Genes
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: This work tackles the hard problem of classifying genetic variants in hearing loss, a disorder that varies widely in phenotype, genes and alleles. The authors built the Deafness Variation Database, an open resource that combines genetic, genomic and clinical data with expert curation for 152 genes linked to syndromic and non-syndromic deafness. Of 876,139 variants, more than 8,100 were classed as pathogenic or likely pathogenic, more than 172,000 as benign or likely benign, and more than 695,000 as uncertain. Expert curation changed the class of 1,270 variants, 300 of them in ways that affect clinical care. More than 96% of coding variants were rare and novel. Pathogenicity depended on allele frequency, variant effect and protein domain, with patterns that differ by gene.

title: Genomic meta-analysis of the interplay between 3D chromatin organization and gene expression programs under basal and stress conditions
synopsis: This study asks how differences in 3D chromatin organization between cell types relate to gene expression, both at baseline and after stimulation. It is a meta-analysis that combines Hi-C data from thirteen cell lines with dozens of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq datasets collected under basal and treated conditions. Shifts in A/B compartments between cell lines were strongly associated with differential expression and transcription factor binding. Baseline compartments also correlated with genes induced after treatment. Still, many differential binding and induction events fell in regions that were A compartment in both cell types, so compartments alone do not explain cell-type-specific programs. The results suggest that enhancer-promoter contacts set up at baseline also shape responses to stimuli.

title: Functional CRISPR screen identifies AP1-associated enhancer regulating FOXF1 to modulate oncogene-induced senescence
synopsis: This study looks for non-coding enhancers needed to establish oncogene-induced senescence, a proliferation arrest that acts as a barrier against cancer. The authors first profiled enhancer RNAs genome-wide to find enhancers switched on by oncogenic stress. Motif analysis of these enhancers pointed to AP-1 as a major regulator. A CRISPR-Cas9 library aimed at senescence-induced, AP-1-linked enhancers was then used in a functional screen. The screen identified an enhancer, named Enh AP1-OIS1, and mutating its AP-1 site allowed cells to bypass senescence. FOXF1 was identified as the enhancer's target gene and shown to carry its effect on senescence. The work shows how CRISPR screens can assign function to regulatory DNA.

title: Genome-wide polygenic scores for common diseases identify individuals with risk equivalent to monogenic mutations
synopsis: This study asks whether genome-wide polygenic scores can find people whose risk is as high as that of carriers of monogenic mutations. The authors developed and validated polygenic scores for five common diseases. The scores flagged 8.0%, 6.1%, 3.5%, 3.2% and 1.5% of the population as having more than threefold increased risk for coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease and breast cancer, respectively. For coronary artery disease, this group is 20 times larger than the share of people carrying rare monogenic mutations with similar risk. The authors argue that polygenic risk prediction should now be considered for clinical care and discuss the issues involved.

title: Bioconda: sustainable and comprehensive software distribution for the life sciences
From genome-wide associations to candidate causal variants by statistical fine-mapping
synopsis: This review covers how to move from GWAS associations to the functional variants that actually influence complex traits. Statistical fine-mapping can pick out and rank candidate causal variants, but the many available methods and study designs make it hard to choose the best approach. The review weighs the strengths and weaknesses of different fine-mapping strategies and the main factors that affect how well they work. Topics include interpreting GWAS results, linkage disequilibrium, statistical fine-mapping methods, trans-ethnic studies, and integrating genomic annotations with other data, along with other analysis and design issues. It is a practical guide for choosing fine-mapping strategies.

title: The Galaxy platform for accessible, reproducible and collaborative biomedical analyses: 2018 update
synopsis: This update describes recent progress on Galaxy, a web-based, open-source platform for analyzing large biomedical datasets, including genomics, proteomics, metabolomics and imaging. Since 2005 Galaxy has aimed to make analyses accessible to all researchers, fully reproducible, and easy to share and extend. Over the last two years, changes to the core framework and user interface have made it possible to analyze tens of thousands of datasets. More than 5,500 tools are now available through the ToolShed. The community has written many high-quality tutorials on common genomic analyses. The numbers of public servers, contributing developers and users of the main server have all grown substantially.

title: The personal and clinical utility of polygenic risk scores
synopsis: This review looks at whether polygenic risk scores give individuals and clinicians useful information. Early GWAS findings showed that most common diseases have a more complex genetic architecture than expected, which led many to conclude that predicting disease from DNA offers little value. More recent work has started to show that polygenic risk profiling can identify groups of people who could benefit from knowing their probabilistic susceptibility to disease. The review collects the evidence on the personal and clinical utility of polygenic risk profiling. It offers a framework for judging when such scores could inform prevention, screening or treatment decisions.

title: Exploring the phenotypic consequences of tissue specific gene expression variation inferred from GWAS summary statistics
synopsis: This study asks how genetically regulated gene expression in different tissues relates to complex traits when only GWAS summary statistics are available. It derives a mathematical formula that reproduces PrediXcan gene-level results from summary data (S-PrediXcan) and shows that the method is accurate and generally robust to mismatched reference panels. Applied to 44 GTEx tissues and more than 100 phenotypes, it produces a public catalog of gene-trait associations that replicates in an independent cohort. Most associations are tissue specific. Some significant, colocalized associations appear in unexpected tissues, which argues for scanning many tissues without prior assumptions. Monogenic disease genes are enriched among associations with related traits, suggesting that milder changes in these genes produce milder phenotypes.

title: FOCS: a novel method for analyzing enhancer and gene activity patterns infers an extensive enhancer–promoter map
synopsis: This paper addresses how to link enhancers to the promoters they regulate using sequencing data that measure the activity of both across many samples. It first shows that existing inference methods produce many false-positive links. It then introduces FOCS, a new inference method. Benchmarked against ChIA-PET, HiChIP and eQTL data, FOCS has lower false discovery rates and higher power. Applying it to 2,630 samples from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, FANTOM5 and a new GRO-seq compendium, the authors build extensive public enhancer-promoter maps. They show how these maps can be used to generate biological hypotheses about gene regulation.

title: An epigenetic biomarker of aging for lifespan and healthspan
synopsis: This study asks whether an epigenetic aging biomarker trained on clinical measures of phenotypic age, rather than on chronological age, can better capture differences in lifespan and healthspan. Using a two-step approach on whole-blood DNA methylation, the authors develop DNAm PhenoAge. It outperforms earlier epigenetic clocks in predicting all-cause mortality, cancers, healthspan, physical functioning and Alzheimer's disease, and it correlates strongly with age in every tissue and cell type tested. In sorted cells, higher epigenetic age relative to chronological age is associated with more active pro-inflammatory and interferon pathways and with weaker transcription/translation, DNA damage response and mitochondrial signatures. A single marker therefore captures risk for many outcomes and points to pathways involved in aging.

title: Heritability enrichment of specifically expressed genes identifies disease-relevant tissues and cell types
synopsis: This paper develops a way to identify the tissues and cell types relevant to a disease by combining gene expression data with GWAS summary statistics. Using stratified LD score regression, it tests whether heritability is enriched around the genes most specifically expressed in each tissue. Across 48 diseases and traits (average N = 169,331), the authors find significant tissue-specific enrichments for 34 traits at FDR below 5%, many of them consistent with known biology. Within the brain, bipolar disorder is enriched in inhibitory over excitatory neurons, while schizophrenia and body mass index are enriched in excitatory over inhibitory neurons. The approach gives a polygenic way to interpret GWAS signals through expression data.

title: QAPA: a new method for the systematic analysis of alternative polyadenylation from RNA-seq data
synopsis: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) affects most mammalian genes but has been hard to profile reliably with conventional RNA-seq. This paper presents QAPA, a method that infers APA from standard RNA-seq data and is faster and more sensitive than existing tools. Applied to neurogenesis, QAPA reveals distinct, temporally coordinated APA programs. Genes regulated by APA overlap little with those regulated by alternative splicing. Modeling these data uncovers a sequence code underlying APA. Because it works on conventional RNA-seq, the method makes regulated APA programs accessible in the many datasets that already exist.

title: Sequential regulatory activity prediction across chromosomes with convolutional neural networks
synopsis: This study asks whether cell-type-specific epigenetic and transcriptional profiles in large mammalian genomes can be predicted from DNA sequence alone. The authors build a convolutional neural network system that identifies promoters and distal regulatory elements and combines their content to predict gene expression. The model's predicted effects of genomic variants on expression align well with causal variants underlying eQTLs in human populations. This makes the model useful for generating mechanistic hypotheses about how noncoding variants act and for fine-mapping disease loci.

title: The Human Cell Atlas
synopsis: This paper describes the Human Cell Atlas, an international collaborative project to define every human cell type by its molecular profile, such as gene expression, and to connect these profiles with classical descriptions like location and morphology. Recent high-throughput single-cell profiling methods make this long-standing goal feasible. The paper sets out the idea, its potential uses, early proofs of concept and design considerations, including a commitment to open data, code and community. An open reference map of healthy human cells would support studies of physiology, development, regulatory circuits and cell interactions. It would also provide a baseline for understanding how cells go wrong in disease.

title: Association analysis identifies 65 new breast cancer risk loci
synopsis: Much of the genetic contribution to breast cancer risk remains unexplained. This study reports a genome-wide association study of 122,977 cases and 105,974 controls of European ancestry and 14,068 cases and 13,104 controls of East Asian ancestry, which identifies 65 new loci for overall breast cancer risk. Most credible risk SNPs fall in distal regulatory elements. Predicted target genes in breast cells overlap strongly with somatic driver genes in breast tumours. Heritability in regulatory features is 2-5-fold enriched relative to the genome-wide average, with strong enrichment at particular transcription factor binding sites. These findings clarify genetic susceptibility and should improve genetic risk scores for screening and prevention.

title: Characterization of noncoding regulatory DNA in the human genome
synopsis: This review asks how the functional noncoding elements of the human genome can be mapped completely, given that most common-disease variants fall outside coding regions. It surveys maps of DNA accessibility and epigenetic marks, which flag putative regulatory elements, and high-throughput reporter assays, which test regulatory activity but remove elements from their chromosomal context and long-range interactions. The authors argue that assigning function definitively requires perturbing elements in place, and that genome-editing screens now make this possible genome-wide. Read properly, such screens could produce an unbiased map of functional noncoding DNA, which is needed to interpret disease-associated variants.

title: 10 Years of GWAS Discovery: Biology, Function, and Translation
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: This review looks back on the first ten years of genome-wide association studies and what the design has delivered. It covers discoveries in population and complex-trait genetics, insights into disease biology, and progress toward new therapeutics. It also looks ahead to the next decade, when GWAS are expected to include millions of array-genotyped samples imputed to large sequenced reference panels, along with hundreds of thousands of whole-genome sequences. It is a broad reference for where association studies have succeeded and where the field is likely to go.

title: The contribution of rare variants to risk of schizophrenia in individuals with and without intellectual disability
synopsis: This study asks how rare, damaging variants contribute to schizophrenia risk and whether that contribution differs by intellectual disability status. It meta-analyzes whole-exome data from 4,133 cases and 9,274 controls, de novo mutations from 1,077 trios, and copy number variants from 6,882 cases and 11,255 controls. Cases carry an excess of rare damaging variants in 3,488 genes that are intolerant of loss-of-function variation. In patients who also have intellectual disability, this burden is concentrated in known neurodevelopmental disorder genes. After those genes are excluded, a burden remains in other constrained genes, and it is present even in patients without intellectual disability. The results point to genetic risk shared between schizophrenia and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Network propagation: a universal amplifier of genetic associations
synopsis: This review looks at how biological networks can boost weak genetic association signals, based on the principle that genes affecting the same phenotype tend to interact. It surveys methods built on random walks, information diffusion and electrical resistance, which have been used to identify disease genes, genetic modules and drug targets. The authors show that all of these methods are variants of one mathematical framework, network propagation. Seeing them this way makes network propagation a general data transformation that can be applied across many kinds of genetic analysis, not a set of unrelated tools.

title: An Expanded View of Complex Traits: From Polygenic to Omnigenic
synopsis: This perspective asks why association signals for complex traits are spread across most of the genome instead of clustering in disease-relevant pathways. The authors propose that gene regulatory networks are so interconnected that any gene expressed in a disease-relevant cell type can affect the core genes that drive the disease. Under this omnigenic model, most heritability comes from small effects of peripheral genes outside the core pathways, not from the core genes themselves. The model changes how GWAS results are interpreted and how the search for causal biology is framed.

title: Development and validation of QRISK3 risk prediction algorithms to estimate future risk of cardiovascular disease: prospective cohort study
synopsis: This study updates the QRISK prediction algorithm for 10-year cardiovascular disease risk by adding new candidate risk factors. Using primary care records from English general practices, the authors fit sex-specific Cox models in 7.89 million patients and validated them in 2.67 million patients from separate practices. All new factors were retained except HIV/AIDS: chronic kidney disease stage 3, blood pressure variability, migraine, corticosteroids, lupus, atypical antipsychotics, severe mental illness and erectile dysfunction. The models were well calibrated, with C statistics of 0.88 in women and 0.86 in men. Overall performance was similar to QRISK2, but the new version can identify more high-risk patients.

title: Nextflow enables reproducible computational workflows
Gfi1Cre mice have early onset progressive hearing loss and induce recombination in numerous inner ear non-hair cells
synopsis: This study asks whether the widely used Gfi1Cre mouse, which is meant to drive recombination only in inner ear hair cells, is as specific and phenotypically neutral as assumed. Using immunofluorescence and flow cytometry, the authors find broad Cre activity in the neonatal inner ear, mostly in resident macrophages, which outnumber hair cells. Heterozygous Gfi1Cre mice develop early-onset progressive hearing loss, though vestibular function stays normal up to 10 months, and they show small but significant changes in hair-cell-enriched transcripts. These findings matter for designing and interpreting conditional knockout and reporter experiments in the inner ear.

title: Overview of the BioBank Japan Project: Study design and profile
synopsis: This report describes the design and participant profile of BioBank Japan, a patient-based biobank set up to support personalized medicine. Between 2003 and 2008, patients with any of 47 common diseases were enrolled at 12 medical institutions across Japan. DNA was collected at baseline, and clinical data and serum were collected annually until 2013. About 200,000 participants were registered (53.1% male, mean age at entry around 62), and survival data, including cause of death, are available for 141,612 of them. Combining genomic data with longitudinal clinical records makes it a major resource for genetic studies of common diseases in East Asian populations.

title: Evaluation of Polygenic Risk Scores for Breast and Ovarian Cancer Risk Prediction in BRCA1 and BRCA2 Mutation Carriers
source: JNCI: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
synopsis: Do common breast and ovarian cancer risk variants found in general-population genome-wide association studies (GWAS) also predict cancer risk in women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations? The study built polygenic risk scores from known susceptibility SNPs and tested them in 15,252 BRCA1 and 8,211 BRCA2 carriers using a weighted cohort analysis of time to diagnosis. In BRCA1 carriers, the estrogen receptor-negative breast cancer score had the strongest effect (HR 1.27 per SD). In BRCA2 carriers, the overall breast cancer score was strongest (HR 1.22). The ovarian score predicted ovarian cancer in both groups. Absolute risks differed by more than 10% between the top and bottom deciles; for example, ovarian cancer risk by age 80 in BRCA2 carriers was 6% versus 19%. Adding these scores could give carriers more personalized risk estimates.

title: Colocalization of GWAS and eQTL Signals Detects Target Genes
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: Most GWAS risk loci lie in non-coding DNA and may act by changing gene expression, but it is hard to tell whether the same variant drives both a GWAS signal and an eQTL signal. Linkage disequilibrium blurs the picture, and some loci contain several causal variants. Existing colocalization methods assume only one causal variant per locus. eCAVIAR is a probabilistic method that allows multiple causal variants and needs only summary statistics. The method was tested on simulated data and then applied to eQTL data from 45 tissues together with loci for glucose- and insulin-related traits. It prioritized likely relevant tissues and target genes, which helps link non-coding association signals to the genes behind them.

title: Systematic mapping of functional enhancer–promoter connections with CRISPR interference
synopsis: Which non-coding regions actually control a gene's transcription? The question is hard to answer from sequence or chromatin marks alone. This study used CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) to systematically silence non-coding regions around the GATA1 and MYC loci. It then measured which regions affect each gene, mapping functional enhancer-promoter connections directly. The approach tests regulatory elements by perturbation rather than inferring them from correlation. It provides an unbiased way to check the results of enhancer-promoter screens and to locate regulatory DNA relevant to gene control.

title: Alternative polyadenylation of mRNA precursors
synopsis: This review covers alternative polyadenylation (APA), an RNA-processing mechanism that produces different 3' ends on mRNAs and other RNA polymerase II transcripts. APA is found across eukaryotes, varies by tissue, and is now seen as a major layer of gene regulation that matters for cell proliferation and differentiation. The review discusses how APA affects mRNA metabolism, protein diversity and protein localization. It also covers the mechanisms that control site choice, including changes in core processing factor levels, RNA-binding proteins and transcription-coupled regulation. It is a useful overview for interpreting 3' end variation in transcriptomic data.

title: HiChIP: efficient and sensitive analysis of protein-directed genome architecture
synopsis: Genome folding is central to gene control but hard to measure efficiently, especially the contacts tied to specific proteins. HiChIP is a protein-centric chromatin conformation method that captures interactions linked to a chosen protein. Compared with ChIA-PET, it yields more than 10 times as many informative reads and needs over 100 times less input material. Applied to cohesin, HiChIP revealed genome architecture at several scales with higher signal-to-background ratios than in situ Hi-C. The method makes protein-anchored 3D genome maps practical for smaller samples and at lower sequencing cost.

title: Basset: learning the regulatory code of the accessible genome with deep convolutional neural networks
synopsis: Most disease-associated non-coding variants have unknown mechanisms, partly because the regulatory code of DNA is poorly understood. Basset is an open-source package that uses deep convolutional neural networks to predict the functional activity of DNA sequence. It was trained on DNase-seq accessibility maps from 164 cell types and predicted accessibility more accurately than previous methods. Its predicted allelic effects on accessibility were much larger for likely causal GWAS SNPs than for nearby SNPs in linkage disequilibrium with them. A single accessibility assay in a new cell type can be used to train a model that scores every possible mutation, which helps interpret non-coding variation.

title: The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship
synopsis: This comment addresses the need for better infrastructure for reusing scholarly data. A group of stakeholders from academia, industry, funding agencies and publishers proposed and endorsed the FAIR Data Principles, a short, measurable set of guidelines for making data findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable. Unlike related efforts aimed mainly at human users, FAIR puts particular weight on letting machines automatically find and use data. The paper is the first formal publication of the principles, with their rationale and example implementations. It has become a common reference point for how genomic and other research data should be shared.

title: 3’UTR Shortening Potentiates MicroRNA-Based Repression of Pro-differentiation Genes in Proliferating Human Cells
synopsis: Proliferating cells tend to use alternative polyadenylation sites that shorten 3'UTRs, which can let mRNAs escape microRNA repression. Because microRNA sites near the ends of a 3'UTR tend to be more active, shortening might instead strengthen repression by sites that end up near the new end. The study used 3' sequencing in several human cell lines to map the 3' ends of human transcripts. Conserved microRNA sites were enriched just upstream of alternative polyadenylation sites, especially in pro-differentiation and anti-proliferative genes. Sites for the miR-17-92 cluster were particularly enriched. This suggests that 3'UTR shortening both frees growth-promoting genes and strengthens repression of anti-proliferative genes.

title: Integrative approaches for large-scale transcriptome-wide association studies
FINEMAP: efficient variable selection using summary data from genome-wide association studies
synopsis: Fine-mapping tries to pinpoint the causal variants behind genome-wide association signals, but current methods that use summary statistics search every possible causal configuration exhaustively, which is computationally expensive. This paper introduces FINEMAP, a software package that uses a shotgun stochastic search to explore only the most important causal configurations in a region. The authors show that FINEMAP gives accurate results in a fraction of the processing time of existing approaches. The speedup makes summary-statistic fine-mapping practical for the growing volume of association and sequencing data, including regions with multiple causal variants.

title: Functional genetic screens for enhancer elements in the human genome using CRISPR-Cas9
synopsis: Most efforts to identify noncoding regulatory elements have relied on large-scale reporter assays, which do not reproduce endogenous chromatin conditions. This study presents two CRISPR-Cas9 genetic screens that test enhancers in their native genomic context by targeting Cas9 to transcription factor binding sites within enhancer regions. The screens identified several functional enhancers and characterized two that mediate p53- and ERα-dependent gene regulation. A tiling screen across the genome also mapped functional domains within individual enhancers at fine resolution. The approach offers a direct way to test the function of noncoding sequence, which is relevant for interpreting regulatory variants.

title: Genome-Wide Polyadenylation Maps Reveal Dynamic mRNA 3′-End Formation in the Failing Human Heart
synopsis: This study asks whether alternative cleavage and polyadenylation, which sets 3′UTR length, regulates gene expression in the human heart and changes in heart failure. The authors used 3′-end RNA sequencing on healthy and failing heart tissue and found disease-specific polyadenylation signatures in many genes. Genes with shortened 3′UTRs in failing hearts were enriched for RNA binding, while lengthened ones were enriched for cytoskeletal and actin-binding functions. RNA-seq in a larger set of hearts showed these genes are often differentially expressed, with 3′UTR length inversely correlated with expression. The APA regulator PABPN1 was strongly reduced in failing hearts, pointing to 3′-end processing as an added layer of regulation in disease.

title: Million Veteran Program: A mega-biobank to study genetic influences on health and disease
synopsis: This paper describes the design and progress of the Million Veteran Program, an observational cohort and mega-biobank within the US Veterans Affairs health care system. Participants provide questionnaire data, access to their electronic health records, and a blood sample for genotyping and other assays. Enrollment began in 2011, and by August 2015 about 397,000 veterans had joined through roughly 50 sites. Among the 199,348 participants with genotype data, 92% are male and most are aged 50 to 69. White (77.2%) and African American (13.5%) participants are well represented. The resource is intended to support large-scale genetic association research and precision medicine.

title: RFX transcription factors are essential for hearing in mice
synopsis: Hair cells in the mammalian inner ear do not regenerate, and little is known about the transcription factors that drive their postnatal maturation. This study applied a cell type-specific functional genomic analysis to transcriptomes of auditory and vestibular sensory epithelia from early postnatal mice. RFX transcription factors emerged as conserved regulators of hair cell-specific gene expression, and several RFX family members were detected in developing hair cells. Conditional knockout of Rfx1 and Rfx3 caused deafness through rapid loss of outer hair cells that had initially formed normally. The results establish RFX factors as essential for outer hair cell survival and hearing.

title: A global reference for human genetic variation
synopsis: This paper reports the completion of the 1000 Genomes Project, which aimed to catalog common human genetic variation across diverse populations. It combined low-coverage whole-genome sequencing, deep exome sequencing and dense genotyping arrays to reconstruct the genomes of 2,504 individuals from 26 populations. The project identified more than 88 million variants, including 84.7 million SNPs, 3.6 million short indels and 60,000 structural variants, all phased into haplotypes. The resource captures over 99% of SNPs with frequency above 1% across many ancestries. It became a standard reference panel for imputation and population-genetic analyses, and the paper discusses implications for studies of common disease.

title: Partitioning heritability by functional annotation using genome-wide association summary statistics
synopsis: This paper asks how heritability of complex traits is distributed across functional categories of the genome. It introduces stratified LD score regression, a computationally tractable method that partitions heritability using only GWAS summary statistics while accounting for linkage disequilibrium. Applied to 17 diseases and traits with an average sample size of 73,599, the method found strong heritability enrichment in conserved regions across many traits. Immune diseases showed very large enrichment in FANTOM5 enhancers, and central nervous system cell types were enriched for body mass index, age at menarche, educational attainment and smoking. The approach links GWAS signals to relevant tissues and cell types and helps prioritize functional follow-up.

title: Genetic variance estimation with imputed variants finds negligible missing heritability for human height and body mass index
synopsis: This study asks how much of the heritability of height and body mass index can be explained by imputed genome-wide variants in unrelated individuals. The authors propose GREML-LDMS, which stratifies variants by LD and minor allele frequency, and show by simulation that imputation captures about 97% of common and 68% of rare variant variation. In 44,126 individuals, about 17 million imputed variants explained 56% of height variance and 27% of BMI variance, with evidence of natural selection on associated variants. Allowing for imperfect tagging, they estimate true heritability at 60-70% for height and 30-40% for BMI, leaving little missing heritability. They conclude that genotyping arrays followed by imputation are currently more cost-effective than whole-genome sequencing.

title: Predicting effects of noncoding variants with deep learning–based sequence model
synopsis: This paper asks whether the functional effects of noncoding variants can be predicted directly from DNA sequence. It introduces DeepSEA, a deep learning framework that learns a regulatory sequence code from large-scale chromatin-profiling data. The trained model predicts how sequence changes alter chromatin features, with sensitivity down to single nucleotides. The authors use these predictions to improve the prioritization of functional variants, including expression quantitative trait loci and disease-associated variants. This matters because most trait-associated variation lies outside coding regions, where its effects are hard to interpret.

title: Mapping Nucleosome Resolution Chromosome Folding in Yeast by Micro-C
synopsis: This study introduces Micro-C, a Hi-C variant that cuts chromatin with micrococcal nuclease instead of restriction enzymes, to map chromosome folding at nucleosome resolution. In budding yeast, the maps reveal many self-associating domains that had not been seen in yeast before. These domains are much smaller than mammalian topologically associating domains and usually span one to five genes. Strong boundaries fall at promoters of highly transcribed genes and at regions of rapid histone turnover, which are often bound by the RSC remodeler. Experiments in mutants implicate RSC, Ssu72, Mediator, Rtt109 and the histone H4 tail in genome folding.

title: A method to predict the impact of regulatory variants from DNA sequence
Mapping long-range promoter contacts in human cells with high-resolution capture Hi-C
synopsis: This study asks how distal regulatory elements contact their target promoters across the human genome, at higher resolution than standard conformation capture methods allow. It applies Capture Hi-C to almost 22,000 promoters in two human blood cell types and finds over 1.6 million shared and cell type-restricted interactions spanning hundreds of kilobases. Active genes contact enhancer-like elements, while inactive genes contact previously uncharacterized elements with repressive marks that may act as silencers. The interacting regions are enriched for disease-associated SNPs, which helps link distal noncoding variants to the genes they may regulate.

title: Disruptions of Topological Chromatin Domains Cause Pathogenic Rewiring of Gene-Enhancer Interactions
synopsis: This study tests whether disrupting topologically associating domains can rewire gene regulation and cause disease. It studies human limb malformations caused by deletions, inversions or duplications at the WNT6/IHH/EPHA4/PAX3 locus and recreates the rearrangements in mice with CRISPR/Cas editing. In mouse limb tissue and patient fibroblasts, the rearrangements create ectopic promoter contacts and move a cluster of Epha4 limb enhancers so that it drives misexpression of another gene. This rewiring happened only when a CTCF-associated boundary was disrupted. The results suggest criteria for predicting the pathogenicity of noncoding structural variants.

title: Understanding multicellular function and disease with human tissue-specific networks
synopsis: This study builds genome-wide functional interaction networks for 144 human tissues and cell types to capture how gene function depends on tissue context. It uses a data-driven Bayesian method that integrates thousands of diverse experiments across tissue and disease states. The networks predict lineage-specific responses to perturbation, show how gene roles change across tissues and reveal relationships among diseases. The authors also introduce NetWAS, which combines nominally significant GWAS genes with tissue-specific networks and identifies disease genes more accurately than GWAS alone. The GIANT webserver makes the networks available for queries, visualization, analysis and download.

title: MAGMA: Generalized Gene-Set Analysis of GWAS Data
synopsis: This paper addresses weaknesses of existing gene and gene-set analysis methods for GWAS, including sensitivity to linkage disequilibrium, poor detection of multi-marker associations and costly permutation testing. It presents MAGMA, which runs gene analysis with a multiple regression model and adds gene-set analysis as a separate regression layer. This design also allows analysis of continuous gene properties and of several gene sets at once. In simulations and Crohn's disease data, MAGMA had more power than other tools, identified more associated genes and gene sets, kept correct type 1 error and ran considerably faster.

title: A DIseAse MOdule Detection (DIAMOnD) Algorithm Derived from a Systematic Analysis of Connectivity Patterns of Disease Proteins in the Human Interactome
synopsis: This study asks which connectivity patterns best describe how disease proteins sit within the human protein interaction network. Analyzing 70 complex diseases, the authors find that disease proteins do not form locally dense communities, and that connectivity significance is the most predictive measure. Based on this, they design DIAMOnD, an algorithm that grows the full disease module around a set of known disease proteins. They evaluate it on controlled synthetic data and validate the modules it finds across a large set of diseases. The work offers a principled basis for network-based discovery of disease genes.

title: UK Biobank: An Open Access Resource for Identifying the Causes of a Wide Range of Complex Diseases of Middle and Old Age
synopsis: This paper describes UK Biobank, a large population-based prospective cohort study. It was set up as an open-access resource for studying the genetic and non-genetic determinants of the diseases of middle and old age. The abstract gives no details on cohort size, data types or findings. The resource matters because it allows researchers to study the causes of a wide range of complex diseases in one large population, and it has become a central dataset for statistical genetics.

title: Second-generation PLINK: rising to the challenge of larger and richer datasets
synopsis: This paper describes a new codebase for PLINK, the widely used toolset for genome-wide association studies and population genetics. Imputed and sequenced datasets have become too large for the original software, and its file format cannot store genotype likelihoods, phase, or multiallelic variants. The first release, PLINK 1.9, uses bit-level parallelism and faster algorithms for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and Fisher's exact tests. Together these changes speed up most operations by one to four orders of magnitude and handle datasets that do not fit in memory. An extended data format that stores the richer genotype information is the basis for PLINK 2.0. As a result, standard analyses of very large genetic datasets can run without high-end computing resources.

title: Uncovering disease-disease relationships through the incomplete interactome
synopsis: This study asks how incomplete protein interaction maps limit what we can learn about mechanistic relationships between diseases. It derives the mathematical conditions under which a disease module, a localized cluster of interacting disease-associated proteins, can be detected in the human interactome. Modules can only be identified for diseases whose data coverage passes a specific threshold. A network-based distance between disease modules predicts molecular similarity: disease pairs with overlapping modules show significant similarity in proteins, gene expression, symptoms, and comorbidity. The approach also links diseases that share no known disease genes, which goes beyond comparing gene lists alone.

title: Integrative analysis of 111 reference human epigenomes
synopsis: Epigenomic research has lacked a reference comparable to the human genome sequence. This paper presents an integrative analysis of 111 reference epigenomes from primary human cells and tissues, generated by the NIH Roadmap Epigenomics Consortium. The data cover histone modifications, DNA accessibility, DNA methylation, and RNA expression. The analysis builds global maps of regulatory elements, defines modules of coordinated regulatory activity, and infers their likely activators and repressors. Variants associated with diseases and traits are enriched in tissue-specific epigenomic marks, which points to the cell types relevant to each trait. The collection is a widely used resource for interpreting noncoding genetic variation and studying gene regulation.

title: LD Score regression distinguishes confounding from polygenicity in genome-wide association studies
lab: the Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium
synopsis: Test statistics in genome-wide association studies are often inflated, and the inflation could come from true polygenic signal or from confounders such as population stratification and cryptic relatedness. Existing methods could not tell these apart. This paper introduces LD Score regression, which regresses association statistics on each variant's linkage disequilibrium score. Polygenic signal increases with LD, while confounding does not. The regression intercept gives a correction factor that is more accurate and more powerful than genomic control. Applied to many large GWAS, the method finds that most of the inflation comes from polygenicity rather than bias. The framework became the basis for heritability and genetic correlation estimation from summary statistics.

title: Tissue-based map of the human proteome
synopsis: Knowing the human genome sequence does not tell us where and how each of the roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes is expressed. This work presents a map of protein expression across 32 human tissues. It combines RNA-level measurements with antibody-based profiling that localizes each protein within tissues. The results are available on an interactive website for exploring expression across the human body. The resource provides a tissue-level reference for protein expression, which helps with interpreting gene function, disease biology, and candidate genes from genetic studies.

title: Pan-cancer network analysis identifies combinations of rare somatic mutations across pathways and protein complexes
synopsis: Cancer mutations follow a long-tail distribution: many genes are mutated in only a few tumors, which makes significantly mutated genes and pathways hard to detect. This study applies HotNet2, a new algorithm that finds significantly mutated subnetworks in an interaction network, to 3,281 tumors from 12 cancer types in The Cancer Genome Atlas. It identifies 16 significantly mutated subnetworks. They include well-known signaling pathways as well as less-characterized complexes such as cohesin and condensin, and many show co-occurring mutations across samples. The subnetworks contain dozens of rarely mutated genes, many with independent evidence of a role in cancer. Network-level analysis can therefore reveal cancer drivers that single-gene tests miss.

title: A 3D Map of the Human Genome at Kilobase Resolution Reveals Principles of Chromatin Looping
synopsis: This study uses in situ Hi-C to map three-dimensional genome architecture in nine cell types, building both haploid and diploid maps. The densest map, from human lymphoblastoid cells, contains 4.9 billion contacts and reaches 1 kb resolution. The genome is divided into contact domains (median 185 kb) that match distinct histone mark patterns and fall into six subcompartments. About 10,000 loops are identified. They often connect promoters to enhancers, correlate with gene activation, and are conserved across cell types and species. Loop anchors usually sit at domain boundaries and bind CTCF, and over 90% of anchor motif pairs face each other in convergent orientation. These findings set out basic principles of chromatin looping.

title: QuantSeq 3′ mRNA sequencing for RNA quantification
Dynamic analyses of alternative polyadenylation from RNA-seq reveal a 3′-UTR landscape across seven tumour types
synopsis: Alternative polyadenylation regulates most human genes, but its role in cancer is poorly characterized because dedicated profiling methods are rarely used. This study introduces DaPars, an algorithm that detects dynamic alternative polyadenylation de novo from standard RNA-seq data. Applied to 358 tumor/normal pairs across seven TCGA cancer types, it finds 1,346 genes with recurrent, tumor-specific polyadenylation changes. In 91% of these genes, tumors have shorter 3' UTRs that can escape microRNA repression; one example is the metabolic enzyme glutaminase.
