Some events add prognostic power beyond standard clinical and molecular variables. The polyadenylation factor CstF64 emerges as a likely master regulator of 3' UTR shortening across tumor types.

title: Integrating Functional Data to Prioritize Causal Variants in Statistical Fine-Mapping Studies
synopsis: The paper asks how to choose which variants at a GWAS risk locus to send for functional testing, given that marginal statistics and simple posterior models ignore functional information. The authors build a probabilistic fine-mapping framework that uses summary association statistics, allows more than one causal variant per locus, and learns from the data how much each functional annotation contributes, sharing these estimates across all risk loci. In simulations based on 1000 Genomes data, it reduced the number of SNPs needed to capture 90% of causal variants from 13.3 to 10.4 per locus, compared with the next-best method. In a meta-analysis of four blood lipid traits, variants in exons and transcription start sites were more likely to be causal and variants in repressed regions less likely, and the 90% confidence sets shrank from 17.5 to 13.5 variants per locus. A cost-to-benefit framework is also provided to decide how many variants to follow up.

title: Rare-Variant Association Analysis: Study Designs and Statistical Tests
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: This review asks how studies looking for rare variants linked to complex traits should be designed and analyzed, since common variants leave much of the heritability unexplained. It walks through a typical analysis pipeline for rare-variant studies and reviews cost-effective sequencing designs and genotyping platforms. It compares gene- or region-based tests, namely burden tests, variance-component tests and combined omnibus tests, in terms of their assumptions and when each performs well. It also covers meta-analysis, adjusting for population stratification, imputation, follow-up studies and heritability due to rare variants. The review closes with practical analysis guidelines and open challenges.

title: RAREMETAL: fast and powerful meta-analysis for rare variants
synopsis: This application note describes RAREMETAL, a software tool for combining rare-variant association results across studies, whether the variants were measured by sequencing or by genotyping arrays. The tool can also analyze individual studies, accepts several input file formats, and works with both related and unrelated individuals. It runs single-variant and burden tests and supports conditional association analysis. Executables, source code and documentation are freely available. The tool targets a practical bottleneck, since large consortia need fast, flexible meta-analysis to have enough power to detect rare-variant effects.

title: Bayesian Test for Colocalisation between Pairs of Genetic Association Studies Using Summary Statistics
synopsis: The paper asks whether two association signals in the same region, such as a disease GWAS hit and an eQTL, reflect one shared causal variant. The authors develop a Bayesian colocalisation test that needs only single-SNP summary statistics, so any two GWAS datasets can be compared. They reanalyzed liver gene expression from 966 samples together with a lipid meta-analysis of more than 100,000 Europeans. The test supported 26 of 38 previously reported eQTL–lipid colocalisations and found 14 new ones. For SYPL2, IFT172 and TBKBP1, the data pointed instead to SORT1, GCKR and KPNB1 as the more likely causal genes. The method gives a formal way to nominate candidate causal genes at GWAS loci.

title: CFIm25 links alternative polyadenylation to glioblastoma tumour suppression
synopsis: The study asks whether RNA 3'-end processing factors that control alternative polyadenylation help cause tumours, since proliferating cells tend to shorten their 3' UTRs and so escape microRNA repression. The authors identify CFIm25 as a broad repressor of proximal poly(A) site use. Applying a regression model to standard RNA-seq data, they found at least 1,450 genes, about 11% of expressed mRNAs, with shortened 3' UTRs after CFIm25 knockdown, along with higher levels of oncogenes such as cyclin D1. Glioblastomas with low CFIm25 showed shortened 3' UTRs in a subset of CFIm25-regulated genes. Depleting CFIm25 increased tumour growth and overexpressing it suppressed growth, linking this processing factor to glioblastoma.

title: Transcriptional enhancers: from properties to genome-wide predictions
synopsis: This review asks how enhancers, the regulatory elements that set precise gene expression patterns, can be found across animal genomes, given that the current picture is still incomplete decades after their discovery. It describes how features of enhancer sequences and chromatin are used to predict enhancers in genome-wide studies. It also covers newer high-throughput methods that identify enhancers directly by measuring their activity. The review ends with recent technological advances and the main open challenges in regulatory genomics, making it a useful overview for interpreting noncoding variation.

title: A general framework for estimating the relative pathogenicity of human genetic variants
synopsis: Most variant annotation methods rely on a single kind of information, such as conservation, or cover only certain variant classes, such as missense changes. CADD combines many diverse annotations into a single C score for each variant, using a support vector machine trained to separate 14.7 million high-frequency human-derived alleles from 14.7 million simulated variants. Scores are precomputed for all 8.6 billion possible single-nucleotide variants, and short indels can also be scored. C scores correlate with allelic diversity, functional annotations, pathogenicity, disease severity, measured regulatory effects and complex trait associations, and they rank known pathogenic variants highly within individual genomes. This gives one genome-wide measure for prioritizing likely deleterious variants across many functional categories.

title: DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types
synopsis: The study asks whether DNA methylation can predict age accurately across many human tissues and cell types, and whether that prediction has biological meaning. A multi-tissue age predictor based on 353 CpG sites was built from 8,000 samples in 82 Illumina array datasets covering 51 healthy tissues and cell types. The estimated age is near zero for embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells, tracks cell passage number, gives a highly heritable measure of age acceleration, and also works in chimpanzee tissues. In 6,000 samples covering 20 cancer types, every cancer type showed significant age acceleration, 36 years on average, which was related to somatic mutation burden, TP53 status and steroid receptor mutations. The freely available clock provides a tool for research on development, cancer and aging.

title: 2013 ACC/AHA Guideline on the Assessment of Cardiovascular Risk
Transposition of native chromatin for fast and sensitive epigenomic profiling of open chromatin, DNA-binding proteins and nucleosome position
synopsis: This paper introduces ATAC-seq, a method for profiling open chromatin by inserting sequencing adaptors directly into native chromatin with a transposase. The protocol has two steps and works with 500 to 50,000 cells. From a single assay, it maps open chromatin, DNA-binding protein footprints, nucleosome positions and chromatin compaction at nucleotide resolution. The authors identify classes of DNA-binding factors that strictly avoid, tolerate or tend to overlap with nucleosomes. Using CD4+ T cells sampled from one person on consecutive days, they show that an individual's epigenome can be profiled fast enough to inform clinical decisions. The method's speed and low input requirements made genome-wide chromatin accessibility profiling widely practical.

title: Alternative cleavage and polyadenylation: extent, regulation and function
synopsis: This review covers alternative cleavage and polyadenylation (APA), in which a gene uses more than one polyadenylation site to produce mRNAs with different 3' ends. A large share of protein-coding and long non-coding genes have multiple polyadenylation sites, so APA is widespread. The resulting isoforms can differ in coding sequence or in 3' untranslated regions. These differences can change an RNA's function, stability, localization and translation efficiency. The review describes the polyadenylation machinery, methods for identifying APA events, the mechanisms that control which poly(A) site is used, and the biological processes and diseases linked to APA. It is a useful overview of an important layer of post-transcriptional gene regulation.

title: The Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project
synopsis: Most variants found by genome-wide association studies do not change protein-coding sequence, which suggests that many act through gene regulation. This paper describes the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project, which was set up to study how genetic variation relates to gene expression across human tissues. The project will build a public database and a tissue bank sampled from many tissues. These resources will allow systematic mapping of expression quantitative trait loci in multiple tissues. The aim is to help explain how noncoding disease-associated variants affect susceptibility, making GTEx a central resource for interpreting association signals.

title: Genome-Wide Quantitative Enhancer Activity Maps Identified by STARR-seq
synopsis: Projects such as ENCODE and modENCODE have annotated many regulatory regions, but how many enhancers animal genomes contain, and where they are, how cell-type-specific they are and how strong they are, remains largely unknown. This paper presents STARR-seq, a massively parallel reporter assay that measures enhancer activity directly and quantitatively across the whole genome. In STARR-seq, candidate DNA fragments are placed so that active enhancers drive their own transcription. Each fragment's activity can then be read out by sequencing. The resulting genome-wide maps of enhancer strength give insight into how the regulatory genome is organized and offer a functional complement to annotations based on chromatin marks.

title: eRNAs Are Required for p53-Dependent Enhancer Activity and Gene Transcription
synopsis: This study asks how the p53 tumor suppressor regulates transcription from binding sites located far from its known target genes. Genome-wide chromatin-binding profiles show that many distal p53-bound regions carry conserved p53 motifs and the hallmarks of enhancers. The authors show that these p53-bound enhancer regions have enhancer activity and contact several neighboring genes on the same chromosome. In a p53-dependent manner, the regions produce enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), and these eRNAs are required for efficient activation of target genes and for p53-dependent cell-cycle arrest. The findings show that a single p53 binding site can regulate multiple genes and give eRNAs a functional role in enhancer activity.

title: Genome-wide Methylation Profiles Reveal Quantitative Views of Human Aging Rates
synopsis: This study asks whether DNA methylation can be used to measure how fast a person is aging, rather than only their chronological age. The authors measured more than 450,000 CpG markers in whole blood from 656 people aged 19 to 101 and built a quantitative model of aging. The model gives each person a methylome aging rate, which the authors find is influenced by sex and genetic variants. Differences in aging rate help explain epigenetic drift and are mirrored in the transcriptome. The model also holds in other tissues and shows faster aging in tumors. It provides a quantitative readout for studying methylation in age-related disease.

title: Bayesian refinement of association signals for 14 loci in 3 common diseases
lab: the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium
synopsis: To narrow down causal variants at known GWAS loci, the authors genotyped 5,500 SNPs across 14 associated regions in 8,000 samples. The samples comprised controls and cases of type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease and Graves' disease. Using Bayesian posterior probabilities, they defined 95% credible sets of SNPs likely to contain the causal variant. At TCF7L2, CTLA4 and CDKN2A-CDKN2B (type 2 diabetes), most of the probability fell on a single SNP. Four other regions had small credible sets that excluded most SNPs. Very few credible-set SNPs had annotated functions, which shows how limited mechanistic understanding remains and how dense fine-mapping can guide functional follow-up.

title: Systematic Localization of Common Disease-Associated Variation in Regulatory DNA
synopsis: This study asks where common disease-associated variants from genome-wide association studies sit relative to regulatory DNA. The authors compared GWAS variants with DNase I hypersensitive sites mapped across many tissues and cell types. They analyzed the overlap by tissue, by disease, and by enrichment in physiologically relevant transcription factor binding sites and networks. Many noncoding disease associations fall within regulatory DNA, often in tissue- and developmental-stage-specific elements. The results suggest that many common risk variants act by changing gene regulation, and they provide a systematic way to link GWAS signals to relevant cell types and regulatory pathways in adult-onset disease.

title: An integrated encyclopedia of DNA elements in the human genome
synopsis: This paper asks what the roughly three billion bases of the human genome actually do, given that most lie outside protein-coding genes. The ENCODE project systematically mapped transcription, transcription factor binding, chromatin structure and histone modifications across the genome. These data assign a biochemical function to 80% of the genome, much of it outside coding regions. Many candidate regulatory elements are physically linked to each other and to expressed genes. The elements are also statistically associated with disease-linked sequence variants. The result is a large functional annotation resource that helps with interpreting non-coding variation and understanding gene regulation.

title: Snakemake—a scalable bioinformatics workflow engine
synopsis: This paper presents Snakemake, a workflow engine for building reproducible bioinformatics pipelines. Workflows are written in a readable, Python-based definition language. The same workflow runs on a single-core workstation or a compute cluster without changes. According to the authors, Snakemake is the first system to infer multiple named wildcards in input and output filenames automatically, which makes it simpler to write rules that generalize across many samples and files. The tool matters for labs that need pipelines that scale and are easy to maintain and share.

title: Alternative Cleavage and Polyadenylation during Colorectal Cancer Development
synopsis: This study asks whether alternative cleavage and polyadenylation (APA), which changes 3′UTR length and therefore post-transcriptional regulation, shifts as colorectal cancer progresses. The authors measured genome-wide APA by next-generation sequencing in 15 patient samples and validated the findings in a cohort of 50 patients that included matched normal/tumor pairs. Many genes showed progressive APA changes. Genes with shortened 3′UTRs were enriched for cell-cycle and nucleic acid processing functions, while genes with lengthened 3′UTRs were enriched for adhesion and extracellular matrix functions. Increased expression of cleavage and polyadenylation factors may drive these changes. Quantitative PCR confirmed shifts in DMKN, PDXK and PPIE, which suggests APA as a source of cancer biomarkers.

title: Optimal Unified Approach for Rare-Variant Association Testing with Application to Small-Sample Case-Control Whole-Exome Sequencing Studies
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics

title: E2F mediates enhanced alternative polyadenylation in proliferation
synopsis: This study asks what mechanisms drive the global 3′UTR shortening through alternative polyadenylation that has been linked to proliferation and cancer. The authors applied deep sequencing of poly(A) sites to two human cell models, each profiled in proliferating, arrested and transformed states. Proliferation was linked to global 3′UTR shortening much more strongly than transformation was. It also increased cleavage at intronic poly(A) sites. Genes encoding 3′-end processing proteins were more highly expressed during proliferation, and E2F transcription factors contributed to this upregulation. The work identifies E2F-mediated co-transcriptional regulation as one mechanism that connects cell proliferation to enhanced alternative polyadenylation.

title: Topological domains in mammalian genomes identified by analysis of chromatin interactions
synopsis: This study asks how mammalian chromosomes are organized in three dimensions at a scale relevant to genome function. The authors used high-resolution Hi-C on human and mouse embryonic stem cells and on differentiated cell types. They found pervasive megabase-sized local interaction domains, which they call topological domains, and these coincide with regions that limit the spread of heterochromatin. The domains are stable across cell types and conserved between species. Domain boundaries are enriched for CTCF binding, housekeeping genes, tRNAs and SINE elements. The work establishes topological domains as a basic unit of genome architecture and points to factors that may form their boundaries.

title: The Poly(A)-Binding Protein Nuclear 1 Suppresses Alternative Cleavage and Polyadenylation Sites
synopsis: This study looks for factors that control alternative cleavage and polyadenylation (APA), which were largely unknown. A reporter-based RNAi screen identified the nuclear poly(A)-binding protein PABPN1 as a regulator. Genome-wide analysis showed that loss of PABPN1 causes extensive 3′UTR shortening through increased use of proximal cleavage sites. In Cyclin D1, this shift weakened microRNA-mediated repression. A triplet-repeat expanded form of PABPN1, which causes oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy, also broadly induced proximal site usage in a mouse model and in human cells. This effect was linked to sequestration of the normal protein in nuclear aggregates. The work establishes PABPN1 as a suppressor of APA with relevance to disease.

title: Systematic dissection and optimization of inducible enhancers in human cells using a massively parallel reporter assay
synopsis: This paper introduces a massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA) for systematically dissecting transcriptional regulatory elements. Microarray-synthesized regulatory sequences paired with unique tags are cloned into reporter plasmids and transfected into cells, and activity is read out by sequencing the tags. The authors tested more than 27,000 variants of two inducible enhancers, a synthetic cAMP-responsive enhancer and the interferon-β enhancer. The data produced single-nucleotide maps of functional binding sites and were used to train quantitative sequence-activity models. Combining models from two cellular states allowed the design of enhancers that maximize induced activity while keeping basal activity low. The approach supports both reading and engineering regulatory sequence.

title: High throughput gene expression analysis of the inner ear
synopsis: This review examines a decade of microarray-based gene expression studies of the mouse inner ear, a tissue made up of many different cell types. The studies it covers searched for deafness genes, developmental transcriptional networks and functional microRNAs. They also profiled responses to ototoxic drugs, hypergravity and caloric restriction, and the pathways downstream of deafness genes. The review assesses these data critically as the field moves toward RNA-seq. Because most of the datasets are deposited in GEO, the authors also show that integrating independent experiments is feasible and can produce new insights, which highlights the value of reusing public expression data in hearing research.

title: Selective inhibition of microRNA accessibility by RBM38 is required for p53 activity
synopsis: This study asks how RNA-binding proteins shape which microRNA targets are actually repressed, and how that ties into p53 signaling. A genetic screen for RNA-binding proteins that control whether microRNAs can reach their target mRNAs identified RBM38, which p53 switches on. RBM38 binds uridine-rich regions near microRNA target sites and blocks repression of some targets but not others. For example, it does little to stop miR-34a from repressing SIRT1. Without this activity, p53 does not work properly. In large human breast cancer cohorts, low RBM38 expression caused by promoter hypermethylation went along with wild-type p53. Together, the results point to a post-transcriptional layer of p53 regulation that its tumor-suppressor role depends on.

title: Cell Type–Specific Transcriptome Analysis Reveals a Major Role for Zeb1 and miR-200b in Mouse Inner Ear Morphogenesis
synopsis: Bulk expression profiles of complex organs mix many cell types, which makes it hard to infer regulatory networks from them. To get around this, the authors developed a protocol that sorts auditory and vestibular tissue from newborn mouse inner ears into its major cell types, and then profiled the transcriptome of each sorted population. The profiles formed cell type-specific expression clusters. Computational analysis then pointed to transcription factors and microRNAs that help set cell identity, in particular the Zeb1/miR-200b pathway, which separates epithelial from mesenchymal identity. This pathway was misregulated in Twirler mutant mice, which have malformed inner ears. The finding suggests a new mechanism behind deafness and balance disorders, and the approach can be applied to other mouse mutants.

title: Matrin 3 Binds and Stabilizes mRNA
synopsis: Matrin 3 is a conserved protein of the inner nuclear matrix with RNA-recognition motifs, and the ATM kinase phosphorylates it, but its function has been largely unknown. This study shows that it binds several RNA-processing proteins in an RNA-dependent way and holds on to RNA through its second RNA-recognition motif. Deep sequencing of the RNA it binds turned up several kinds of small noncoding RNA. Microarray analysis found 77 transcripts whose levels depended on Matrin 3, and nine of these were validated and also found bound to its complex. Experiments showed that Matrin 3 is needed to keep several of these mRNAs stable. The authors conclude that the tightly regulated level of Matrin 3 may control the stability of a group of transcripts.

title: Rare-Variant Association Testing for Sequencing Data with the Sequence Kernel Association Test
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: Classical single-marker tests have little power to detect rare variants associated with complex traits in sequencing studies. This paper introduces SKAT, a kernel regression method that tests all variants in a region, rare and common together, for association with a continuous or binary trait while adjusting for covariates. Because it is a score-based variance-component test, p-values are calculated analytically after fitting only the null model. As a result, a genome-wide study of 1000 individuals split into 30 kb regions runs in about 7 hours on a laptop. In simulations and in triglyceride data from the Dallas Heart Study, SKAT clearly outperformed several other rare-variant tests. The paper also gives analytic power and sample-size calculations for designing sequencing studies.

title: Integration of Transcriptomics, Proteomics, and MicroRNA Analyses Reveals Novel MicroRNA Regulation of Targets in the Mammalian Inner Ear
synopsis: This study aims to find which microRNA-target interactions actually matter in the inner ear, where a microRNA mutation is already known to cause deafness. The authors combined microRNA, transcriptome and proteome profiles of microdissected auditory and vestibular sensory epithelia and analyzed them with the FAME algorithm. They detected 157 microRNAs, of which 53 differed between cochlea and vestibule. Important microRNAs were identified by looking for targets enriched or depleted in the data in the direction expected from microRNA repression. Many targets showed up only in the protein data, which points to translational suppression. The authors validated that miR-135b regulates PSIP1-P75 in vestibular hair cells, suggesting that this microRNA helps create differences between cochlear and vestibular hair cells.

title: Complex and dynamic landscape of RNA polyadenylation revealed by PAS-Seq
synopsis: Alternative polyadenylation is an important way of regulating genes after transcription, but microarrays cannot measure it comprehensively or quantitatively. This paper introduces PAS-Seq, a deep-sequencing method that maps poly(A) junctions across the transcriptome and measures the relative abundance of polyadenylated RNAs. Applied to human and mouse samples, it found that 40-50% of expressed genes produce alternatively polyadenylated mRNAs. It also detected conserved polyadenylation of histone mRNAs and new features of mitochondrial RNA polyadenylation. Profiling of mouse embryonic stem cells, neural progenitors and neurons found more poly(A) sites than the whole mouse EST database. It also showed widespread 3' UTR lengthening as stem cells differentiate, which shows that polyadenylation is dynamically regulated during development.

title: Network medicine: a network-based approach to human disease
synopsis: This review argues that disease rarely comes from a defect in a single gene. Instead, it reflects disruption of the network of molecular interactions inside and between cells, tissues and organs. The authors describe network medicine tools for systematically mapping the molecular complexity of a disease, which can reveal disease modules and pathways as well as molecular links between diseases that look unrelated. They argue that this framework is needed to find new disease genes and to interpret disease-associated variants from genome-wide association and whole-genome sequencing studies. It should also help identify drug targets and biomarkers for complex diseases, which makes network approaches central to understanding human disease.

title: SPIKE: a database of highly curated human signaling pathways
synopsis: As knowledge of signaling pathways grows quickly, researchers need repositories that store and organize it in a usable way. SPIKE is a database of carefully curated interactions for selected human signaling pathways, and each interaction comes with literature-referenced details about its nature. It uses a simple data model and shows pathways as maps that reflect each curator's understanding. Current coverage is mainly the DNA damage response, cell cycle, programmed cell death and hearing-related pathways, and pathways are updated and added over time. The whole database and individual maps can be exported freely in several formats, and a stand-alone tool supports analysis and dynamic visualization of pathways.

title: A Pumilio-induced RNA structure switch in p27-3′ UTR controls miR-221 and miR-222 accessibility
synopsis: This study asks why the tumour suppressor p27 stays highly expressed in quiescent cells even though its inhibitors, miR-221 and miR-222, are abundant. The work shows that in quiescent cells these microRNAs are largely inactive on the p27 3' UTR because their target sites are hidden. When growth factors stimulate the cells, the RNA-binding protein Pumilio-1 is upregulated and phosphorylated. It then binds the p27 3' UTR and changes the local RNA structure, which exposes the target sites. This lets the microRNAs repress p27 and the cells enter the cell cycle quickly. The finding describes a new mechanism in which an RNA-binding protein switches microRNA regulation on by reshaping RNA structure.

title: Major role for mRNA stability in shaping the kinetics of gene induction
synopsis: This study asks how much mRNA stability, rather than transcription alone, shapes the timing of gene expression responses. Researchers usually explain waves of gene induction by transcription factors switching on one after another. Analyzing many expression datasets, the study found a strong genome-wide anti-correlation between how quickly a gene is induced and how stable its mRNA is, as a kinetic mathematical model predicts. For suppressed genes the relationship was weaker. Many normally stable mRNAs dropped faster after stimulation than even a complete transcriptional shutdown could explain, which points to active regulation of RNA decay. The results show that mRNA stability is a key factor in the kinetics of mammalian transcriptional networks.

title: Expander: from expression microarrays to networks and functions
synopsis: This protocol describes Expander, an integrated software platform for analyzing gene expression microarray data that is free for academic use. The aim is to turn large volumes of raw expression data into biological insight. The workflow imports the data and then normalizes and filters it. Next it performs clustering and network-based analyses. The resulting gene groups are tested for enrichment in Gene Ontology functions, for co-regulation using transcription factor and microRNA target predictions, and for co-location in the genome. Each step offers several visualizations, and the full protocol takes about one hour. The tool gives researchers a single environment that covers the whole path from raw data to regulatory networks.

title: Associating Genes and Protein Complexes with Disease via Network Propagation
synopsis: This study addresses how to identify disease-causing genes using networks of protein-protein or functional interactions. Genes linked to similar diseases tend to cluster together in such networks, but most existing methods use only local network information and predict single genes. The proposed method, PRINCE, is a global network propagation approach. It constrains the prioritization to be smooth over the network and to use prior knowledge, and it can also predict associations with protein complexes. In cross-validation on 1,369 OMIM diseases, it ranked the true causal gene first for 34% of diseases and outperformed existing approaches. It also identified 139 coherent disease-related complexes. Predictions for prostate cancer, Alzheimer's disease and type 2 diabetes matched the literature and suggested new candidate genes.

title: Comprehensive Mapping of Long-Range Interactions Reveals Folding Principles of the Human Genome
synopsis: This study asks how the human genome is folded in the nucleus, since contacts between nearby and distant loci can affect gene expression. The authors developed a method that captures all interactions between genomic loci in the nucleus and reads them out by deep sequencing. They used it to map the spatial proximity of loci across the human genome at one-megabase resolution. The map shows that the genome divides into two spatial compartments that track local chromatin state. When the chromatin state changes, the compartments are remodeled accordingly. The work provides a genome-wide view of three-dimensional chromatin organization and a general tool for studying it.

title: Widespread Shortening of 3′UTRs by Alternative Cleavage and Polyadenylation Activates Oncogenes in Cancer Cells
synopsis: This study asks why oncogene proteins are sometimes overexpressed in cancer cells even when the genes themselves are not altered. Compared with non-transformed cell lines that proliferate at similar rates, cancer cell lines often expressed mRNA isoforms with shorter 3' UTRs, mostly through alternative cleavage and polyadenylation. The shorter isoforms were more stable and typically produced ten-fold more protein, partly because they escaped microRNA repression. Expressing the short isoform of the proto-oncogene IGF2BP1/IMP-1 caused much more oncogenic transformation than expressing the full-length mRNA. The results suggest that alternative polyadenylation is a widespread way for cancer cells to activate oncogenes without genetic mutation.

title: Potential etiologic and functional implications of genome-wide association loci for human diseases and traits
synopsis: This study introduces an online catalog of SNP-trait associations from published genome-wide association studies and uses it to examine where associated variants fall in the genome. The reported variants were common (median risk allele frequency 36%) and had modest effects (median odds ratio 1.33). Compared with random array SNPs, they were enriched only at nonsynonymous sites (OR 3.9) and in 5 kb promoter regions (OR 2.3). Although 88% lay in introns or intergenic regions, they were not enriched in introns and were depleted in intergenic regions (OR 0.44). There was little evidence of enrichment in regions under positive selection. The catalog is meant to guide functional follow-up of common variants in complex disease.

title: WGCNA: an R package for weighted correlation network analysis
synopsis: This paper presents WGCNA, an R package for weighted correlation network analysis. The method is commonly used to describe correlation patterns among genes across expression samples. Different parts of the method had been published separately, and the package brings them together in one consistent, user-friendly implementation with tutorials. Its functions cover network construction, detection of modules of highly correlated genes, and summarizing modules by eigengenes or hub genes. They also relate modules to each other and to external traits, compute module membership and topological properties, and support simulation, visualization and links to other software. The approach has been used in cancer, mouse and yeast genetics, and brain imaging. Although it was built for gene expression data, it applies to other kinds of data and helps screen candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

title: Proliferating Cells Express mRNAs with Shortened 3' Untranslated Regions and Fewer MicroRNA Target Sites
synopsis: This study asks whether the length of messenger RNA 3' untranslated regions changes systematically with cell state. After activating primary mouse CD4+ T cells, the authors saw a conserved shift toward mRNAs that end at upstream polyadenylation sites, which gives shorter 3'UTRs. The same pattern tracked with proliferation across many cell types and tissues. Expressing full-length 3'UTRs lowered protein output, and in some cases deleting predicted microRNA target sites in the variable region reversed this. The work points to a coordinated program in which proliferating cells shed much of the 3'UTR-based regulation of their transcripts, including microRNA control.

title: SPIKE – a database, visualization and analysis tool of cellular signaling pathways
synopsis: SPIKE is a knowledge base built to help researchers gather, visualize and interpret the fast-growing data on cellular signaling pathways. It has three parts. The first is a database that keeps carefully curated literature information in a tier separate from large public data sources. The second is an interactive visualization package that can overlay genomic and proteomic data on pathway maps. The third is an inference engine that searches the networks for new functional interactions. Registered users can upload their own data, so the database is meant to grow as a community effort, with each group contributing pathways from its own field of expertise.

title: PLINK: A Tool Set for Whole-Genome Association and Population-Based Linkage Analyses
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
synopsis: Whole-genome association studies produce datasets too large for many existing genetic analysis tools. PLINK is an open-source C/C++ tool set that can quickly manipulate and analyze hundreds of thousands of markers genotyped in thousands of individuals. It covers five areas: data management, summary statistics, population stratification, association analysis, and identity-by-descent estimation. The paper focuses on estimating identity-by-state and identity-by-descent between individuals. These estimates can detect and correct for population stratification and can find long chromosomal segments shared by distant relatives. Patterns of shared segments may support population-based linkage mapping of disease loci that carry multiple rare variants.

title: Genome-Wide Mapping of in Vivo Protein-DNA Interactions
synopsis: This work maps where transcription factors bind DNA in living cells across a whole mammalian genome. The authors developed ChIP-Seq, which pairs chromatin immunoprecipitation with ultrahigh-throughput sequencing, and used it to locate binding of the repressor NRSF/REST at 1946 sites in the human genome. Binding positions were resolved to within about 50 base pairs, which helped with motif discovery and revealed noncanonical NRSF motifs. The data had high sensitivity and specificity (ROC area at least 0.96) and strong statistical confidence. They also suggested new candidate targets, including key transcription factors in pancreatic islet development, and the method set the pattern for genome-wide binding studies that followed.

title: Newborn Hearing Screening — A Silent Revolution
EXPANDER – an integrative program suite for microarray data analysis
synopsis: Gene expression microarray experiments produce large datasets, and biologists need integrated, easy-to-use tools to turn them into biological insight. EXPANDER 2.0 is a 'one-stop shop' software package covering the whole microarray analysis workflow. It runs normalization and filtering, clustering and biclustering, functional enrichment analysis to find active biological processes, and promoter analysis to identify transcription factors likely behind the observed response. The package ships with precompiled Gene Ontology annotations and promoter sequence data for yeast, worm, fly, rat, mouse and human. This lets researchers move from raw expression data to regulatory hypotheses within a single tool, and it is freely available to academic users.

title: Transcription profiling of inner ears from Pou4f3ddl/ddl identifies Gfi1 as a target of the Pou4f3 deafness gene
synopsis: Pou4f3 is a transcription factor needed for inner ear hair cell development, and a mutation in it causes the human progressive hearing loss DFNA15. To find its downstream targets, the authors compared microarray expression profiles of embryonic inner ears from wild-type mice and deaf Pou4f3 mutants. Gfi1 stood out as a candidate target. RT-PCR and in situ hybridization confirmed that Gfi1 expression drops significantly without Pou4f3 and follows the same expression pattern as Pou4f3. Gfi1 mutant mice showed outer hair cell degeneration similar to that in Pou4f3 mutants. Gfi1 is thus the first known downstream target of a hair cell-specific transcription factor and may account for much of the hair cell loss in Pou4f3-related deafness.

title: Prediction of Mammalian MicroRNA Targets
synopsis: When this study was done, the genes regulated by vertebrate microRNAs were essentially unknown. The authors predicted targets by finding mRNAs with conserved pairing to the 5' region of each miRNA and scoring the number and quality of matching sites. This identified more than 400 candidate targets of conserved vertebrate miRNAs. Shuffled-miRNA controls put the false-positive rate at 31% for targets conserved across human, mouse and rat, and 22% when pufferfish was also required. Eleven of 15 tested predictions were supported in a HeLa reporter assay. The predicted targets were enriched for transcriptional regulators but spanned a broad range of functions, which pointed to widespread post-transcriptional regulation by miRNAs.

title: STRING: a web-server to retrieve and display the repeatedly occurring neighbourhood of a gene
synopsis: Genes that repeatedly sit near each other across different genomes often encode functionally related proteins. STRING (search tool for recurring instances of neighbouring genes) is a web server that finds the genes a query gene repeatedly clusters with across genomes. It searches iteratively and displays the results in their genomic context, which yields a set of candidate functional partners for the query. The authors illustrate its use by suggesting a functional context for an RNA methylase whose specificity was unknown. The tool offers a way to infer protein function from genome organization when there is no direct experimental evidence.

title: Connexin 26 mutations in hereditary non-syndromic sensorineural deafness
synopsis: This study asks which genes underlie non-syndromic sensorineural deafness, the most common inherited sensory disorder, which affects about 1 in 1,000 children. The authors studied a family with autosomal dominant deafness and found a mutation in the gap-junction protein connexin 26 (Cx26) that segregates with profound deafness. They also found Cx26 mutations that create premature stop codons in three autosomal recessive families linked to the DFNB1 locus on chromosome 13q11-12. Immunostaining showed high Cx26 expression in human cochlear cells. This was the first susceptibility gene identified for non-syndromic autosomal sensorineural deafness, and it points to Cx26 as a key component of the cochlea.
